Hamiltonian Lattice Gauge Theories:
emergent properties from tensor network methods

Giovanni Cataldi

See main-frn.pdf

Abstract

This thesis develops advanced Tensor Network (TN) methods to address Hamiltonian Lattice Gauge Theories (LGTs), overcoming limitations in real-time dynamics and finite-density regimes. A novel dressed-site formalism is introduced, enabling efficient truncation of gauge fields while preserving gauge invariance for both Abelian and non-Abelian theories. This formalism is successfully applied to SU(2) Yang-Mills LGTs in two dimensions, providing the first TN simulations of this system and revealing critical aspects of its phase diagram and non-equilibrium behavior, such as a Quantum Many-Body (QMB) scarring dynamics. A generalization of the dressed-site formalism is proposed through a new fermion-to-qubit mapping for general lattice fermion theories, revealing powerful for classical and quantum simulations. Numerical innovations, including the use of optimal space-filling curves such as the Hilbert curve to preserve locality in high-dimensional simulations, further enhance the efficiency of these methods. Together with high-performance computing techniques, these advances open current and future development pathways toward optimized, efficient, and faster simulations on scales comparable to Monte Carlo state-of-the-art.

Introduction

Quantum field theory (QFT) is a foundational framework in particle physics, offering a comprehensive description of how particles interact. It integrates the principles of quantum mechanics with special relativity to provide insights into the behavior of particles under different forces. Gauge invariance is a fundamental principle in QFT, representing a special symmetry where the equations describing a physical system remain unchanged under local transformations of the fields. Then, a gauge theory is a framework that imposes these local symmetries as constraints, ensuring that certain transformations can occur independently at each point in space and time without altering the observable outcomes. The Standard Model (SM) of particle physics [442] represents the current state-of-the-art in our understanding of gauge theories, as it successfully unifies the electromagnetic, weak, and strong interactions under a common theoretical framework, incorporating both Abelian and non-Abelian gauge symmetries. It has proven remarkably successful in explaining a wide range of experimental results and predicting new phenomena.

However, non-Abelian gauge theories, particularly QCD, pose significant challenges, especially in the low-energy, non-perturbative regime. At high energies, where the gauge coupling constant is small, perturbation theory is an effective tool for making predictions, such as those concerning high-energy collisions in particle accelerators. However, at lower energies, typical of the hadronic scale (below 1 GeV), the gauge coupling constant becomes large, making perturbative methods inadequate. To overcome these limitations, lattice gauge theories (LGTs) provide a non-perturbative framework for studying QCD and other gauge theories [443, 444, 445], allowing numerical simulations to be performed. LGTs discretize spacetime into a lattice grid where matter and gauge fields occupy lattice sites and links respectively. One of the most successful applications of LGTs is lattice QCD [446, 447, 448], which has been instrumental in computing the hadronic spectrum, such as the masses of protons and neutrons, and understanding phenomena like confinement [449, 450, 451, 452, 453, 454], chiral symmetry breaking [455, 456, 457, 458], and the role of topology in QCD at finite temperatures [459, 460, 461, 450]. In these terms, Monte Carlo (MC) simulations of LGTs play a critical role by providing statistically meaningful results for observables that are otherwise inaccessible through analytical methods [462, 459, 463, 464, 465, 466, 467, 468, 469, 470, 471, 472]. Despite these successes, MC simulations face challenges, particularly the sign problem, which hampers the simulation of a wide class of physical settings described by complex or negative actions (finite charge-density phases, fermions, real-time dynamics), whose numerical investigations remain – to date – an open problem [473, 474].

According to Feynman, all these challenges could have been solved by attacking quantum systems with a quantum computer, where traditional classical numerical methods could be circumvented, particularly in handling quantum correlations (i.e. entanglement). After his seminal proposal and the recent fast development of quantum hardware, there is growing interest in experimental platforms for simulating LGTs, such as ultra-cold atoms, optical lattices, and superconducting circuits. Recently, quantum-inspired strategies have been applied to LGTs, attempting to reproduce their quantum dynamics [475, 476, 477, 478, 479, 480].

While awaiting noiseless and scalable quantum hardware, in the current Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) era, MC problems have inspired the development of novel classical numerical algorithms based on Tensor Networks (TN) [481, 482, 483, 484]. These techniques exploit the area-law entanglement bounds satisfied by a large class of quantum many-body (QMB) systems [485] and allow for an efficient representation of the low-energy sector by retaining in memory only the relevant states that contribute to equilibrium and non-equilibrium properties. This is achieved by compressing the exponentially large wavefunctions into a network of tensors interconnected through auxiliary indices with bond dimension χ\chi. The main TN anzätze for representing QMB states are Matrix Product States (MPS) for 1D systems [486, 487, 488, 489, 490], Projected Entangled Pair States (PEPS) [491, 492, 481, 493, 494, 495, 496, 497, 498, 499, 500, 501, 502, 503], Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) [504, 505, 506, 484, 507] and Multiscale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz (MERA) [507, 508, 509], which can be defined in any dimension.

Recent advances in TN methods offered promising alternatives for studying LGTs without MC limitations like the sign problem. Indeed, TNs are particularly valuable for attacking non-perturbative LGT phenomena in the Hamiltonian formulation, accessing real-time dynamics and finite-density phases. Exploiting TN algorithms, noteworthy results have been produced for Abelian LGTs in one [510, 511, 512, 513, 514, 515, 516, 517, 518, 519, 520, 521, 522, 523] and higher spatial dimensions [524, 525, 526]. As for non-Abelian LGTs, TN-based simulations were so far limited to one spatial dimension [527, 528, 529], but recently, they have been successfully applied to two dimensional systems [437].

Despite all these achievements, one main challenge for numerical and quantum simulations of LGTs remains the finite-dimensional encoding of the continuous gauge fields, especially beyond one spatial dimension, where decoupling the gauge field’s longitudinal component is required [530]. Among known truncation recipes are Quantum Link Models (QLM) [531, 532, 533, 534, 535], an approach already considered for practical quantum simulation of LGTs [536, 537, 538, 539, 540, 541, 542, 543, 544, 545, 546], finite subgroups [517, 521, 547], digitization of gauge fields [548], and fusion-algebra deformation [549]. Whatever the adopted solution, further effort is required to satisfy gauge symmetry at each local site, which involves the concurrent evaluation of all the gauge links and the attached matter site [550, 551, 528]. As it represents the highest energy-scale of the model, any violation of this constraint would prevent the correctness of simulations.

Another important issue to be faced in simulating LGTs is to account for the Fermi statistics of matter fields. In several TN methods as well on well-established conventional digital quantum simulation platforms (e.g. superconducting qubits, trapped-ions, Rydberg arrays, quantum dots) [552, 553, 554, 555, 556], which are built on distinguishable, spatially localized qubits (or qudits), fermionic algebra (mutually-anticommuting operations) must be econded into a genuinely local algebra (mutually-commuting operations) of qudits. Standard fermion-to-qubit encodings, such as the Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation [557], and other modern approaches [558, 559, 560] make any fermionic Hamiltonian interaction inherently long-range and expensive from a computational perspective. Together with the truncation of the gauge fields and the Gauss’s law constraint, these challenges necessitate further advancements in numerical and quantum simulation strategies to accurately capture the ground-state and dynamical properties of LGTs.

In this thesis, we address these challenges: we discuss a theoretical and numerical formalism that provides a controllable gauge field truncation (in Casimir spectrum) and directly accesses the Hilbert subspace of gauge invariant states where gauge and matter fields are combined in a dressed-site encoded with a bosonic statistics. Such a formalism is detailed and quantitatively discussed in [437, 440] for both Abelian and non-Abelian LGT, yet successfully generalizes to lattice fermion theories without gauge invariance occurring in condensed matter [439]. We exploit this approach to perform numerical simulations of the SU(2) Yang-Mills LGT in and out of equilibrium, exploring compelling regimes in the phase diagram [437] and exotic behaviors like QMB scarring dynamics [438]. In parallel, we review the state-of-the-art TN methods for Hamiltonian LGTs, providing and testing optimal encodings for high-dimensional Hamiltonians [436] and figuring strategies for parallelized high-performance large-scale simulations of LGTs [440].

All the achievements conveyed in this work [437, 440, 439, 438, 436] not only advance the theoretical and numerical understanding of LGT by means of TN methods, but also provide valuable benchmarks for experimental quantum simulations [561, 562, 563, 564, 565, 566, 567, 568, 569, 570, 571, 572, 573, 574], contributing to systematically identify the quantum advantage threshold [575, 576] towards a deeper understanding of the fundamental interactions governing particle and condensed matter physics.

The thesis is structured as follows: in Chapter 1, we provide a detailed overview of all the fundamental ingredients of an LGT. Starting from the basics of QFT, we discuss the main effects arising from the lattice discretization of the theory, with a special focus on fermion fields and energy cutoffs. The whole discussion is based on the Hamiltonian formalism, as it will be lately exploited for all the presented numerical results. The innovative part of this chapter starts from the dressed-site formalism discussed in Section 1.2, a theoretical scheme that reveals extremely useful for simulating LGTs via TN and quantum hardware. Such an approach is detailed and quantitatively applied first to the challenging non-Abelian SU(2) Yang-Mills theory (Section 1.3) and secondly to the Abelian U(1) case (Section 1.4). In both scenarios, we derive a pedagogical strategy to simulate the LGT in any spatial dimensions, with a controllable and scalable truncation of the gauge fields, where Gauss law is automatically satisfied. The resulting theories are made out of bosonic degrees of freedom, preventing simulations from the challenging sign problem that characterizes MC methods.

In Chapter 2, we discuss the state-of-the-art numerical methods for attacking QMB Hamiltonians and, more in detail, the previously discussed LGTs. We start reviewing Exact Diagonalization (ED) methods and the numerical strategies to exploit the global symmetries such as particle-number or momentum conservation via block diagonalization. These features are currently implemented in the ED-LGT Python library [441], developed throughout these three years for simulating and benchmarking QMB systems and dressed-site formulated LGTs such as the ones presented in Chapter 1. We then switch to reviewing TN methods, from the fundamental tensor operations to advanced algorithms for ground-state search and time evolution of QMB systems tailored for MPS and TTN ansätze.

A noteworthy section compares different ways of mapping high-dimensional Hamiltonians onto TN structures, demonstrating the Hilbert curve [436] as the optimal ordering for preserving distances and quantum correlations when simulating large scale high-dimensional QMB systems. We conclude the chapter by discussing the status of TN methods dedicated to LGTs, providing current and future lines of development towards optimized, efficient, and faster simulations on scales comparable to MC state-of-the-art. All these strategies are conveyed in a recent roadmap [440] and stimulate benchmarking tests for quantum simulations of LGTs.

After discussing all theoretical and numerical tools that are necessary for simulating LGTs, we devote the second part of the thesis to the presentation of the most compelling results achieved and conveyed in the following recent scientific works: [437, 439, 438]. In Chapter 3, we present the first TN simulations of a SU(2) Yang-Mills LGT with flavorless fermionic dynamical matter in two spatial dimensions [437]. The simulations rely on the hardcore-gluon approximation, the smallest nontrivial electric-truncation of the SU(2) gauge fields discussed in Section 1.3.5. However, they provide a clear phase diagram of the model both at zero and finite baryon density, exploring challenging regimes of the couplings and addressing the continuum limit location.

In Chapter 4, we discuss the non-equilibrium properties of LGTs, with compelling regard to the non-ergodic behaviors observed in non-Abelian LGTs. After a pedagogical introduction to classical and quantum ergodicity, we expose the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) for isolated QMB systems concerning their spectral and dynamical properties. We review the first experimental and numerical observations of QMB systems with scarring dynamics, an exotic behavior that weakly violates ETH. We highlight the strong connection between the main features of QMB scars and the fundamental mechanism appearing in Abelian LGTs. Remarkably, we extend such a relation to non-Abelian LGTs by simulating a one-dimensional truncated SU(2) Yang-Mills LGT and observing all the spectral and dynamical properties of a scarring dynamics [438]. These phenomena are further explained through meson-baryon creation processes that are intrinsically due to the non-Abelian nature of the model.

Finally, Chapter 5 focuses on the recent work [438], where we discuss an extension of the dressed-site formalism for generic lattice fermion theories without gauge invariance. In detail, we propose an efficient fermion-to-qubit mapping that is suitable for classical and (digital) quantum simulations. We test its applicability on the spin-(1/21/2) Fermi-Hubbard model in two spatial dimensions investigating both equilibrium and non-equilibrium properties via TN methods. We demonstrate the perfect equivalence with the original model and recover interesting features of the expected physics. The presented encoding is then compared in detail with other theoretical strategies to remove Fermi statistics, revealing efficient, scalable, and competitive.

Chapter 1 Hamiltonian Lattice Gauge Theories

As anticipated, gauge theories form the backbone of our understanding of fundamental interactions in particle physics. Central to gauge theories is the principle of gauge invariance, where physical laws remain unchanged under local transformations of certain fields. Different realizations of gauge theories correspond to different symmetry groups and interaction structures. In Quantum Electrodynamics (QED), the U(1) symmetry group governing electromagnetic interactions, with the photon as the associated gauge boson. Non-Abelian gauge theories, such as those based on SU(2) and SU(3) symmetry groups, describe the weak and strong interactions, respectively. These groups allow for more complex transformations, where the gauge bosons themselves interact with one another. For instance, in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD), the SU(3) gauge theory of the strong force, gluons are the gauge bosons that mediate interactions between quarks and also interact among themselves due to the non-Abelian nature of the theory.

Lattice Gauge Theories (LGTs) [443, 444, 445] offer a non-perturbative framework for studying these models, particularly in regimes where perturbative methods fail, such as in low-energy QCD [446, 447, 448]. By discretizing spacetime into a lattice, LGTs enable numerical simulations of gauge theories, allowing us to explore compelling phenomena such as confinement [449, 450, 451, 452, 453, 454], chiral symmetry breaking [455, 456, 457, 458], the hadronic spectrum, and the dynamics of quarks and gluons [577].

In traditional Monte Carlo (MC) approach to LGTs [462, 459, 463, 464, 465, 466, 467, 468, 469, 470, 471, 472], the action of a continuum gauge theory is regularized by working on a finite and discrete Euclidean spacetime, where both space and (imaginary) time are discretized [464]. Instead, Tensor Networks (TN) and quantum simulations typically rely on the Hamiltonian formalism, where time remains a real continuous variable, while space is discretized on a DD-dimensional lattice. The Hamiltonian discretization of gauge theories explicitly breaks Lorentz invariance, which is however restored in the continuum limit. Simultaneously, Hamiltonian LGTs present features that distinguish them from other QMB systems commonly simulated via TN or quantum hardware [443]. Next, we discuss these properties in more detail and outline the main steps that have to be taken to exploit TN algorithms. Without any loss of generality, we focus on matter-coupled LGTs of the Yang-Mills type, routinely employed in high-energy physics to describe nature’s fundamental interactions.

We start from a pedagogical review of lattice discretization in Section 1.1, with special regard for fermion fields within the staggered fermion solution in Section 1.1.3 and gauge fields in Section 1.1.4. The original contribution of this chapter starts from Section 1.2, where we present the dressed-site formalism, a theoretical scheme that is suitable for attacking LGTs via TNs and quantum hardware directly within the gauge-invariant sector, where all the logical degrees of freedom undergo a bosonic statistics. In Sections 1.3 and 1.4, we respectively detail two specific realizations of this formalism, SU(2) for the non-Abelian and U(1) for the Abelian scenario. Such an approach has been successfully applied to obtain all the numerical results detailed in Chapters 3 and 4 (see also [437, 438, 440, 578]) and is generalized to pure fermion theories (without gauge fields, i.e. no LGTs) in [439] and Chapter 5.

1.1 Lattice discretization

Let us consider continuous (D+1) spacetime domain (ℝD×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{D}\times\mathbb{R}) identified by the (D+1)-dimensional point r=(t,𝐫)r=(t,\mathbf{r}), where 𝐫=(r1,…​rD)\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\dots r_{D}). When performing spatial discretization, the time variable tt remains continuous, while the spatial domain ℝD\mathbb{R}^{D} is replaced by a hyper-cubic D-dimensional lattice Λ\Lambda, whose sites are equally spaced by lattice constant a0a_{0} (see Fig. 1.1). Lattice sites are then labelled by coordinates 𝐧=(n1,…,nD)\mathbf{n}=(n_{1},\dots,n_{D}), where rk=a0​nkr_{k}=a_{0}n_{k} and nk∈{1​…​Nk}n_{k}\in\quantity{1\dots N_{k}}, with NkN_{k} denoting the number of lattice sites along the kthk^{\text{th}} direction ∀k=1,…,D\forall k=1,\dots,D. Then, if N=∏k=1DNkN=\prod_{k=1}^{D}N_{k} is the total number of lattice sites, with the corresponding lattice volume given by V=a0D​NV=a_{0}^{D}N. Additionally, we define the unit lattice vectors ±𝝁k\pm{\bf\it\mu}_{k} pointing along the ±kth\pm k^{\text{th}} direction, assuming ±𝝁k=𝝁±k\pm{\bf\it\mu}_{k}={\bf\it\mu}_{\pm k}. We use the convention where summations over lattice vectors include only positive directions. Then, the lattice link connecting two neighboring sites 𝐧\mathbf{n} and 𝐧+𝝁k{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}}_{k} along the direction +𝝁k+{\bf\it\mu}_{k}, is denoted by the couple (𝐧,𝝁k)({\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}_{k}) or equivalently with (𝐧+𝝁k,−𝝁k)(\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{k},-{\bf\it\mu}_{k}). For future purposes, we refer to an even (odd) site, if (−1)𝐧=(−1)∑knk(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}=(-1)^{\sum_{k}n_{k}} is even (odd).

∫ℝDd​rD​|f⁡(𝐫)|2=L<∞,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{D}}dr^{D}\absolutevalue{f(\vecpos)}^{2}=L<\infty\,, (1.1.1)

1.1.2 Continuum limit and Lorentz invariance

The main physical consequence of the ultraviolet cutoff is the following: the discretized theory does not describe physics at scales (momenta) smaller (larger) than the lattice spacing a0a_{0} (π/a0\pi/a_{0}), i.e., all the short-distance (high-energy) phenomena [443].

Another effect of lattice discretization is the loss of the Lorentz invariance (the symmetry of special relativity), as the lattice spacing a0a_{0} introduces a preferred reference frame. In the Lagrangian formalism, where both space and time are discretized, the spacetime lattice does not support continuous Lorentz transformations, but the theory retains a discrete version of spacetime symmetry, such as discrete rotations or translations. On the contrary, the spatial discretization performed in Hamiltonian LGTs breaks the symmetry between space and time, which is a crucial part of Lorentz invariance. In these terms, the Hamiltonian formalism is said to explicitly break Lorentz invariance.

Restoring the continuum theory and the Lorentz invariance requires to take the continuum limit, where a0→0a_{0}\to 0, N→∞N\to\infty, while keeping a0⋅Na_{0}\cdot N fixed [579]. In this regime, maximum momentum 𝐩max\mathbf{p}_{\max} and energy EmaxE_{\max} become infinite and the lattice approximates the continuous space. The continuum limit is typically associated with the process of renormalization, where the theory is adjusted to correctly reproduce physical observables (which should be insensitive to the discretization) as the lattice spacing goes to zero. Unfortunately, the continuum limit location is non trivial and requires a lot of attention in understanding the relation between the lattice spacing and the Hamiltonian parameters. A comprehensive dissertation about the continuum limit would require a dedicated effort out of the purposes of the thesis. Nonetheless, we will partially discuss it in Sections 1.1.3 and 1.1.4 by using simple dimensional analysis. For a deeper discussion, see [444, 449, 459, 579, 580, 581, 582].

1.1.3 Discretization of fermions fields

Discretization of more complex objects such as fermion fields, i.e. spinors, requires more attention and encounters a set of problems whose solutions are not univocal nor perfect. Throughout this section, we will cover these challenges by focusing on one of the possible solutions: staggered fermions. For a more general and complete discussion about fermion discretization, see [583, 449, 579].

Let us start from the continuum Dirac equation for a massive free fermion. Assuming the spacetime coordinate r=(t,𝐫)r=(t,\mathbf{r}) and the metric ημ​ν=diag⁡(+1,−1,−1,−1)\eta^{\mu\nu}=\rm{diag}(+1,-1,-1,-1), we have:

(iℏγμ∂μ−m0c)ψ(r)=(iℏcγ0∂t−iℏγk∂k−m0c)ψ(r)=0,(i\hbar\gamma^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}-m_{0}c)\psi(r)=\quantity(i\frac{\hbar}{\lspeed}\gamma^{0}\partial_{t}-i\hbar\gamma^{k}\partial_{k}-\mass[0]\lspeed)\psi(r)=0\,, (1.1.7)

where cc is the speed of light, ℏ\hbar is the Planck constant, m0m_{0} is the mass parameter, and γμ\gamma^{\mu} are the 4×44\times 4 Dirac matrices satisfying Clifford’s algebra

{γμ,γν}=2​ημ​ν.\quantity{\gamma^{\mu},\gamma^{\nu}}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}\,. (1.1.8)

The field ψ⁡(r)\psi(r) is a 4-dimensional spinor, whose Hermitian conjugate is ψ¯​(r)=ψ†​(r)​γ0\overline{\psi}(r)=\psi^{\dagger}(r)\gamma^{0}. The corresponding quantized version satisfies the canonical equal-time commutation relations

{ψ^α​(t,𝐫),ψ^β†​(t,𝐫′)}=i​ℏ​δα​β​δ3​(𝐫−𝐫′),\quantity{\hpsi_{\alpha}(t,\vecpos),\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\beta}(t, \vecpos')}=i\hbar\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta^{3}(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\,, (1.1.9)

where the α\alpha and β\beta indices label spinor components. In the Hamiltonian form, Eq. 1.1.7 reads:

−iℏ∂tψ^(t,𝐫)=(icℏγ0γk∂k+m0c2γ0)ψ^(t,𝐫).-i\hbar\partial_{t}\hat{\psi}(t,\mathbf{r})=\quantity(i\lspeed\hbar\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}\partial_{k}+\mass[0]\lspeed^{2}\gamma^{0})\hat{\psi}(t,\mathbf{r})\,. (1.1.10)

Omitting the time dependence, the Dirac Hamiltonian in this form becomes

H^Dirac=∫d​𝐫​H^​(𝐫)=∫d​𝐫​[ψ^†(𝐫)(icℏγ0γk∂k+m0c2γ0)ψ^(𝐫)],\hat{H}_{\rm{Dirac}}=\int d\mathbf{r}\hat{H}(\mathbf{r})=\int d\mathbf{r}\quantity[\hpsi^{\dagger}(\vecpos)(i\lspeed\hbar\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}\partial_{k}+\mass[0]\lspeed^{2}\gamma^{0})\hpsi(\vecpos)]\,, (1.1.11)

When discretizing the space on a D-dimensional spatial lattice Λ\Lambda, we replace ψ^​(t,𝐫)→ψ^𝐧​(t)\hat{\psi}(t,\mathbf{r})\to\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}(t), where 𝐫=a0​𝐧\mathbf{r}=a_{0}\mathbf{n}. Correspondingly, the canonical equal-time commutation relations become:

{ψ^𝐧,α​(t),ψ^𝐧′,β†​(t)}=i​ℏ​δα​β​δ𝐧,𝐧′.\quantity{\hpsi_{\vecsite, \alpha}(t),\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite^{\prime}, \beta}(t)}=i\hbar\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\,. (1.1.12)

Unless required, from now on, we will omit the temporal dependence, by simply focusing on ψ^𝐧\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}. Similarly, spatial derivatives ∂kψ^​(𝐫)\partial_{k}\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{r}) are replaced by (symmetric) finite differences:

∂kψ^​(𝐫)⟶12​a0​[ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−ψ^𝐧−𝝁k].\partial_{k}\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{r})\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2a_{0}}\quantity[\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-\hpsi_{\vecsite-\latvec[k]}]\,. (1.1.13)

By recalling Eq. 1.1.2, the lattice Dirac Hamiltonian reads

H^Diraclatt=a0D​∑𝐧,kψ^𝐧†​[i​c​ℏ​γ0​γk2​a0​(ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−ψ^𝐧−𝝁k)]+a0D​m0​c2​∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†​γ0​ψ^𝐧.\hat{H}_{\rm{Dirac}}^{\rm{latt}}=a_{0}^{D}\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[i\lspeed\hbar\frac{\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}}{2\lspace}(\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-\hpsi_{\vecsite-\latvec[k]})]+a_{0}^{D}m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\gamma^{0}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}\,. (1.1.14)

We then redefine ψ^𝐧→a0−D/2ψ^𝐧\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}\to a_{0}^{-D/2}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}} and obtain

H^Diraclatt=∑𝐧,kψ^𝐧†​[i​c​ℏ​γ0​γk2​a0​(ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−ψ^𝐧−𝝁k)]+m0​c2​∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†​γ0​ψ^𝐧.\hat{H}_{\rm{Dirac}}^{\rm{latt}}=\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[i\lspeed\hbar\frac{\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}}{2\lspace}(\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-\hpsi_{\vecsite-\latvec[k]})]+m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\gamma^{0}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}\,. (1.1.15)

This choice makes the lattice fermion fields adimensional, even if their hidden dependence on the lattice spacing becomes important when considering the continuum limit location.

Fermion Doubling Problem

An artifact of the lattice discretization of fermions is the appearance of extra solutions of the Dirac equation, known as doublers [444]. In a DD-dimensional space, these doublers lead to the appearance of 2D−12^{D}-1 extra fermion species with respect to the continuum theory: namely, each spatial direction kk contributes a factor of 2 to the number of solutions (one at pk=0p_{k}=0 and one at pk=π/a0p_{k}=\pi/a_{0}).

In order to formally visualizes these extra solutions, let us transform the lattice spinor field to the momentum space using the previously defined Fourier transform:

ψ^𝐧=1V​∑𝐩ei​𝐩⋅𝐧​a0​ψ^​(𝐩),\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{p}}e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{n}a_{0}}\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})\,, (1.1.16)

where 𝐩\mathbf{p} is the lattice momentum, while VV is the lattice volume. Substituing Eq. 1.1.16 into the discretized derivative, we have:

ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−ψ^𝐧−𝝁k2​a0=1V​∑𝐩ei​𝐩⋅𝐧​a0​ei​pk​a0−e−i​pk​a02​a0​ψ^​(𝐩)=1V​∑𝐩ei​𝐩⋅𝐧​a0​i​sin⁡(pk​a0)a​ψ^​(𝐩).\frac{\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}}{2a_{0}}=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{p}}e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{n}a_{0}}\frac{e^{ip_{k}a_{0}}-e^{-ip_{k}a_{0}}}{2a_{0}}\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})=\frac{1}{V}\sum_{\mathbf{p}}e^{i\mathbf{p}\cdot\mathbf{n}a_{0}}\frac{i\sin(\mom[k]\lspace)}{a}\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})\,. (1.1.17)

Then, the lattice Dirac Hamiltonian in the momentum space becomes

H^​(𝐩)=ψ^​(𝐩)†​[−∑k=13γ0γkc​ℏa0sin⁡(pk​a0)+m0c2γ0]​ψ^​(𝐩).\hat{H}(\mathbf{p})=\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})^{\dagger}\quantity[-\sum_{k=1}^{3}\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}\frac{\lspeed\hbar}{\lspace}\sin(\mom[k]\lspace)+\mass[0]\lspeed^{2}\gamma^{0}]\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})\,. (1.1.18)

From the eigenvalue equation H⁡(𝐩)​ψ^​(𝐩)=E⁡(𝐩)​ψ^​(𝐩)H(\mathbf{p})\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})=E(\mathbf{p})\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p}), we have

[−∑k=13γ0γkc​ℏa0sin⁡(pk​a0)+m0c2γ0]​ψ^​(𝐩)=E⁡(𝐩)​ψ^​(𝐩)\quantity[-\sum_{k=1}^{3}\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}\frac{\lspeed\hbar}{\lspace}\sin(\mom[k]\lspace)+\mass[0]\lspeed^{2}\gamma^{0}]\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})=E(\mathbf{p})\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p}) (1.1.19)

Squaring both sides of the eigenvalue equation, we have:

γ0​[−∑k=13c​ℏ​γka0sin⁡(pk​a0)+m0c2]​γ0​[−∑k′=13c​ℏ​γk′a0sin⁡(pk′​a0)+m0c2]​ψ^​(𝐩)=E2​(𝐩)​ψ^​(𝐩)[∑k=13(c​ℏa0​sin⁡(pk​a0))2+m02​c4]​ψ^​(𝐩)=∗\begin{split}\gamma^{0}\quantity[-\sum_{k=1}^{3}\frac{\lspeed\hbar\gamma^{k}}{\lspace}\sin(\mom[k]\lspace)+\mass[0]\lspeed^{2}]\gamma^{0}\quantity[-\sum_{k'=1}^{3}\frac{\lspeed\hbar\gamma^{k'}}{\lspace}\sin(\mom[k']\lspace)+\mass[0]\lspeed^{2}]\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})&=E^{2}(\mathbf{p})\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})\\ \quantity[\sum_{k=1}^{3}\qty(\frac{\lspeed\hbar}{\lspace}\sin(\mom[k]\lspace))^{2}+\mass[0]^{2} c^{4}]\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{p})&\underset{*}{=}\end{split} (1.1.20)

where, in the second passage, we canceled all the mixed terms by exploiting the following properties from the Cliffor’s algebra in Eq. 1.1.8:

γ0​γ0\displaystyle\gamma^{0}\gamma^{0} =𝟙\displaystyle=\mathbb{1} γ0​γk+γk​γ0\displaystyle\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}+\gamma^{k}\gamma^{0} =0\displaystyle=0 γj​γk+γk​γj\displaystyle\gamma^{j}\gamma^{k}+\gamma^{k}\gamma^{j} =2​δj​k​𝟙.\displaystyle=2\delta^{jk}\mathbb{1}\,. (1.1.21)

Clearly, when pk​a0≪1p_{k}a_{0}\ll 1, then sin⁡(pk​a0)∼pk​a0\sin(\mom[k]\lspace)\sim p_{k}a_{0} and the energy reduces to the familiar dispersion relation of relativistic particles: E⁡(𝐩)=±c2​ℏ2​𝐩2+m02​c4E(\mathbf{p})=\pm\sqrt{c^{2}\hbar^{2}\mathbf{p}^{2}+m_{0}^{2}c^{4}}. However, the sine function sin⁡(pk​a0)\sin(\mom[k]\lspace) has an additional zero at pk=π/a0p_{k}=\pi/a_{0}, which yields another low-energy solution at the border of the BZ. Therefore, in DD spatial dimensions, we obtain 2D2^{D} fermion species. The extra degrees of freedom affect the extrapolation to the continuum limit such that the correct continuum results can not be recovered.

Nielsen & Ninomiya Theorem

Handling and removing fermion doublers is neither easy nor without cost. Indeed, according to the Nielsen and Ninomiya no-go theorem [584, 585], any local, hermitian, lattice fermion theory, with translational invariance and chiral symmetry, necessary displays fermion doublers. Hence, any attempt to remove doublers requires violating at least one of the four hypotheses of the theorem. Choosing which of these characteristics to compromise allows for different strategies, with the Wilson fermion [449] and staggered fermion [583] methods being some of the most well-known approaches. While the former one being already studied for quantum simulations [586, 587, 588, 589], throughout the whole thesis, we will rely on the second solution, staggered fermions, introduced by Kogut and Susskind in [579], which has been widely exploited in numerical and quantum simulations [528, 524, 525, 522, 590, 437, 438, 578].

Staggered Fermions

Staggered fermions do not completely resolve the Fermion doubling problem, yet they represent a compromise that reduces the number of doublers by distributing the components of the Dirac spinor across multiple lattice sites. This doubles the periodicity of the lattice, from a0a_{0} to 2​a02a_{0}, and halves the Brillouin zone to [−π2​a0,π2​a0]D[-\frac{\pi}{2a_{0}},\frac{\pi}{2a_{0}}]^{D}. Such a solution looses locality, but maintains a modified translational invariance with a checkerboard pattern and a remnant of chiral symmetry, which is important for maintaining some of the physical characteristics of massless lattice fermions [589].

The practical realization of staggered fermions strongly depends on the spatial dimension of the lattice, as it affects the representation of spinors and gamma matrices [591]. In detail, we need to adjust the matrices γ0\gamma^{0} and γ0​γk\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k} for k=1​…​Dk=1\dots D while maintaining all the Clifford’s algebra properties.

(1+1)D Case

In one spatial dimension, 𝐧=n1\mathbf{n}=n_{1}, and the four-component spinor reduces to a two-spinor with the 0t​h0^{th} (time) component and the 3r​d3^{rd} (space) component: (ψ^0ψ^3)\quantity(\begin{smallmatrix}\hpsi_{0}\\ \hpsi_{3}\end{smallmatrix}). Correspondingly, γ0\gamma^{0} and γ0​γ1\gamma^{0}\gamma^{1} can be any two Pauli matrices, for example σz\sigma^{z} and σx\sigma^{x}. We have then:

H^𝐧1​D=(ψ^0,𝐧†ψ^3,𝐧†)​(m0​c2icℏ∂1icℏ∂1−m0​c2)​(ψ^0,𝐧ψ^3,𝐧).\hat{H}^{\rm{1D}}_{\mathbf{n}}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\psi}_{0,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}&\hat{\psi}_{3,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}m_{0}c^{2}&ic\hbar\partial_{1}\\ ic\hbar\partial_{1}&-m_{0}c^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\psi}_{0,\mathbf{n}}\\ \hat{\psi}_{3,\mathbf{n}}\end{pmatrix}\,. (1.1.22)

Then, in the staggered fermion solution, we decompose the spinor components by placing ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} on even sites (where (−1)n1=+1(-1)^{n_{1}}=+1) and ψ^3\hat{\psi}_{3} on odd sites (where (−1)n1=−1(-1)^{n_{1}}=-1). Then, for even sites, we have:

H^even1​D=m0​c2​∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+i​c​ℏ2​a0​∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†​(ψ^𝐧+𝝁1−ψ^𝐧−𝝁1),\hat{H}^{\rm{1D}}_{\rm{even}}=m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}+\frac{ic\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{1}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}_{1}})\,, (1.1.23)

whereas, for odd sites, we have

H^odd1​D=+i​c​ℏ2​a0∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†(ψ^𝐧+𝝁1−ψ^𝐧−𝝁1)−m0c2∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†ψ^𝐧.\hat{H}^{\rm{1D}}_{\rm{odd}}=+\frac{ic\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{1}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}_{1}})-m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}\,. (1.1.24)

Notice that each of these two contributions contains the hermitian conjugate of the hopping term of the other one. Therefore, combining even and odd sites, the (1+1)D Dirac Hamiltonian via staggered fermions reads:

H^Dirac1​D=∑𝐧[i​c​ℏ2​a0​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁1+h.c]+m0​c2​∑𝐧(−1)𝐧​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧,\begin{split}\hat{H}_{\rm{Dirac}}^{\rm{\rm{1D}}}&=\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[\frac{i\lspeed\hbar}{2\lspace}\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[1]}+\hc]+m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}\,,\end{split} (1.1.25)
(2+1)D Case

The case of two-spatial dimensions is less trivial, as there are multiple ways of defining the matrices (γ0,γ0​γ1,γ0​γ2)(\gamma^{0},\gamma^{0}\gamma^{1},\gamma^{0}\gamma^{2}). For instance, using two-spinors, there are two solutions: (γ0,γ0​γ1,γ0​γ2)→(σz,σx,±σy)(\gamma^{0},\gamma^{0}\gamma^{1},\gamma^{0}\gamma^{2})\to(\sigma^{z},\sigma^{x},\pm\sigma^{y}). Choosing the case with +σy+\sigma^{y}, we obtain:

H^𝐧2​D=(ψ^0,𝐧†ψ^3,𝐧†)​(m0​c2icℏ(∂1−i∂2)icℏ(∂1+i∂2)−m0​c2)​(ψ^0,𝐧ψ^3,𝐧).\hat{H}^{\rm{2D}}_{\mathbf{n}}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\psi}_{0,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}&\hat{\psi}_{3,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}m_{0}c^{2}&ic\hbar(\partial_{1}-i\partial_{2})\\ ic\hbar(\partial_{1}+i\partial_{2})&-m_{0}c^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\psi}_{0,\mathbf{n}}\\ \hat{\psi}_{3,\mathbf{n}}\end{pmatrix}\,. (1.1.26)

The decomposition of the spinor components along the lattice is similar to the (1+1)D case: we place ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} in even sites (where (−1)n1+n2=+1(-1)^{n_{1}+n_{2}}=+1) and ψ^3\hat{\psi}_{3} in odd ones (where (−1)n1+n2=−1(-1)^{n_{1}+n_{2}}=-1). Then, for even sites, we have:

H^even2​D=m0​c2​∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+i​c​ℏ2​a0​∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†​(ψ^𝐧+𝝁1−ψ^𝐧−𝝁1)+c​ℏ2​a0​∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†​(ψ^𝐧+𝝁2−ψ^𝐧−𝝁2)\hat{H}^{\rm{2D}}_{\rm{even}}=m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}+\frac{ic\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{1}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}_{1}})+\frac{c\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{2}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}_{2}}) (1.1.27)

As for the odd sites, we have

H^odd2​D=−m0c2∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†ψ^𝐧+i​c​ℏ2​a0∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†(ψ^𝐧+𝝁1−ψ^𝐧−𝝁1)−c​ℏ2​a0∑𝐧ψ^𝐧†(ψ^𝐧+𝝁2−ψ^𝐧−𝝁2)\hat{H}^{\rm{2D}}_{\rm{odd}}=-m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}+\frac{ic\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{1}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}_{1}})-\frac{c\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}(\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{2}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}_{2}}) (1.1.28)

Combining the two cases and noting the hermitian conjugate of the hopping terms, we find

H^2​D=c​ℏ2​a0​∑𝐧[[i​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁1+(−1)n1+n2​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁2]+h.c]+m0​c2​∑𝐧(−1)𝐧​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧.\begin{split}\hat{H}^{\rm{2D}}=&\frac{c\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[\qty[i\hpsi_{\vecsite}^{\dagger}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[1]} +(-1)^{\site[1]+\site[2]}\hpsi_{\vecsite}^{\dagger}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[2]}]+\hc]+m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}\,.\end{split} (1.1.29)
(3+1)D Case

In the three-dimensional case, we have to use the full 4-component spinor and the original definition of the gammma matrices:

γ0\displaystyle\gamma^{0} =(𝟙2−𝟙2)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{1}_{2}&\\ &-\mathbb{1}_{2}\end{pmatrix} and γk\displaystyle\gamma^{k} =(σkσk).\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}&\sigma^{k}\\ \sigma^{k}&\end{pmatrix}\,. (1.1.30)

Correspondingly, we have:

H^𝐧3​D=(ψ^0,𝐧†ψ^1,𝐧†ψ^2,𝐧†ψ^3,𝐧†)​(m0​c2icℏ∂3icℏ(∂1−i∂2)m0​c2icℏ(∂1+i∂2)−icℏ∂3icℏ∂3icℏ(∂1−i∂2)−m0​c2icℏ(∂1+i∂2)−icℏ∂3−m0​c2)​(ψ^0,𝐧ψ^1,𝐧ψ^2,𝐧ψ^3,𝐧).\hat{H}^{\rm{3D}}_{\mathbf{n}}{=}\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\psi}_{0,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}&\hat{\psi}_{1,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}&\hat{\psi}_{2,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}&\hat{\psi}_{3,\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}m_{0}c^{2}&&ic\hbar\partial_{3}&ic\hbar(\partial_{1}-i\partial_{2})\\ &m_{0}c^{2}&ic\hbar(\partial_{1}+i\partial_{2})&-ic\hbar\partial_{3}\\ ic\hbar\partial_{3}&ic\hbar(\partial_{1}-i\partial_{2})&-m_{0}c^{2}&\\ ic\hbar(\partial_{1}+i\partial_{2})&-ic\hbar\partial_{3}&&-m_{0}c^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\psi}_{0,\mathbf{n}}\\ \hat{\psi}_{1,\mathbf{n}}\\ \hat{\psi}_{2,\mathbf{n}}\\ \hat{\psi}_{3,\mathbf{n}}\end{pmatrix}. (1.1.31)

In this case, decomposing the spinor components along the lattice is less intuitive, but effordable. Namely, we place the component ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} at site 𝐧=(0,0,0)\mathbf{n}=(0,0,0): it couples with ψ^3\hat{\psi}_{3} at sites where n1+n2n_{1}+n_{2} is odd and n3n_{3} is even, with ψ^2\hat{\psi}_{2} at sites where n1+n2n_{1}+n_{2} is even and n3n_{3} is odd, with ψ^1\hat{\psi}_{1} at sites where n1+n2n_{1}+n_{2} is odd and n3n_{3} is odd, and finally with ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} at sites where n1+n2n_{1}+n_{2} is even and n3n_{3} is even. Correspondingly, H^3​D\hat{H}^{\rm{3D}} decomposes into four separate sub-theories, with each theory touching a single fermion specie per site. In particular, ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} and ψ^1\hat{\psi}_{1} occupy even sites, while ψ^2\hat{\psi}_{2} and ψ^3\hat{\psi}_{3} occupy odd sites. As for the mass term, it acts positively on ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} and ψ^1\hat{\psi}_{1} (even sites), and negatively on ψ^2\hat{\psi}_{2} and ψ^3\hat{\psi}_{3} (odd sites). As for the xx-derivative, it acts positively everywhere, while the yy- and zz-derivatives act positively on ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} and ψ^2\hat{\psi}_{2} (where n1+n2n_{1}+n_{2} is even) and negatively on ψ^1\hat{\psi}_{1} and ψ^3\hat{\psi}_{3} (where n1+n2n_{1}+n_{2} is odd). Summarizing, we obtain:

H^Dirac3​D=+c​ℏ2​a0∑𝐧[[i​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁1+(−1)n1+n2​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁2+i​(−1)n1+n2​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁3]+h.c]+m0c2∑𝐧(−1)𝐧ψ^𝐧†ψ^𝐧,\begin{split}\hat{H}^{\rm{3D}}_{\rm{Dirac}}=&+\frac{c\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[\qty[ i\hpsi_{\vecsite}^{\dagger}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[1]} +(-1)^{\site[1]+\site[2]} \hpsi_{\vecsite}^{\dagger}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[2]} +i(-1)^{\site[1]+\site[2]} \hpsi_{\vecsite}^{\dagger}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[3]}]+\hc]\\ &+m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}},\end{split} (1.1.32)

which perfectly matches [583]. We stress that the staggered phases in the hopping and the mass term are fundamental for recovering correct resultss.

1.1.4 Discretization of gauge fields

In QFT, the principle of gauge invariance underlies the interactions between matter fields (such as fermions) and gauge fields (such as bosons, e.g. photons or gluons). Such an interaction is ruled by local (gauge) transformations from a corresponding gauge group.

Basics of group theory

Let us consider a generic compact Lie group 𝒢\mathcal{G} (e.g., SU(N) or U(1)), whose algebra has generators TaT^{a}, where a∈{1​…​dim𝒢}a\in\quantity{1\dots\dim\gaugegroup}. In the fundamental representation of non-Abelian groups 𝒢\mathcal{G} like SU(N), these generators could be the Gell-Mann matrices for SU(3), or Pauli matrices for SU(2). In general, the generators TaT^{a} satisfy the following commutations rules

[Ta,Tb]=i​fa​b​c​Tc,[T^{a},T^{b}]=if^{abc}T^{c}\,, (1.1.33)

where fa​b​cf^{abc} are the structure constants of the gauge group 𝒢\mathcal{G}. For a non-Abelian group, these constants are fully antisymmetric in the indices a,b,ca,b,c, encoding the non-commuting relation between the generators (and correspondingly between the resulting transformations). For instance, in the SU(2) case, fa​b​cf^{abc} is the Levi-Civita symbol ϵa​b​c\epsilon^{abc}. Conversely, in the Abelian scenario, like U(1), the generator is unique and scalar T=1T=1 and fa​b​c=0f^{abc}=0.

Then, any group element Ω⁡(r)\Omega(r) can vary from point to point in spacetime and is defined as

Ω⁡(r)\displaystyle\Omega(r) =exp⁡(i​θa​(r)​Ta)\displaystyle=\exp(i\theta^{a}(\pos)T^{a}) with Ω⁡(r)​Ω†​(r)=Ω†​(r)​Ω​(r)=𝟙,\displaystyle\Omega(r)\Omega^{\dagger}(r)=\Omega^{\dagger}(r)\Omega(r)=\mathbb{1}\,, (1.1.34)

where θa​(r)\theta^{a}(r) are the local parameters of the gauge transformation. For example, in the case of SU(2), Ω⁡(r)\Omega(r) could be a 2×22\times 2 unitary matrix with determinant 1. For U(1) (electromagnetism), Ω⁡(r)\Omega(r) would simply be a phase factor exp⁡(i​θ​(r))\exp(i\theta(\pos)).

Matter fields

Assuming a single matter flavor in the fundamental representation of the gauge group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, gauge transformations of spinors are generated by the charge operator 𝒬^a​(r)\hat{\mathcal{Q}}^{a}(r), defined as:

𝒬^a​(r)=∑α,βψ^α†​(r)​Tα​βa​ψ^β​(r).\hat{\mathcal{Q}}^{a}(r)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\alpha}(r)T^{a}_{\alpha\beta}\hat{\psi}_{\beta}(r). (1.1.35)

This operator represents how the matter fields interact with the gauge fields and underlies the dynamics of the gauge theory when multiple flavors are present. Correspondingly, under a local gauge transformation Ω⁡(r)\Omega(r), matter fields transform as follows:

ψ^​(r)→ψ^′​(r)=Ω⁡(r)​ψ^​(r).\hat{\psi}(r)\rightarrow\hat{\psi}^{\prime}(r)=\Omega(r)\hat{\psi}(r). (1.1.36)
The covariant derivative

The original Dirac equation of Eq. 1.1.7 is clearly not invariant under local gauge transformations such as the ones in Eq. 1.1.36; indeed when transforming the derivative, we find:

∂μψ^​(r)→∂μψ^′​(r)=∂μ(Ω⁡(r)​ψ^​(r))=(∂μΩ⁡(r))​ψ^​(r)+Ω⁡(r)​∂μψ^​(r),\partial_{\mu}\hat{\psi}(r)\rightarrow\partial_{\mu}\hat{\psi}^{\prime}(r)=\partial_{\mu}\quantity(\Omega(\pos) \hpsi(\pos))=(\partial_{\mu}\Omega(r))\hat{\psi}(r)+\Omega(r)\partial_{\mu}\hat{\psi}(r)\,, (1.1.37)

so that the transformed Dirac equation reads

0=i​ℏ​γμ​[(∂μΩ⁡(r))​ψ^​(r)+Ω⁡(r)​∂μψ^​(r)]−m0​c​Ω​(r)​ψ^​(r)=Ω⁡(r)​(i​ℏ​γμ​∂μψ^​(r)−m0​c​ψ^​(r))+i​ℏ​γμ​(∂μΩ⁡(r))​ψ^​(r).\begin{split}0&=i\hbar\gamma^{\mu}\quantity[(\partial_{\mu} \Omega(\pos)) \hpsi(\pos) + \Omega(\pos) \partial_{\mu} \hpsi(\pos)]-m_{0}c\Omega(r)\hat{\psi}(r)\\ &=\Omega(r)\quantity(i\hbar\gamma^{\mu} \partial_{\mu} \hpsi(\pos) - \mass[0]\lspeed\hpsi(\pos))+i\hbar\gamma^{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}\Omega(r))\hat{\psi}(r).\end{split} (1.1.38)

To impose invariance under this transformation, the extra term i​ℏ​γμ​(∂μΩ⁡(r))​ψ​(r)i\hbar\gamma^{\mu}(\partial_{\mu}\Omega(r))\psi(r) must vanish. This would spontaneously happen just in case Ω⁡(r)\Omega(r) is constant (which corresponds to a global, rather than local, gauge transformation). In general, to achieve gauge invariance, the ordinary derivative ∂μ\partial_{\mu} must be replaced by the covariant derivative D^μ\hat{D}_{\mu}, which transforms covariantly under gauge transformations thereby canceling the extra terms introduced by the local gauge transformation. Namely, we have:

D^μ​ψ^​(r)=(∂μ−iqℏA^μ(r))​ψ^​(r)=(∂μ−ig0A^μ(r))​ψ^​(r),\hat{D}_{\mu}\hat{\psi}(r)=\quantity(\partial_{\mu} - i \frac{\charge}{\hbar}\vecpot_{\mu}(\pos))\hat{\psi}(r)=\quantity(\partial_{\mu} - i \coupling[0]\vecpot_{\mu}(\pos))\hat{\psi}(r)\,, (1.1.39)

where qq is the charge, g0=q/ℏg_{0}=q/\hbar is the gauge coupling, while A^μ​(r)=A^μa​(r)​Ta\hat{A}_{\mu}(r)=\hat{A}_{\mu}^{a}(r)T^{a} is the full gauge field operator obtained by contracting the gauge field components A^μa​(r)\hat{A}_{\mu}^{a}(r) to the generators TaT^{a} via the gauge group index aa. The gauge field operator transforms as follows:

A^μ​(r)→A^μ′​(r)=Ω⁡(r)​A^μ​(r)​Ω†​(r)+ig0​Ω​(r)​∂μΩ†​(r).\hat{A}_{\mu}(r)\rightarrow\hat{A}_{\mu}^{\prime}(r)=\Omega(r)\hat{A}_{\mu}(r)\Omega^{\dagger}(r)+\frac{i}{g_{0}}\Omega(r)\partial_{\mu}\Omega^{\dagger}(r)\,. (1.1.40)

Correspondingly, the continuum Dirac Hamiltonian in Eq. 1.1.11 is made covariant as follows:

H^Dirac=∫d​𝐫​[ψ^†(𝐫)(icℏγ0γk(∂k−ig0A^k)+m0c2γ0)ψ^(𝐫)].\hat{H}_{\rm{Dirac}}=\int d\mathbf{r}\quantity[\hpsi^{\dagger}(\vecpos)(i\lspeed\hbar\gamma^{0}\gamma^{k}(\partial_{k}-i\coupling[0]\vecpot_{k}) +\mass[0]\lspeed^{2}\gamma^{0})\hpsi(\vecpos)]\,. (1.1.41)
The pure gauge Hamiltonian

To make the Dirac equation gauge invariant, we needed to introduce an extra d.o.f., a gauge field, whose dynamics needs to be properly accounted and added to the Dirac Hamiltonian. In the continuum, the dynamics of gauge fields is captured by the field strength tensor F^μ​ν​(r)\hat{F}_{\mu\nu}(r), which for a generic non-Abelian gauge field A^μ​(r)\hat{A}_{\mu}(r) is given by:

F^μ​ν​(r)=∂μA^ν​(r)−∂νA^μ​(r)−i​g0​[A^μ​(r),A^ν​(r)]F^μ​νa​(r)​Ta=[∂μA^νa​(r)−∂νA^μa​(r)+g0​fa​b​c​A^μb​(r)​A^νc​(r)]​Ta.\begin{split}\hat{F}_{\mu\nu}(r)&=\partial_{\mu}\hat{A}_{\nu}(r)-\partial_{\nu}\hat{A}_{\mu}(r)-ig_{0}\quantity[\vecpot_{\mu}(\pos), \vecpot_{\nu}(\pos)]\\ \hat{F}_{\mu\nu}^{a}(r)T^{a}&=\quantity[\partial_{\mu} \vecpot_{\nu}^{a}(\pos) - \partial_{\nu} \vecpot_{\mu}^{a}(\pos) + \coupling[0] f^{abc} \vecpot_{\mu}^{b}(\pos) \vecpot_{\nu}^{c}(\pos)]T^{a}.\end{split} (1.1.42)

To move towards the Hamiltonian formalism, we separate its electric and magnetic components:

E^ka​(r)\displaystyle\hat{E}_{k}^{a}(r) =F^0​ka​(r)=1c​∂tA^ka​(r)−∂kA^0a​(r)−g0​fa​b​c​A^0b​(r)​A^kc​(r)\displaystyle=\hat{F}_{0k}^{a}(r)=\frac{1}{c}\partial_{t}\hat{A}_{k}^{a}(r)-\partial_{k}\hat{A}_{0}^{a}(r)-g_{0}f^{abc}\hat{A}_{0}^{b}(r)\hat{A}_{k}^{c}(r) (1.1.43a)
B^ia​(r)\displaystyle\hat{B}_{i}^{a}(r) =−12​ϵi​j​k​F^j​ka​(r)=ϵi​j​k​(∂jA^ka​(r)−g02​fa​b​c​A^jb​(r)​A^kc​(r)),\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_{ijk}\hat{F}_{jk}^{a}(r)=\epsilon_{ijk}\quantity(\partial_{j}\vecpot_{k}^a(\pos) - \frac{\coupling[0]}{2} f^{abc} \vecpot_{j}^b(\pos)\vecpot_{k}^c(\pos)), (1.1.43b)

where i,j,ki,j,k are spatial indices. In the Coulomb gauge, where A^0​(r)=0\hat{A}^{0}(r)=0, the electric field reduces to E^ka​(r)=F^0​ka​(r)=∂tA^ka​(r)/c\hat{E}_{k}^{a}(r)=\hat{F}_{0k}^{a}(r)=\partial_{t}\hat{A}_{k}^{a}(r)/c. This choice does not change the physics, as it simply exploits an extra freedom in defining the gauge fields.

The corresponding Hamiltonian of the pure gauge fields is

H^gauge=∫d​𝐫​[ϵ02​E^ka​(r)​E^ka​(r)+12​μ0​B^ka​(r)​B^ka​(r)].\hat{H}_{\rm{gauge}}=\int d\mathbf{r}\quantity[\frac{\permittivity}{2} \eleE_{k}^{a}(\pos)\eleE_{k}^{a}(\pos)+ \frac{1}{2\permeability}\magn_{k}^{a}(\pos)\magn_{k}^{a}(\pos)]\,. (1.1.44)

where ϵ0\epsilon_{0} and μ0=(c2​ϵ0)−1\mu_{0}=(c^{2}\epsilon_{0})^{-1} correspond to the vacuum permittivity and permeability respectively. In dimensioned units (such as SI), the physical dimensions of the constants read

[ϵ0]\displaystyle\quantity[\permittivity] =(charge)2​(length)2−D​(energy)−1\displaystyle=(\text{charge})^{2}(\text{length})^{2-D}(\text{energy})^{-1} (1.1.45)
[μ0]\displaystyle\quantity[\permeability] =(charge)−2​(length)D−2​(energy)⋅(length)−2​(time)2\displaystyle=(\text{charge})^{-2}(\text{length})^{D-2}(\text{energy})\cdot(\text{length})^{-2}(\text{time})^{2}
=(charge)−2​(length)D−4​(energy)​(time)2.\displaystyle=(\text{charge})^{-2}(\text{length})^{D-4}(\text{energy})(\text{time})^{2}\,.

Correspondingly, the electric and magnetic fields have the following dimensions:

[E^]\displaystyle\quantity[\eleE] =(charge)−1​(length)−1​(energy)\displaystyle=(\text{charge})^{-1}(\text{length})^{-1}(\text{energy}) (1.1.46)
[B^]\displaystyle\quantity[\magn] =(charge)−1​(length)−2​(energy)​(time).\displaystyle=(\text{charge})^{-1}(\text{length})^{-2}(\text{energy})(\text{time})\,.

As for the coupling constant g0g_{0}, its dimensional analysis reads

[g0]=(charge)​(energy)−1​(time)−1,\quantity[\coupling[0]]=(\text{charge})(\text{energy})^{-1}(\text{time})^{-1}\,, (1.1.47)

while for the vector potential we have:

[A^]=(charge)−1​(length)−1​(energy)​(time).\quantity[\vecpot]=(\text{charge})^{-1}(\text{length})^{-1}(\text{energy})(\text{time})\,. (1.1.48)
Discretized gauge fields

When moving from the continuum to the lattice, each spatial component kk of the covariant derivative in Eq. 1.1.39 is replaced by the parallel transport11 1 Parallel transports have several names in literature. Sometimes they are also called connections referring to a differential geometry framework. Sometimes, they are called comparators. U^𝐧,𝝁k​(t)\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}(t), a dimensionless link variable reflecting the gauge field’s influence along the link connecting neighboring lattice sites 𝐧\mathbf{n} and 𝐧+𝝁k\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{k}. Omitting again the time dependence, we define the parallel transport as:

D^k=(∂k−ig0A^k)⟶U^𝐧,𝝁k=exp⁡(i​g0​∫𝐧𝐧+𝝁kA^k​(𝐫)​𝑑ℓ)∼exp⁡(i​g0​a0​A^k),\hat{D}_{k}=(\partial_{k}-ig_{0}\hat{A}^{k})\quad\longrightarrow\quad\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}=\exp(i\coupling[0] \int_{\vecsite}^{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}\vecpot^{k}(\vecpos)d\ell)\sim\exp(i\coupling[0]\lspace\vecpot^{k})\,, (1.1.49)

where in the second step we assumed A^k​(r)∼A^𝐧k\hat{A}^{k}(r)\sim\hat{A}^{k}_{\mathbf{n}} to be almost constant along the lattice link (𝐧,𝝁k)({\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}_{k}) of length a0a_{0}. Assuming a0a_{0} to be sufficiently small, we can further expand the parallel transporter up to the first order and notice that:

[i​ψ^𝐧†​U^𝐧,𝝁k​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k2​a0+h.c]=i​[ψ^𝐧†​U^𝐧,𝝁k​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−ψ^𝐧+𝝁k†​U^𝐧,𝝁k†​ψ^𝐧2​a0]=i​[ψ^𝐧†​U^𝐧,𝝁k​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−ψ^𝐧†​U^𝐧−𝝁k,𝝁k†​ψ^𝐧,−𝝁k2​a0]=i​ψ^𝐧†​[U^𝐧,𝝁k​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−U^𝐧−𝝁k,𝝁k†​ψ^𝐧,−𝝁k]2​a0∼i​ψ^𝐧†2​a0​[(1−i​g0​A^𝐧k​a0)​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−(1+i​g0​A^𝐧−𝝁kk​a0)​ψ^𝐧,−𝝁k]=iψ^†𝐧[ψ^𝐧+𝝁k−ψ^𝐧−𝝁k2​a0−i​g0​A^𝐧k​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k†]→a0→0iψ^†(𝐫)(∂k−ig0A^k(𝐫))ψ^(𝐫).\begin{split}&\quantity[\frac{i\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite}\Apara_{\vecsite, \latvec[k]}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}}{2\lspace}+\hc]=i\quantity[\frac{\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite}\Apara_{\vecsite, \latvec[k]}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}\Apara^{\dagger}_{\vecsite, \latvec[k]}\hpsi_{\vecsite}}{2\lspace}]\\ &\qquad=i\quantity[\frac{\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite}\Apara_{\vecsite, \latvec[k]}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite}\Apara^{\dagger}_{\vecsite-\latvec[k], \latvec[k]}\hpsi_{\vecsite, -\latvec[k]}}{2\lspace}]\\ &\qquad=i\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\frac{\quantity[\Apara_{\vecsite, \latvec[k]}\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-\Apara^{\dagger}_{\vecsite-\latvec[k], \latvec[k]}\hpsi_{\vecsite, -\latvec[k]}]}{2a_{0}}\\ &\qquad\sim\frac{i\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}}{2a_{0}}\quantity[(1-i\coupling[0]\vecpot^{k}_{\vecsite}\lspace)\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-(1+i\coupling[0]\vecpot^{k}_{\vecsite-\latvec[k]}\lspace)\hpsi_{\vecsite, -\latvec[k]}]\\ &\qquad=i\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[\frac{\hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}-\hpsi_{\vecsite-\latvec[k]}}{2\lspace} -i\coupling[0]\vecpot^{k}_{\vecsite} \hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite+\latvec[k]}]\xrightarrow{a_{0}\to 0}i\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{r})(\partial_{k}-ig_{0}\hat{A}^{k}(\mathbf{r}))\hat{\psi}(\mathbf{r}).\end{split} (1.1.50)

Then, the lattice version of the covariant Dirac Hamiltonian with staggered fermions is

H^Dirac=c​ℏ2​a0​∑𝐧,𝝁[s𝐧,𝝁​ψ^𝐧​U^𝐧,𝝁​ψ^𝐧+𝝁+h.c]+m0​c2​∑𝐧s𝐧​ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧,𝝁,\begin{split}\hat{H}_{\rm{Dirac}}=&\frac{c\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}\quantity[s_{\genlink}\hpsi_{\vecsite} \Apara_{\genlink} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec} + \hc]+m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}s_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}},\end{split} (1.1.51)

where s𝐧,𝝁s_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} and s𝐧s_{\mathbf{n}} are phases that arise when using staggered fermions.

Similarly to the vector potential, gauge transformations of the parallel transporter read:

U^𝐧,𝝁k→Ω𝐧​U^𝐧,𝝁k​Ω𝐧+𝝁k†,\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}\rightarrow\Omega_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}\Omega^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}\,, (1.1.52)

where Ω𝐧\Omega_{\mathbf{n}} is the gauge transformation matrix at site 𝐧\mathbf{n}. In general, due to the non-commuting algebra in Eq. 1.3.32, the left Ω𝐧\Omega_{\mathbf{n}} and the right Ω𝐧+𝝁k†\Omega^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}_{k}} gauge transformations are different and generated by the dimensionless conjugate fields L^𝐧,𝝁a\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a} and R^𝐧,𝝁a\hat{R}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a} respectively, which satisfy the following relations:

[L^𝐧,𝝁a,U^α​β𝐧′,𝝁′]\displaystyle\commutator*{\eleL^{a}_{\genlink}}{\NApara_{\genlinkprime}} =−δ𝐧​𝐧′δ𝝁​𝝁′∑γTaα​γU^𝐱,𝝁γ​β,\displaystyle=-\delta_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{{\bf\it\mu}{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}\sum_{\gamma}T^{a}_{\alpha\gamma}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{x,{\bf\it\mu}}}^{\vphantom{dagger}\gamma\beta}\,, (1.1.53a)
[R^𝐧,𝝁a,U^α​β𝐧′,𝝁′]\displaystyle\commutator*{\eleR^{a}_{\genlink}}{\NApara_{\genlinkprime}} =+δ𝐧​𝐧′δ𝝁​𝝁′∑γU^𝐱,𝝁α​γTaγ​β,\displaystyle=+\delta_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{{\bf\it\mu}{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}\sum_{\gamma}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{x,{\bf\it\mu}}}^{\vphantom{dagger}\alpha\gamma}T^{a}_{\gamma\beta}\,, (1.1.53b)

where α,β,γ,δ\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta span the matrix indices of the group generators TaT^{a}. In the Abelian U(1) case, where there is only one generator, there is only one electric field and the parallel transporter acts as a raising operator. Namely, we have:

E^𝐧,𝝁\displaystyle\hat{E}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} =L^𝐧,𝝁=R^𝐧,𝝁\displaystyle=\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}=\hat{R}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} [E^𝐧,𝝁,U^𝐧,𝝁]\displaystyle\commutator*{\eleE_{\genlink}}{\Apara_{\vecsite, \latvec}} =U^𝐧,𝝁.\displaystyle=\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}\,. (1.1.54)
The pure gauge lattice Hamiltonian

Once we have discretized all the gauge fields, we can build the corresponding lattice version of the pure gauge Hamiltonian in Eq. 1.1.44. The electric energy density is given by the Casimir operator:

E^𝐧,𝝁2=L^𝐧,𝝁a​L^𝐧,𝝁a=R^𝐧,𝝁a​R^𝐧,𝝁a.\hat{E}^{2}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}=\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}=\hat{R}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}\hat{R}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}\,. (1.1.55)

To make the Casimir operator adimensional, the electric Hamiltonian is redefined as follows:

H^elec\displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm{elec}} =ϵ02​∫dD​𝐫​E^k​(r)​E^k​(r)\displaystyle=\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}\int d^{D}\mathbf{r}\hat{E}_{k}(r)\hat{E}_{k}(r) →\displaystyle\to H^eleclatt\displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm{elec}}^{\rm{latt}} =a0D​ϵ02​∑𝐧,kq2​a02−2​Dϵ02​E^𝐧,𝝁k2=∑𝐧,kq2​a02−D2​ϵ0​E^𝐧,𝝁k2.\displaystyle=a_{0}^{D}\frac{\epsilon_{0}}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\frac{q^{2}a_{0}^{2-2D}}{\epsilon_{0}^{2}}\hat{E}^{2}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}=\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\frac{q^{2}a_{0}^{2-D}}{2\epsilon_{0}}\hat{E}^{2}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}\,. (1.1.56)

We can recast the latter in dimensionless units, by redefining the gauge coupling constant as

g=g0​ℏc​ϵ0​a03−D2=q​a03−D2c​ℏ​ϵ0=q​a03−D2​c​μ0ℏ.g=g_{0}\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{c\epsilon_{0}}}a_{0}^{\frac{3-D}{2}}=q\frac{a_{0}^{\frac{3-D}{2}}}{\sqrt{c\hbar\epsilon_{0}}}=qa_{0}^{\frac{3-D}{2}}\sqrt{\frac{c\mu_{0}}{\hbar}}\,. (1.1.57)

By doing so, we obtain

H^eleclatt=∑𝐧,kg2​c​ℏ2​a0​E^𝐧,𝝁k2.\hat{H}_{\rm{elec}}^{\rm{latt}}=\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\frac{g^{2}c\hbar}{2a_{0}}\hat{E}^{2}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}_{k}}\,. (1.1.58)

Notice that the new gauge coupling constant gg is dimensionless yet depends on the lattice spacing. As discussed for the matter fields, such an hidden relation becomes important when discussing the continuum limit.

Correspondingly, the simplest way to describe the magnetic energy density on the lattice is by using Wilson loops [579, 449], i.e. gauge-invariant loops made out of parallel transporters U^\hat{U}. On a hypercubic lattice, the smallest non-trivial loop is represented by a plaquette operator

U^□=∑α,β,γ,δU^α​β𝐧,𝝁U^𝐧+𝝁,𝝁′β​γU^𝐧+𝝁′,𝝁γδ†U^𝐧,𝝁′δγ†,\hat{U}_{\mathbf{\square}}^{\vphantom{dagger}}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}\hat{U}^{\alpha\beta}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}^{\beta\gamma}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime},{\bf\it\mu}}^{\gamma\delta\dagger}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}^{\delta\gamma\dagger}, (1.1.59)

where 𝝁{\bf\it\mu} and 𝝁′{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime} span the plaquette’s plane. Since the parallel transporters in Eq. 1.1.49 commutes when acting on different links (and so the vector potentials do), one can notice that:

U^□=exp⁡(i​g0​∮∂□A^k​d​ℓk)​=∗​exp⁡(i​g0​∮□∇⁣×⁡𝐀^⋅𝑑𝐬)=exp⁡(i​g0​∮□𝐁^⋅𝑑𝐬)∼exp⁡(i​g0​a02​B^).\begin{split}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{\square}}^{\vphantom{dagger}}=\exp(i\coupling[0]\oint_{\partial\square}\vecpot_{k}d\ell_{k})\underset{*}{=}\exp(i\coupling[0]\oint_{\square}\curl\vb{\vecpot}\cdot d\vb{s})=\exp(i\coupling[0]\oint_{\square}\vb{\magn}\cdot d\vb{s})\sim\exp(i\coupling[0]\lspace^{2}\magn)\,.\end{split} (1.1.60)

where in the ∗* we used the Stokes theorem, while in the last step we assumed the magnetic field to be almost constant in the plaquette of area a02a_{0}^{2}. Given these assumptions, we have:

Tr⁡(U^□+U^□†)=2​cos⁡(g0​a02​B^)∼2​[1−12​g02​a04​B^2],\begin{split}\Tr(\plaq+\plaq*)=2\cos(\coupling[0]\lspace^{2}\magn)\sim 2\quantity[1-\frac{1}{2}\coupling[0]^{2}\lspace^{4}\magn^{2}],\end{split} (1.1.61)

from which we obtain that

B^2∼−1g02​a04​Tr⁡(U^□+U^□†).\hat{B}^{2}\sim-\frac{1}{g_{0}^{2}a_{0}^{4}}\Tr(\plaq+\plaq*). (1.1.62)

Then, the magnetic Hamiltonian can be discretized as follows:

H^magn\displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm{magn}} =12​μ0​∫dD​𝐫​Bk​(r)​Bk​(r)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\mu_{0}}\int d^{D}\mathbf{r}B_{k}(r)B_{k}(r) →\displaystyle\to H^magnlatt\displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm{magn}}^{\rm{latt}} =−12​μ0​g02​a04−D∑□Tr⁡(U^□+U^□†).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2\mu_{0}g_{0}^{2}a_{0}^{4-D}}\sum_{\square}\Tr(\plaq+\plaq*). (1.1.63)

Finally, by using the dimensionless gauge coupling in Eq. 1.1.57, we obtain:

H^magnlatt=−c​ℏ2​g2​a0∑□Tr⁡(U^□+U^□†).\displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm{magn}}^{\rm{latt}}=-\frac{c\hbar}{2g^{2}a_{0}}\sum_{\square}\Tr(\plaq+\plaq*)\,. (1.1.64)

Notice that plaquette terms only exist in D>1D>1, contributing to the increased complexity of quantum and TN simulations of LGTs in higher dimensions [541].

The lattice gauge Hamiltonian with staggered fermions

Summarizing and combining all the ingredients (matter and gauge fields), the general Kogut-Susskind Hamiltonian via staggered fermions [443] reads:

HLGT=c​ℏ2​a0​∑𝐧,𝝁∑α,β[s𝐧,𝝁​ψ^𝐧,α​U^𝐧,𝝁α​β​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β+h.c]+m0​c2​∑𝐧,αs𝐧​ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧,𝝁+c​ℏ​g22​a0∑𝐧,𝝁E^2𝐧,𝝁−c​ℏ2​g2​a0∑□Tr⁡(U^□+U^□†),\begin{split}H_{\rm LGT}=&\frac{c\hbar}{2a_{0}}\sum_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\quantity[s_{\genlink}\hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha} \NApara_{\genlink} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec, \beta} + \hc]+m_{0}c^{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}s_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}\\ &+\frac{c\hbar g^{2}}{2a_{0}}\sum_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}\hat{E}^{2}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}-\frac{c\hbar}{2g^{2}a_{0}}\sum_{\square}\Tr(\plaq+ \plaq*)\,,\end{split} (1.1.65)

where we expressed the dependence on the matrix indices α,β\alpha,\beta of the gauge algebra generators.

1.2 Dressed-site model for Hamiltonian Lattice Gauge Theories

We have seen all the ingredients for discretizing an LGT with dynamical matter. However, there remain fundamental challenges to be faced for attacking Hamiltonians like Eq. 1.1.65 with numerical methods.

First of all, we need to achieve a finite-dimensional encoding of the continuous gauge fields such as U(1) or SU(N), especially beyond one spatial dimension, where decoupling the gauge field’s longitudinal component is required [530]. Among known truncation recipes are Quantum Link Models (QLM) [531, 532, 533, 534, 535], finite subgroups [517, 521, 547], digitization of gauge fields [548], and fusion-algebra deformation [549]. Whatever the adopted solution, further effort is required to satisfy gauge symmetry at each local site, which involves the concurrent evaluation of all the gauge links and the attached matter site. In practice, an extensive number of local constraints (energy penalties), which corresponds to QMB operators concurrently acting on 2D+1 sites (2D gauge links and 1 matter site), where D is the number of spatial dimensions. Moreover, since the Gauss law represents the fundamental conservation law underpinning the theory (the highest energy scale of the model), enforcing it is essential for the simulation to remain meaningful. Any small violation of these local constraints would incur a significant energy cost, reflecting the critical role of gauge invariance in reproducing the correct physical behavior.

Another important issue to be faced in simulating LGTs is to account for the Fermi statistics of matter fields. In several TN methods as well on well-established conventional digital quantum simulation platforms (e.g. superconducting qubits, trapped-ions, Rydberg arrays, quantum dots) [552, 553, 554, 555, 556], fermionic algebra (mutually-anticommuting operations) must be encoded into a genuinely local algebra (mutually-commuting operations) of qubits. Standard fermion-to-qubit encodings, such as the Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation [557], and other modern approaches [558, 559, 560, 592, 497, 498] make any fermionic Hamiltonian interaction inherently long-range and expensive from a computational perspective.

In numerical methods such as TNs, as well as in quantum computations, all these requirements significantly impact the computational resources needed for the simulations, as well as their efficiency. In this section, we present a theoretical scheme which is able to order achieve a finite and controllable gauge field truncation, avoid the Fermi statistics of matter fields and directly access the gauge invariant subspace, revealing suitable for TN methods as well as for quantum simulations of LGTs. Building on the work of [564, 593], we dress every physical matter site with the information related to its adjacent gauge links. A pictorial scheme of this approach is outlined in Fig. 1.1[Right]: (a) starting from the original description matter fields on sites and gauge fields on links in Eq. 1.1.65, we truncate the gauge group imposing an energy cut-off on the Casimir operator. Then, (b) we express each truncated gauge link as a pair of fermionic rishon modes ζ^\hat{\zeta} and (c) constrain their link dynamics according to the original gauge group algebra. Ultimately, (d) we merge each of these modes to its adjacent matter site, ending up in a compact dressed-site formalism [564, 593, 550]. The resulting effective Hamiltonian is made out of only bosonic operators and directly acts on the gauge invariant Hilbert sub-space. Correspondingly, as done in Loop String Hadrons methods [594], the original (Abelian/non-Abelian) gauge invariance is exactly rewritten into an Abelian, nearest-neighbor, diagonal selection rule, and the explicit dependence on the fermionic matter is eliminated [524, 550, 551]. Such an approach is especially suitable when dealing with LGTs in high-dimensional lattices.

We will practically apply the dressed-site formalism on two paradigmatic examples that have been exploited for numerical simulations [437, 438, 440]: SU(2) in Section 1.3 and U(1) in Section 1.4.

1.2.1 Gauge field truncation

The link Hilbert space is the space of square-integrable functions on the gauge group 𝒢\mathcal{G}, L2​(𝒢)L^{2}(\mathcal{G}), which is infinite-dimensional for continuous groups such as U(1) or SU(N) [595].

In one space dimension, gauge degrees of freedom are unphysical (absence of transverse polarizations) and can thus be integrated out, albeit at the price of introducing non-local interactions [596]. Beyond one dimension, the removal is much more delicate, because it requires first decoupling the gauge field’s longitudinal component [530]. When impossible or inconvenient to remove, gauge degrees of freedom might have to be truncated to perform TN or quantum simulation. Among known truncation recipes are Quantum Link Models (QLM) [531, 532, 533, 534, 535], an approach already considered for practical quantum simulation of LGTs [536, 537, 538, 539, 540, 541, 542, 543, 544, 545, 546], finite subgroups [517, 521, 547], digitization of gauge fields [548], and fusion-algebra deformation [549].

Another approach is to truncate the spectrum of the electric energy density operator ‖E^2‖≤Θ\norm{\casimir}\leq\Theta on each link [437, 590]. The cutoff is conveniently imposed in the irreducible representation (irrep) basis {|j​mL​mR⟩}\{\ket{\spin\mL\mR}\} [595] of L2​(𝒢)L^{2}(\mathcal{G}), where E^2\hat{E}^{2} is diagonal:

E^2​|j​mL​mR⟩=C2​(j)​|j​mL​mR⟩.\hat{E}^{2}\ket{\spin\mL\mR}=C_{2}(j)\ket{\spin\mL\mR}\,. (1.2.1)

Here, mLm_{\mathrm{L}} and mRm_{\mathrm{R}} are indices in the jj-irrep of 𝒢\mathcal{G} and C2​(j)C_{2}(j) is the quadratic Casimir of jj [595]. In the strong coupling limit, where the electric energy term dominates HLGTH_{\rm LGT}, this truncation is equivalent to an energy cutoff [590].

1.2.2 Gauss law and the dressed site

The most distinctive feature of gauge theories is arguably the presence of local constraints, analogous to the Gauss law of classical electrodynamics, relating the configuration of the gauge field to the spatial distribution of charges [597]. At the quantum level, Gauss law is the statement that only gauge invariant states are physical, namely, G^𝐧a​|Ψphys⟩=0​∀𝐧,a\hat{G}_{\mathbf{n}}^{a}\ket*{\Psi_{\text{phys}}}=0\;\forall\mathbf{n},a, where G^𝐧a\hat{G}_{\mathbf{n}}^{a} are the generators of local gauge transformations at 𝐧\mathbf{n}:

G^𝐧a=𝒬^𝐧a+q𝐧a+∑𝝁[L^𝐧,𝝁a+R^𝐧−𝝁,𝝁a],\hat{G}_{\mathbf{n}}^{a}=\hat{\mathcal{Q}}^{a}_{\mathbf{n}}+q^{a}_{\mathbf{n}}+\sum_{{\bf\it\mu}}[\hat{L}^{a}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}+\hat{R}^{a}_{{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu},{\bf\it\mu}}}]\,, (1.2.2)

with q𝐧aq^{a}_{\mathbf{n}} representing eventual static background charges (typically vanishing). Lattice Gauss law provides a set of vertex constraints, each involving a lattice site and its 2D neighboring links.

Due to Gauss law, the physical Hilbert space of LGTs is much smaller than the tensor product of all local sites and link Hilbert spaces. Properly exploiting gauge symmetries can thus significantly speed up numerical simulations [593]. Strategies that solve Gauss law by eliminating (partially or entirely) either the gauge fields or the matter fields have been developed. Nonetheless, such approaches come with specific limitations: the range of interaction has to be extended, moreover, integrating-out gauge fields become problematic in D>1D>1 [530], while the recipe for removing matter is a model (matter content) dependent [551].

Another possibility is to enforce Gauss law using a dressed site construction [564, 593, 550, 551], sketched in Fig. 1.1 and outlined below. Dressed sites have local dimensions typically larger than those resulting from the aforementioned approaches, but they are obtained from a model-independent prescription which has the advantage of preserving the locality of the interactions [593, 590].

As a first step, we factorize each gauge link in a pair of modes, living at its edges. Namely, every link is decomposed into a pair of left (LL) and right (RR) rishon d.o.f., each associated with a Hilbert space spanned by the basis states |j​m⟩\ket{\spin m}, identifying |j​mL​mR⟩↪|j​mL⟩⊗|j​mR⟩\ket{j \mL\mR}\hookrightarrow\ket{j \mL}\otimes\ket{j \mR}, and writing parallel transporters as rishon bilinears [437]:

U^α​β𝐧,𝝁→∑iζ^L⁡(i)​α𝐧,+𝝁ζ^R(i)β†𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁.\hat{U}^{\alpha\beta}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}\to\sum_{i}\hat{\zeta}^{L(i)\alpha}_{\mathbf{n},+{\bf\it\mu}}\hat{\zeta}^{R(i)\beta\,\dagger}_{{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}},-{\bf\it\mu}}\,\,. (1.2.3)

Physical gauge link configurations, i.e. those with the left and right rishons in the same irrep, are selected introducing a local link symmetry at the TN simulation level [441, 593, 590]. Notice that such a constraint is always Abelian, regardless of the Abelian or non-Abelian nature of the gauge group.

1.2.3 Projecting dressed site operators onto the gauge-invariant basis

Crucially, the gauge generators G^𝐧a\hat{G}_{\mathbf{n}}^{a} now involve only the matter site at 𝐧\mathbf{n} and its 2​D2D neighboring rishons. Fusing these degrees of freedom in a composite site, Gauss law becomes an internal constraint that singles out the dressed site Hilbert space as its gauge invariant subspace:

ℋdress=ker⁡G⊂ℋmatt⊗(ℋrish)⊗2​D.\mathcal{H}_{\text{dress}}=\ker G\subset\mathcal{H}_{\text{matt}}\otimes(\mathcal{H}_{\text{rish}})^{\otimes 2D}\,. (1.2.4)

Therefore, the effective operators of the resulting dressed-site Hamiltonian should be obtained by projecting the obtained ones on the subspace generated by a gauge-invariant basis MM. Namely, for any dressed-site operator OO among the previously defined, the corresponding effective operator OeffO^{\text{eff}} acting on gauge-invariant states reads:

Oeff\displaystyle O^{\text{eff}} =M†⋅O⋅M,\displaystyle=M^{\dagger}\cdot O\cdot M\,, where M†⋅M\displaystyle M^{\dagger}\cdot M =𝟙\displaystyle=\mathbb{1} and (M⋅M†)2\displaystyle\quantity(M\cdot M^{\dagger})^{2} =(M⋅M†).\displaystyle=\quantity(M\cdot M^{\dagger})\,. (1.2.5)

The practical computation of the gauge-invariant basis MM can be determined as the kernel of the Gauss Law operator of the corresponding LGT (see Section 1.3 for SU(2) and Section 1.4 for U(1)). The expansion of the gauge singlet basis states of ℋdress\mathcal{H}_{\text{dress}} in terms of the matter and rishon bases is computed via Clebsch-Gordan decomposition [590].

The resulting operators OeffO^{\text{eff}}, for any spatial dimension D and any value of the gauge truncation jmaxj_{\max}, are available for U(1) and SU(2) in the GitHub repository ed-lgt [441], which also allows for simulations of these LGTs via Exact Diagonalization.

1.2.4 Defermionization

As aforementioned in the introduction, an important challenge to be faced in simulating LGTs is to account for the Fermi statistics of matter fields. In several TN methods and conventional digital quantum simulation platforms [552, 553, 554, 555, 556], fermionic (anticommuting) algebra must be encoded into a genuinely local (commuting) algebra of qub(d)its. Standard fermion-to-qubit encodings, such as the Jordan-Wigner (JW) transformation [557], and other modern approaches [558, 559, 560] make any fermionic Hamiltonian interaction inherently long-range and expensive from a computational perspective [481], especially for higher-dimensional LGTs.

Within the dressed-site formalism, it is additionally possible resolve this problem and effectively eliminate the Fermi statistics of matter fields. This is possible for any gauge theory where the gauge field has a well-defined parity. Specifically, a local parity operator P^𝐧,𝝁=P^𝐧,𝝁†\hat{P}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}=\hat{P}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{\dagger} such that P^𝐧,𝝁2=1\hat{P}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{2}=1 must satisfy {U^𝐧,𝝁,P^𝐧,𝝁}=0\{\hat{U}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}},\hat{P}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}\}=0, as it happens for ℤ2​N\mathbb{Z}_{2N}, U(N), and SU(2N) [550, 551, 437]. In these cases, it is possible to consider rishons with a Fermi statistics, and, as a result, all physical (gauge invariant) dressed site operators are genuinely local, i.e. they mutually commute at a nonzero distance (as spins or bosons) [439].

As the resulting Hamiltonian in the dressed site formalims is made out of different fermions (matter fields and gauge rishons), it is convenient to rule the tensor product of general fermion operators. For a fermionic QMB system with particles arbitrarily sorted along a certain path, any tensor product of fermionic operators should take into consideration the proper anti-commutation rules. Namely, a generic fermionic operator F^𝐧\hat{F}_{\mathbf{n}} acting on the 𝐧t​h\mathbf{n}^{th} position along the path reads:

F^𝐧=(f^11…f^1​Nf^N​1…f^N​N)F=⋯⊗P^𝐧−𝝁⊗F^𝐧⊗𝟙𝐧+𝝁⊗…,\hat{F}_{\mathbf{n}}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{f}_{11}&\dots&\hat{f}_{1N}\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ \hat{f}_{N1}&\dots&\hat{f}_{NN}\\ \end{pmatrix}_{F}=\dots\otimes\hat{P}_{{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}}}\otimes\hat{F}_{\mathbf{n}}\otimes\mathbb{1}_{{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}}}\otimes\dots\,, (1.2.6)

where P^𝐧=P^𝐧†=P^𝐧−1\hat{P}_{\mathbf{n}}=\hat{P}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}=\hat{P}_{\mathbf{n}}^{-1} is a fermion parity operator that gets inverted after the action of a fermionic operator:

{P^𝐧,F^𝐧}=0[P^𝐧,F^𝐧′≠𝐧]=0∀𝐧,𝐧′∈Λ.\quantity{\parity_{\vecsite},\hat{F}_{\vecsite}}=0\qquad\quantity[\parity_{\vecsite},\hat{F}_{\vecsite^{\prime}\neq\vecsite}]=0\qquad\forall\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}\in\Lambda\,. (1.2.7)

Therefore, matter fields admit a notion of parity satisfying Eq. 1.2.7. For Dirac fermions

ψ^Dirac\displaystyle\hat{\psi}_{\text{Dirac}} =(0100)F\displaystyle=\quantity( \begin{array}{cc} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array})_{F} P^Dirac\displaystyle\hat{P}_{\text{Dirac}} =(+100−1),\displaystyle=\quantity( \begin{array}{cc} +1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{array})\,,

where the subscript FF is a reminder that the ψ^\hat{\psi} matrix is meant ’as a fermion’, with the global action in Eq. 1.2.6. Similarly, as for Majorana fermions, we have:

γ^Majorana\displaystyle\hat{\gamma}_{\text{Majorana}} =(0110)F\displaystyle=\quantity( \begin{array}{cc} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{array})_{F} P^Majorana\displaystyle\hat{P}_{\text{Majorana}} =(+100−1).\displaystyle=\quantity( \begin{array}{cc} {+}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{array})\,.

Similarly, as for the incoming (fermion) rishon-operators, we will provide an adequate notion of parity (see Eq. 1.3.30 for SU(2) and Eq. 1.4.13 for U(1)).

1.3 SU(2) Yang-Mills Lattice Gauge Theory

In this section, we apply the dressed-site formalism to a non-Abelian scenario, focusing on the SU(2) Yang-Mills (YM) LGT, including dynamical matter. For simplicity we will focus on a (2+1)D system, where both the electric and magnetic gauge contributions play a non-trivial role. Generalizations to the (3+1)D are trivial, provided to consider the correct phase factors in Eq. 1.1.32 due to staggered fermions. Restrictions to the (1+1)D case are considered in Section 1.3.5 and applied in [528, 578, 438].

1.3.1 The model

Before introducing the SU(2) YM Hamiltonian, let us recall the main properties of the SU(2) gauge theory. First, the SU(2) algebra generators are the Pauli matrices T^a=σ^a/2\hat{T}^{a}=\hat{\sigma}^{a}/2, while the structure constants are equal to the Levi-Civita tensor fa​b​c=εa​b​cf^{abc}=\varepsilon^{abc}. Correspondingly, left/right generators of SU(2) gauge transformations L^𝐧,𝝁/R^𝐧,𝝁\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}/\hat{R}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} are hermitian and related each other as follows: for a,b,c∈{x,y,z}a,b,c\in\quantity{x,y,z}

[L^𝐧,𝝁a,R^𝐧,𝝁b]\displaystyle\quantity[\eleL_{\genlink}^{a},\eleR_{\genlink}^{b}] =0\displaystyle=0 [L^𝐧,𝝁a,L^𝐧′,𝐧′+𝝁′b]\displaystyle\quantity[\eleL_{\genlink}^{a},\eleL^{b}_{\vecsite^{\prime},\vecsite^{\prime}+\latvec'}] =i​δ𝐧​𝐧′​δ𝝁​𝝁′​ϵa​b​c​L^𝐧,𝝁c\displaystyle=i\delta_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{{\bf\it\mu}{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}\epsilon_{abc}\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{c} (same with R^\hat{R}) \displaystyle\,. (1.3.1)

Their trace yields the Casimir operator

E^𝐧,𝝁2=∑aL^𝐧,𝝁a​L^𝐧,𝝁a=∑aR^𝐧,𝝁a​R^𝐧,𝝁a,\hat{E}^{2}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}=\sum_{a}\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}\hat{L}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}=\sum_{a}\hat{R}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}\hat{R}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{a}\,, (1.3.2)

and the commutations rules with the parallel transporter U^α​β\hat{U}^{\alpha\beta} read

[L^a𝐧,𝝁,U^α​β𝐧′,𝝁′]\displaystyle\quantity[\eleL^{a}_{\genlink},\NApara_{\genlinkprime}] =−δ𝐧​𝐧′δ𝝁′∑γσα​γa2U^𝐧,𝝁γ​β,\displaystyle=-\delta_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}\sum_{\gamma}\frac{{\sigma}^{a}_{\alpha\gamma}}{2}\hat{U}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{\gamma\beta}, [R^𝐧,𝝁a,U^𝐧′,𝝁′α​β]\displaystyle[\hat{R}^{a}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}},\hat{U}^{\alpha\beta}_{{\mathbf{n}{\prime},{\bf\it\mu}{\prime}}}] =+δ𝐧​𝐧′δ𝝁​𝝁′∑γU^𝐧,𝝁α​γσγ​βa2.\displaystyle=+\delta_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{{\bf\it\mu}{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}\sum_{\gamma}\hat{U}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}^{\alpha\gamma}\frac{{\sigma}^{a}_{\gamma\beta}}{2}\,. (1.3.3)

Then, when introducing dynamical matter, we focus on single-flavor matter fields with SU(2)-color 1/2, expressed in terms of SU(2)-color staggered (Dirac) fermions ψ^𝐧,α\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha} [583] and satisfying

{ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧′,β}\displaystyle\quantity{\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha}\hpsi_{\vecsite^{\prime},\beta}} =i​ℏ​δ𝐧,𝐧′​δα,β,\displaystyle=i\hbar\delta_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{\alpha,\beta}, where α,β\displaystyle\alpha,\beta ∈{r,g}\displaystyle\in\quantity{\rla,\gla} are SU(2)-colors \displaystyle\,. (1.3.4)

From Eq. 1.2.2 and assuming no background charges, Gauss Law operators are defined as

G^𝐧a\displaystyle\hat{G}^{a}_{\mathbf{n}} =𝒬^𝐧a+∑𝝁(R^𝐧−𝝁,𝐧a+L^𝐧,𝝁a),\displaystyle=\hat{\mathcal{Q}}^{a}_{\mathbf{n}}+\sum_{{\bf\it\mu}}\quantity(\eleR^{a}_{\vecsite-\latvec,\vecsite} + \eleL^{a}_{\genlink})\,, where 𝒬^𝐧a\displaystyle\hat{\mathcal{Q}}^{a}_{\mathbf{n}} =∑α​βψ^𝐧,α†​σα​βa2​ψ^𝐧,β\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha\beta}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\frac{\sigma^{a}_{\alpha\beta}}{2}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\beta} (1.3.5)

rotates the quark field at 𝐧\mathbf{n}, and, if squared, it yields the matter color density, i.e. the quadratic Casimir operator of the matter field gauge group transformations:

S^matt,𝐧2=∑a𝒬^𝐧a​𝒬^𝐧a.\hat{S}^{2}_{\rm{matt},\mathbf{n}}=\sum_{a}\hat{\mathcal{Q}}^{a}_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\mathcal{Q}}^{a}_{\mathbf{n}}. (1.3.6)

Correspondingly, L^𝐧−𝝁,𝐧a\hat{L}^{a}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu},\mathbf{n}} and R^𝐧,𝝁a\hat{R}^{a}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} account for the transformation of the gauge links at its left and its right respectively [565].

Then, the corresponding (2+1)D Hamiltonian with staggered fermions (see Section 1.1.3) reads:
