As for LGTs such as the ones described in Chapter 1 and simulated in Chapters 3 and 4, there is a global U(1) symmetry related to the invariants of the matter fields under rotations ψ^𝐧→ei​θ​ψ^𝐧\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}\to e^{i\theta}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}} and corresponds to the conservation of charge: baryon number for non-Abelian LGTs such as SU(2) Yang Mills in Section 1.3 and electric charge for Abelian ones such as QED in Section 1.4. In the former case, a^𝐧\hat{a}_{\mathbf{n}} corresponds to the baryon number density bb defined in Eq. 3.1.8; in the latter case, a^𝐧=q^𝐧≡ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧−((1)𝐧−1)/2\hat{a}_{\mathbf{n}}=\hat{q}_{\mathbf{n}}\equiv\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}-((1)^{\mathbf{n}}-1)/2 [525, 524, 522]. Due to the aforementioned sign-problem, accessing sectors with finite baryon number density bb or finite electric charge is challenging for MC based algorithms, while being straightforward for ED simulations (by exploiting block diagonalization) [441] or TN methods, where the U(1) sector is directly selected in the TN ansatz, ensuring that the symmetry is preserved throughout the simulation [624, 625, 482, 484].

Momentum conservation

In a QMB system with translational symmetry, as in the case of periodic boundary conditions (PBC), the corresponding Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} is invariant under translations of particle positions or lattice sites. This means shifting all particles or lattice sites by a unit (or a set of units) leaves the physical properties of the system unchanged [623]. For simplicity, let us focus on a 1D lattice, whose sites are labeled by n∈{0,…,N}n\in\quantity{0,\dots,\Nsites}.

We define a translation operator T^\hat{T} which moves every particle from site nn to site n+1n+1, i.e., T^​|n⟩=|n+1⟩\hat{T}\ket{\site}=\ket{\site+1}, with T^N=𝟙\hat{T}^{N}=\mathbb{1}. Due to translational symmetry, T^​H^=H^​T^\hat{T}\hat{H}=\hat{H}\hat{T}, meaning that H^\hat{H} and T^\hat{T} admit a common set of eigenstates. Thanks to Bloch’s theorem, these eigenstates can be expressed as wave functions with a definite momentum, characterized by a wave vector p=2​π​n/Np=2\pi n/N:

|φp⟩=1Nφ​∑n=0Nφ−1e−i​p​n​T^n​|φ⟩,\ket{\varphi_{\mom}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{\varphi}}}\sum_{n=0}^{N_{\varphi}-1}e^{-ipn}\hat{T}^{n}\ket{\varphi}, (2.1.4)

where |φ⟩\ket{\varphi} is a reference state. To construct the momentum basis for given pp, we need a set of reference states resulting in a complete set of normalizable orthogonal states. Clearly, for two states |φp⟩\ket{\varphi_{\mom}} and |φp′⟩\ket{\varphi^{\prime}_{\mom}} to be orthogonal, the corresponding representatives must obey T^r​|φ⟩≠|φ′⟩​∀r∈{1,…,N}\hat{T}^{r}\ket{\varphi}\neq\ket{\varphi^{\prime}}\,\forall r\in\quantity{1,\dots, \Nsites}. Therefore, for each set of translated states {|φ⁡(r)⟩=T^r|φ⟩}\{\ket{\varphi(r)}=\hat{T}^{r}\ket{\varphi}\}, only one of them should be used as a reference state [623]. The normalization factor NφN_{\varphi} in Eq. 2.1.4 takes into account the periodicity of the reference state |φ⟩\ket{\varphi}, which in general could be smaller to NN: T^Nφ​|φ⟩=|φ⟩\hat{T}^{N_{\varphi}}\ket{\varphi}=\ket{\varphi} for some Nφ<NN_{\varphi}<N.

Once we have selected an orthonormal set of reference states, we can build the corresponding momentum basis via Eq. 2.1.4 and express the Hamiltonian as follows:

H^p​p′=⟨ψp|H^|ψp′⟩,\hat{H}_{pp^{\prime}}=\matrixelement{\psi_{\mom}}{\ham}{\psi_{\mom^{\prime}}}, (2.1.5)

where, due to the translational invariance, H^p​p′=0\hat{H}_{pp^{\prime}}=0 for p≠p′p\neq p^{\prime}. Eigenvalues and eigenstates of the Hamiltonian in a particular momentum sector pp are obtained diagonalizing the block H^p​p\hat{H}_{pp}.

When dealing with QMB systems where translational invariance involves a logical basis of Nb>1N^{b}>1 sites, the translational symmetry unit is expanded from a single site to NbN^{b} sites. Correspondingly, we have to update the momentum vetor definition in Eq. 2.1.4 with a normalization factor that matches the total number of unit cells L=NNbL=\frac{N}{N^{b}} or a smaller periodicity LφL_{\varphi}:

|φp⟩=1Lφ​∑n=0Lφ−1e−i​p​n​T^Nb​n​|φ⟩.\ket{\varphi_{\mom}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{L_{\varphi}}}\sum_{n=0}^{L_{\varphi}-1}e^{-ipn}\hat{T}^{N^{b}n}\ket{\varphi}. (2.1.6)

For instance, in LGTs employing the staggered fermion solution, the corresponding Hamiltonian is invariant under translations of two sites along each spatial direction. For instance, ED simulations of the (1+1)D SU(2) Yang-Mills LGT in PBC (see Section 4.4 and [438]) have been obtained in the zero momentum, since the scarred initial states of the dyanmics belong to that sector.

2.1.2 Basic Tensor Operations

Aside by block diagonalization and the use of symmetries, by accurately manipulating the coefficient tensor TT in Eq. 2.1.1, we can further extract a lot of information, such as quantum correlations, entanglement, and few-body observables, sometimes accessing only a portion of all its entries. The main operations which can be performed over Ti1,…,iNT_{i_{1},\dots,i_{N}} involve the indices labelling its links. In particular, it is possible to distinguish among at least three different kinds of operations affecting links: manipulations, contractions, and decompositions. Below, we briefly discuss each of them. For an equivalent pictorial representation, see Fig. 2.2.

Manipulations

Link manipulations involve operations like permutation, which reorders tensor indices, fusion, which combines adjacent links into a single index, and splitting, which breaks down a link into multiple smaller indices.

Link permutation

It reorders the links i1​…​iNi_{1}\dots i_{N} of the tensor TT by moving the link at position ℓ\ell into k=σ⁡(ℓ)k=\sigma(\ell) of the permuted tensor T[p]T^{[p]}:

Tiσ⁡(1)​…​iσ⁡(N)[p]=Ti1​…​iN.T^{[p]}_{i_{\sigma(1)}\dots i_{\sigma(N)}}=T_{i_{1}\dots i_{N}}. (2.1.7)
Link fusion

It combines m−k+1m-k+1 adjacent links (ik​…​imi_{k}\dots i_{m}) of dimensions (dk​…​dm)(d_{k}\dots d_{m}) into a fused link jj defined as follows:

j=fuse​(ik​…​im)=1+∑r=km(ir−1)∏j=1r−kdjwherej∈𝕁=𝟙k×⋯×𝟙m=1+(ik−1)​dk0+(ik+1−1)​dk+1+⋯+(im−1)​dmm−k.\begin{split}j=\text{fuse}(i_{k}\dots i_{m})&=1+\sum_{r=k}^{m}(i_{r}-1)\prod_{j=1}^{r-k}d_{j}\quad\text{where}\quad j\in\mathbb{J}=\mathbb{1}_{k}\times\dots\times\mathbb{1}_{m}\\ &=1+(i_{k}-1)d_{k}^{0}+(i_{k+1}-1)d_{k+1}+\dots+(i_{m}-1)d^{m-k}_{m}.\end{split} (2.1.8)
Link splitting

It replaces a given link kk with index jkj_{k} and dimension dkd_{k} with m−k+1m-k+1 links ik​…​imi_{k}\dots i_{m} of dimensions dk′​…​dm′d_{k^{\prime}}\dots d_{m^{\prime}} such that dk=dk′×⋯×dm′d_{k}=d_{k^{\prime}}\times\dots\times d_{m^{\prime}}:

Ti1​…​ik−1​(ik+1​…​im)​im+1​…​iN′=Ti1​…​ik−1,jk,im+1​…​iN.T^{\prime}_{i_{1}\dots i_{k-1}(i_{k+1}\dots i_{m})i_{m+1}\dots i_{N}}=T_{i_{1}\dots i_{k-1},\;j_{k},\;i_{m+1}\dots i_{N}}. (2.1.9)

Link fusion and splitting are very useful for decomposing large tensors into manageable parts.

Contractions

Whenever two tensors A and B, with links {a1,…​an}\quantity{a_{1},\dots a_{n}} and {b1​…​bm}\quantity{b_{1}\dots b_{m}} of dimensions respectively {d1​…​nA}\quantity{d^{A}_{1\dots n}} and {d1​…​mB}\quantity{d^{B}_{1\dots m}}, have a set of kk common links sjs_{j} (where {dn−k+jA}={djB}={djs}\{d^{A}_{n-k+j}\}=\{d^{B}_{j}\}=\{d^{s}_{j}\} for j=1​…​kj=1\dots k), we can contract them over {s1​…​sk}\quantity{s_{1}\dots s_{k}}, obtaining a single tensor C:

Ca​b​=s​p​l​i​t​Ca1,…​an−k​bk+1​…​bm=∑s1​…​skAa1,…​an−k​s1​…​sk​Bs1​…​sk​bk+1​…​bm​=f​u​s​e​∑sAa​s​Bs​b,C_{ab}\underset{split}{=}C_{a_{1},\dots a_{n-k}b_{k+1}\dots b_{m}}=\sum_{s_{1}\dots s_{k}}A_{a_{1},\dots a_{n-k}s_{1}\dots s_{k}}B_{s_{1}\dots s_{k}b_{k+1}\dots b_{m}}\underset{fuse}{=}\sum_{s}A_{as}B_{sb}\,, (2.1.10)

where in the 1s​t1^{st} and in the 3r​d3^{rd} equalities we exploited the link splitting and fusing operations respectively, obtaining the single links ss, aa, and bb, with dimensions respectively:

ds\displaystyle d_{s} =d1s×⋯×dks\displaystyle=d_{1}^{s}\times\dots\times d_{k}^{s} da\displaystyle d_{a} =d1a×⋯×dn−ka\displaystyle=d_{1}^{a}\times\dots\times d_{n-k}^{a} db\displaystyle d_{b} =dk+1b×⋯×dmb.\displaystyle=d_{k+1}^{b}\times\dots\times d_{m}^{b}. (2.1.11)
Decompositions

A tensor decomposition replaces a single input tensor with two or more output tensors, connected through a certain number of auxiliary links; correspondingly, it preserves with a given distribution, all the physical links of the input tensor. To perform a decomposition we need to:

  1. 1.

    choose a bipartition of the physical links of the input tensor TT: (i1​…​ir)​(ir+1​…​iN)(i_{1}\dots i_{r})\;(i_{r+1}\dots i_{N}).

  2. 2.

    fuse these latter into two single row and column links: T(i1​…​ir)​(ir+1​…​iN)=Ta​bT_{(i_{1}\dots i_{r})(i_{r+1}\dots i_{N})}=T_{ab}

  3. 3.

    decompose the obtained tensor into two factor matrices and (eventually) a diagonal one:

    Ta​b=∑k=1dkAa​k​λk​Bk​b;T_{ab}=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{k}}A_{ak}\lambda_{k}B_{kb}; (2.1.12)
  4. 4.

    split the links initially fused to restore the initial network geometry.:

    T(i1​…​iN)=∑kA(i1​…​ir),k​λk​Bk,(ir+1​…​iN).T_{(i_{1}\dots i_{N})}=\sum_{k}A_{(i_{1}\dots i_{r}),k}\lambda_{k}B_{k,(i_{r+1}\dots i_{N})}. (2.1.13)

Noticeable examples are the QR decomposition and the SVD decomposition.

QR decomposition

We can split TT into two tensors, namely QQ and RR:

T(i1​…​ir)​(ir+1​…​iN)=Ta​b​=QR​∑k=1dkQa​k​Rk​b=∑k=1dkQ(i1​…​ir)​k​Rk⁡(ir+1​…​iN).T_{(i_{1}\dots i_{r})(i_{r+1}\dots i_{N})}=T_{ab}\underset{\rm{QR}}{=}\sum_{k=1}^{d_{k}}Q_{ak}R_{kb}=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{k}}Q_{(i_{1}\dots i_{r})k}R_{k(i_{r+1}\dots i_{N})}. (2.1.14)

The matrix Rk​bR_{kb} is an upper trapezoidal matrix, whereas Qa​kQ_{ak} is a semi-unitary matrix w.r.t. kk, that is ∑aQa​k​Qa​k′∗=δk​k′\sum_{a}Q_{ak}Q^{*}_{ak^{\prime}}=\delta_{kk^{\prime}}. The minimal dimension dkd_{k} is such that

dk=min⁡{a,b}=min⁡{(i1⋅⋯⋅ir),(ir+1⋅⋯⋅iN)}.d_{k}=\min\quantity{a,b}=\min\quantity{(i_{1}\cdot\dots\cdot i_{r}),(i_{r+1}\cdot\dots\cdot i_{\Nsites})}. (2.1.15)
Singular value decomposition (SVD)

In this case, we split TT into three tensors:

T(i1​…​ir)​(ir+1​…​iN)=Ta​b​=SVD​∑k=1dkSa​k​Vk​k​Dk​b=∑k=1dkSa​k​λk​Dk​b=∑k=1dkS(i1​…​ir)​k​λk​Dk⁡(ir+1​…​iN),T_{(i_{1}\dots i_{r})(i_{r+1}\dots i_{N})}=T_{ab}\underset{\rm{SVD}}{=}\sum_{k=1}^{d_{k}}S_{ak}V_{kk}D_{kb}=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{k}}S_{ak}\lambda_{k}D_{kb}=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{k}}S_{(i_{1}\dots i_{r})k}\lambda_{k}D_{k(i_{r+1}\dots i_{N})}, (2.1.16)

where VV is a diagonal and positive real matrix, whereas SS and DD are semi unitary matrices (S†​S=𝟙=D​D†S^{\dagger}S=\mathbb{1}=DD^{\dagger}). This decomposition is quite useful to mention the possibility of truncation for an index. Indeed, since the diagonal elements of V are real, positive, and hence lower bounded from below by 0, they can be ordered (for instance) in descending order:

[V11=λ1≥V22=λ2​⋯≥0].\quantity[V_{11}=\lambda_{1}\geq V_{22}=\lambda_{2}\dots\geq 0]. (2.1.17)

Moreover, if λk<ϵ\lambda_{k}<\epsilon ∀k>χ\forall k>\chi for χ∈{1,…,dk}\chi\in\quantity{1,\dots, d_{k}}, it is possible to disregard some of the singular values λk\lambda_{k} with a precision ϵ\epsilon. In other words, whenever the singular values decay fast enough after some λχ\lambda_{\chi}, we can neglect them. Correspondingly, the matrices SS and DD can be truncated, and dkd_{k} reduced to χ\chi. Such a reduction introduces an error in the original representation of the tensor Ti​jT_{ij}, which can be estimated as follows:

‖Ti​j−∑k=1χSi​k​λk​Dk​j‖=‖∑k=m+1dkSi​k​λk​Dk​j‖<∑k=χ+1dk‖Si​k​Dk​j‖<ϵ​C\norm{\tensor_{ij}-\sum_{k=1}^{\chi}S_{ik}\lambda_{k}D_{kj}}=\norm{\sum_{k=m+1}^{d_{k}}S_{ik}\lambda_{k}D_{kj}}<\sum_{k=\chi+1}^{d_{k}}\norm{S_{ik}D_{kj}}<\epsilon C (2.1.18)

for a finite constant C. As we will see in Section 2.2, in the context of Tensor Networks, the parameter χ\chi will correspond to the bond dimension.

Schmidt Decomposition

Let us consider a bipartition according to which the first NAN_{A} particles belong to a subsystem AA with Hilbert space ℋA=⨂k=1NAℋk\mathcal{H}_{A}=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{N_{A}}\mathcal{H}_{k}, whereas, the remaining NB=N−NAN_{B}=N-N_{A} particles belong to the subsystem BB with Hilbert space ℋB=⨂k=1NBℋk\mathcal{H}_{B}=\bigotimes_{k=1}^{N_{B}}\mathcal{H}_{k}; globally, we have ℋ=ℋA⊗ℋB\mathcal{H}=\mathcal{H}_{A}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{B}. Assuming all system sites with the same dd-dimensional Hilbert space, i.e. dimℋk=d​∀k\dim\mathcal{H}_{k}=d\,\forall k, then the QMB state and its coefficient tensor can be arranged as a linear superposition of products of states of the two sub-partitions:

|ΨQMB⟩=∑n=1NA∑m=1NBCn​m​|an⟩​|bm⟩,\ket{\psiqmb}=\sum_{n=1}^{N_{A}}\sum_{m=1}^{N_{B}}C_{nm}\ket{a_{n}}\ket{b_{m}}\,, (2.1.19)

where {|an⟩}n=1NA∈ℋA\quantity{\ket{a_{n}}}_{n=1}^{N_{A}}\in\mathcal{H}_{A} and {|bm⟩}m=1NB∈ℋB\quantity{\ket{b_{m}}}_{m=1}^{N_{B}}\in\mathcal{H}_{B} are orthonormal basis of A and B. The corresponding density matrix ρ\rho associated to (2.1.19) reads

ρ=|ΨQMB⟩​⟨ΨQMB|=∑n,n′∑m,m′Cn​m​Cn′​m′∗​|an⟩​|bm⟩​⟨an′|​⟨bm′|=∑n,n′∑m,m′ρn​mn′​m′​|an⟩​⟨an′|⊗|bm⟩​⟨bm′|,\begin{split}\rho=\ket{\psiqmb}\bra{\psiqmb}&=\sum_{n,n^{\prime}}\sum_{m,m^{\prime}}C_{nm}C^{*}_{n^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\ket{a_{n}}\ket{b_{m}}\bra{a_{n^{\prime}}}\bra{b_{m^{\prime}}}\\ &=\sum_{n,n^{\prime}}\sum_{m,m^{\prime}}\rho_{nm}^{n^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\ket{a_{n}}\bra{a_{n^{\prime}}}\otimes\ket{b_{m}}\bra{b_{m^{\prime}}}\,,\end{split} (2.1.20)

where we grouped the coefficient matrix Cn​mC_{nm} and its complex conjugate Cn′​m′∗C^{*}_{n^{\prime}m^{\prime}} into a single 4−4-order coefficient tensor ρn​mn′​m′\rho_{nm}^{n^{\prime}m^{\prime}}. The reduced density matrix of subsystem A is then given by tracing ρ\rho over all the states of B:

ρA=∑ℓ=1NB⟨bℓ|ρ|bℓ⟩=∑n,n′∑ℓ∑m,m′ρn​mn′​m′​|an⟩​⟨an′|⊗⟨bℓ|bm⟩​⟨bm′|bℓ⟩=∑n,n′=1NA∑ℓ=1NBρn​ℓn′​ℓ​|an⟩​⟨an′|,\begin{split}\rho_{A}=\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_{B}}\matrixelement{b_{\ell}}{\rho}{b_{\ell}}&=\sum_{n,n^{\prime}}\sum_{\ell}\sum_{m,m^{\prime}}\rho_{nm}^{n^{\prime}m^{\prime}}\ket{a_{n}}\bra{a_{n^{\prime}}}\otimes\innerproduct{b_{\ell}}{b_{m}}\innerproduct{b_{m^{\prime}}}{b_{\ell}}\\ &=\sum_{n,n^{\prime}=1}^{N_{A}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_{B}}\rho_{n\ell}^{n^{\prime}\ell}\ket{a_{n}}\bra{a_{n^{\prime}}}\,,\end{split} (2.1.21)

where we recall the partial trace not to depend on the choice of the basis of the partition we trace out. Then, if λ1,λ2,…​λNA\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\dots\lambda_{N_{A}} are the eigenvalues of ρA\rho_{A} and |α1⟩​…​|αNA⟩\ket{\alpha_{1}}\dots\ket{\alpha_{\Nsites_{A}}} are the corresponding eigenvectors, we can rewrite |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} in terms of {|αn⟩}n=1NA\quantity{\ket{\alpha_{n}}}_{n=1}^{N_{A}} as follows:

|ΨQMB⟩=∑n,m𝒞n​m​|αn⟩​|bm⟩,\ket{\psiqmb}=\sum_{n,m}\mathcal{C}_{nm}\ket{\alpha_{n}}\ket{b_{m}}\,, (2.1.22)

where 𝒞n​m\mathcal{C}_{nm} is a new coefficient tensor. We can then build up a new basis also for the subsystem B, in such a way that each vector is a clever superposition of vectors of the old basis:

|βk⟩=∑m=1NB𝒞k​mλk​|bm⟩.\ket{\beta_{k}}=\sum_{m=1}^{N_{B}}\frac{\mathcal{C}_{km}}{\lambda_{k}}\ket{b_{m}}. (2.1.23)

Since the matrix 𝒞k​m/λk\mathcal{C}_{km}/\lambda_{k} is unitary for each kk, then {|βk⟩}\quantity{\ket{\beta_{k}}} is an orthonormal basis, and we can rewrite (2.1.19) and (2.1.20) in terms of the Schmidt decomposition:

|ΨQMB⟩=∑n,m𝒞n​m​|αn⟩​|bm⟩=∑nλn​|αn⟩​|βn⟩ρ=∑n,mλn​λm∗​|αn⟩​⟨αm|⊗|βn⟩​⟨βm|.\ket{\psiqmb}=\sum_{n,m}\mathcal{C}_{nm}\ket{\alpha_{n}}\ket{b_{m}}=\sum_{n}\lambda_{n}\ket{\alpha_{n}}\ket{\beta_{n}}\qquad\rho=\sum_{n,m}\lambda_{n}\lambda^{*}_{m}\ket{\alpha_{n}}\bra{\alpha_{m}}\otimes\ket{\beta_{n}}\bra{\beta_{m}}. (2.1.24)

It is then clear that both the reduced density matrices ρA\rho_{A} and ρB\rho_{B} are diagonal in the Schmidt basis, and display the same positive spectrum:

ρA=∑q⟨βq|ρ|βq⟩=∑n,m∑qλn​λm∗​⟨βq|βn⟩​|αn⟩​⟨αm|​⟨βm|βq⟩\displaystyle\rho_{A}=\sum_{q}\matrixelement{\beta_{q}}{\rho}{\beta_{q}}=\sum_{n,m}\sum_{q}\lambda_{n}\lambda_{m}^{*}\bra{\beta_{q}}\ket{\beta_{n}}\ket{\alpha_{n}}\bra{\alpha_{m}}\bra{\beta_{m}}\ket{\beta_{q}} =∑q|λq|2​|αq⟩​⟨αq|\displaystyle=\sum_{q}\absolutevalue{\lambda_{q}}^{2}\ket{\alpha_{q}}\bra{\alpha_{q}} (2.1.25a)
ρB=∑k⟨αk|ρ|αk⟩\displaystyle\rho_{B}=\sum_{k}\matrixelement{\alpha_{k}}{\rho}{\alpha_{k}} =∑k|λk|2​|βk⟩​⟨βk|.\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\absolutevalue{\lambda_{k}}^{2}\ket{\beta_{k}}\bra{\beta_{k}}. (2.1.25b)

Such a Schmidt decomposition is very exploitable when computing quantum correlations between bipartitions of a system in a pure state. Conversely, it reveal useless for multipartite descriptions or when applied to mixed states, where no expression in terms of single partitions is available.

Physical perspective

What may appear as just a series of algebraic or technical manipulations on purely mathematical objects, is firmly connected to the control of quantum correlations and entanglement in a QMB system [626, 627]. From a purely physical perspective, if the coefficient tensor T(i1​…​iN)T_{(i_{1}\dots i_{N})} describes the state of a NN-body system, then, every decomposition or contraction allows to move from a many-body description (with a single large tensor), to a single site or partite description (made of several small physical tensors) and the other way around, with eventual intermediate steps. The auxiliary link kk along which decompositions/contractions are performed deserves special regard: in absence of loops in the TN structure, its dimension dkd_{k} quantifies the number of shared degrees of freedom between the arisen subsystems (e.g. QR in Eq. 2.1.15, SVD in Eq. 2.1.16, or Schmidt in Eq. 2.1.24 decompositions). In turn, these shared d.o.f. provide the amount of quantum correlations through which the partitions are mutually entangled. Therefore, the larger the truncation performed on dk→χd_{k}\to\chi (see Eq. 2.1.18), the smaller the entanglement between the partition we keep in track. For instance, exploiting the entanglement entropy [485], we have:

𝒮A=−∑k=1χλklogλk.\mathcal{S}_{A}=-\sum_{k=1}^{\chi}\lambda_{k}\log\lambda_{k}. (2.1.26)

2.1.3 Entanglement area law

As anticipated in Section 2.1, ED simulations of a QMB system, even resolving all its symmetries, are not feasible for a large number system size NN, as the total Hilbert space grows exponentially with NN. Nonetheless, a great variety of natural QMB systems happens to be described by ground and thermal equilibrium states that own little-to-moderate entanglement content. The physical states of these systems live in a small corner of the total Hilbert space, which can be efficiently targeted and parameterized without the exponential cost required by an exact representation.

This property is formally described as entanglement area law, fulfilled by low-energy states of local QMB Hamiltonians [485]: the entanglement between a partition of the system and the rest is proportional to the area of the boundary between them, instead of its volume, as happens for the majority of states in the Hilbert space. Thus, a state obeying area law contains much fewer quantum correlations than expected for a generic (or random) QMB state22 2 Small corrections to the area law exist for instance close to a transition point for one-dimensional quantum systems (logarithmic corrections). However, the entanglement remains overall moderate [628].. From a theoretical point of view, the entanglement area law has been rigorously proven for (i) one-dimensional gapped local Hamiltonians, where the locality means that a lattice site interacts only with neighboring sites, without two-body all-to-all interactions [629, 630, 631]; (ii) for quantum states at thermal equilibrium, independently from the dimensionality of the system [632]. Even though rigorous proof for QMB systems in higher dimensions is lacking, several numerical and phenomenological shreds of evidence suggest that area law still holds in the presence of local interactions [633, 634, 485, 635, 494].

2.2 Tensor Networks Methods

We are then ready to present a general overview of Tensor Networks (TN), which are based on controlled wave-function variational ansätze exploiting the area-law entanglement bounds satisfied by locally interacting QMB systems. Thus, TN admit an efficient representation of the low-energy sectors contributing to the equilibrium properties and (low-entangled) time evolution [485], without suffering from the aforementioned sign problem [622]. Before looking at specific TN realizations, it is convenient to provide the general idea behind a TN geometry.

2.2.1 Tensor Network state

The area law described in Section 2.1.3 has important implications on the numerical simulation of QMB models: indeed, for ground-states and first excited states of local Hamiltonians where the entanglement content is low-to-moderate, it is possible to obtain an approximate but efficient representation capable of describing the main properties of these states [485]. TNs give a natural language for this representation, by replacing the complete rank-NN tensor Ti1,…,iNT_{i_{1},\dots,i_{N}} of Eq. 2.1.1 with a chain of QQ smaller tensors T[q]T^{[q]} with q∈{1,…,Q}q\in\quantity{1,\dots,Q} connected via auxiliary links {α}q\quantity{\alpha}_{q}:

Ti1​…​iN=∑α1,…​αLT{i}1,{α}1[1]​T{i}2,{α}2[2]​…​T{i}Q,{α}Q[Q].T_{i_{1}\dots i_{N}}=\sum_{\alpha_{1},\dots\alpha_{L}}T^{[1]}_{\quantity{i}_{1},\quantity{\alpha}_{1}}T^{[2]}_{\quantity{i}_{2},\quantity{\alpha}_{2}}\dots T^{[Q]}_{\quantity{i}_{Q},\quantity{\alpha}_{Q}}. (2.2.1)

Each sigle tensor T[q]T^{[q]} has a set of physical indices {i}q\{i\}_{q} of dimension dd (one for each lattice site), whereas the dimension of the auxiliary indices {α}q\quantity{\alpha}_{q} is upper bounded by a control parameter χ\chi that is called maximal bond dimension.

The advantage of passing from the exact representation of Eq. 2.1.1 to a TN representation like Eq. 2.2.1 is that the number of TN parameters is of the order O⁡(poly⁡(d)​poly​(N)​poly​(χ))O(\mathrm{poly}(d)\mathrm{poly}(N)\mathrm{poly}(\chi)), e.g., 𝒪⁡(N​χ​max⁡(χ,d)2)\mathcal{O}(N\chi\max(\chi,d)^{2}) for the TTN [440]. The scaling with the system size and consequently the computational complexity is now polynomial and not exponential, as in the exact representation of the QMB state. It is worth noting that the bond dimension χ\chi determines the degree of entanglement and quantum correlations encoded in the TN. Namely, for χ=1\chi=1, the TN describes a separable state (product state, no entanglement), whereas one recovers the exact but inefficient representation in the limit χ≲dN\chi{\lesssim}d^{N} assuming the system to be strongly entangled. Tuning χ\chi properly allows interpolating between these two extreme regimes, efficiently reproducing the entanglement of the quantum state by exploiting decompositions like Schmidt/QR/SVD discussed in Section 2.1.2 [495, 484]. For example, dynamical problems characterized by a slow entanglement entropy growth, as in the many-body scars dynamics observed in Section 4.4, can be efficiently and accurately described by MPS ansatz with small or intermediate bond dimensions [481, 490].

Gauge invariance

More in general, the employment of auxiliary links clearly adds in the TN state some information redundancy with respect to the quantum state it describes. Such a redundancy corresponds to a set of linear transformations of the TN, which leave the quantum state unchanged. We usually refer to these transformations as gauge transformations, as they corresponds to local and invertible manipulations on the auxiliary TN links {α}q\quantity{\alpha}_{q} without affecting the physical degrees of freedom.

To give an example, let us focus on the following portion of Eq. 2.2.1

T[q+q′]{i},{i′}=∑αηT[q]{i},{α}|η,αηT[q′]{i′},{α′}|η,αη,T^{\quantity[q+q^{\prime}]}_{\quantity{i},\quantity{i^{\prime}}}=\sum_{\alpha_{\eta}}T^{[q]}_{\quantity{i},\quantity{\alpha}_{|_{\eta}},\alpha_{\eta}}T^{[q^{\prime}]}_{\quantity{i^{\prime}},\quantity{\alpha^{\prime}}_{|_{\eta}},\alpha_{\eta}}, (2.2.2)

where {α}|η\quantity{\alpha}_{|_{\eta}} collects the auxiliary links of the tensor except for η\eta connecting the nodes qq and q′q^{\prime} with dimension χη\chi_{\eta}. Then, given a χη′×χη\chi^{\prime}_{\eta}\times\chi_{\eta} left-invertible matrix Yαη​αη′Y_{\alpha_{\eta}\alpha^{\prime}_{\eta}}, such that

∑α′(Y−1)α​α′​Yα′​α′′=δα​α′′≠∑α′Yα​α′​(Y−1)α′​α′′,\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}}\big(Y^{-1}\big)_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}Y_{\alpha^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime\prime}}=\delta_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime\prime}}\neq\sum_{\alpha^{\prime}}Y_{\alpha\alpha^{\prime}}\big(Y^{-1}\big)_{\alpha^{\prime}\alpha^{\prime\prime}}, (2.2.3)

the TN state in Eq. 2.2.2 is left unchanged if the tensors T[q]T^{[q]} and T[q′]T^{[q^{\prime}]} transform as follows:

T[q]{i},{α}|η,αη\displaystyle T^{[q]}_{\quantity{i},\quantity{\alpha}_{|_{\eta}},\alpha_{\eta}} ⟶T~[q]{i},{α}|η,αη=∑βYαη​bηT[q]{i},{α}|η,bη\displaystyle\longrightarrow\tilde{T}^{[q]}_{\quantity{i},\quantity{\alpha}_{|_{\eta}},\alpha_{\eta}}=\sum_{\beta}Y_{\alpha_{\eta}b_{\eta}}T^{[q]}_{\quantity{i},\quantity{\alpha}_{|_{\eta}},b_{\eta}} (2.2.4)
T[q′]{i′},{α′}|η,αη\displaystyle T^{[q^{\prime}]}_{\quantity{i^{\prime}},\quantity{\alpha^{\prime}}_{|_{\eta}},\alpha_{\eta}} ⟶T~[q′]{i′},{α′}|η,αη=∑γ(Y−1)αη​γηT[q′]{i′},{α′}|η,γη.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\tilde{T}^{[q^{\prime}]}_{\quantity{i^{\prime}},\quantity{\alpha^{\prime}}_{|_{\eta}},\alpha_{\eta}}=\sum_{\gamma}\big(Y^{-1}\big)_{\alpha_{\eta}\gamma_{\eta}}T^{[q^{\prime}]}_{\quantity{i^{\prime}},\quantity{\alpha^{\prime}}_{|_{\eta}},\gamma_{\eta}}.

Overall, these contractions on the two edges of the link η\eta leaves the composite tensor T[q+q′]T^{\quantity[q+q^{\prime}]} in Eq. 2.2.2 invariated. Therefore, since the state |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} in Eq. 2.2.1 depends on T[q]T^{\quantity[q]} and T[q′]T^{\quantity[q^{\prime}]} via T[q+q′]T^{\quantity[q+q^{\prime}]}, it is insensitive to such a transformation. The intrinsic presence of gauge invariances arising from the TN prescription is going to be numerically exploited when contracting |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} with its corresponding ⟨ΨQMB|\bra{\psiqmb} through the Hamiltonian or other many-body operators.

2.2.2 Loopless Tensor Networks ansätze

The most widely used TN architectures are represented in Fig. 2.3. For 1D systems, Matrix Product States (MPS) [636, 488, 495, 637, 487] represent the landmark of TN simulations, and are largely employed for Density Matrix Renormalization Group’s (DMRG) techniques [638, 639]. Beyond one dimension, there are Projected Entangled Pair States (PEPS) [501, 481, 640, 502, 499, 500, 641], Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) [506, 484, 504, 505] and Multi-scale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz (MERA) [508, 509, 642].

In this thesis, we focus on TTNs, which together with MPS, are loopless Tensor Networks [484], a special class of TN geometries which have found increasing applications for QMB and LGT simulations on finite lattices [481, 482, 436, 643, 511, 512, 541, 571, 535, 524, 525, 437]. Of course, the main concepts and ideas of these two ansätze can be easily generalized and applied to other TN structures, such as PEPS or MERA, which we briefly outline in Section 2.2.5.

Loopless Tensor Network attributes

Before exploring MPS and TTN geometries, it is convenient to review all the TN attributes linked to an intrinsic loopless geometry, which hold for the all the loopless TN realizations. As the name says, loopless TNs can be thought as network graphs which contain no circles among the single tensors. The main consequences of the absence of loops for TNs are the followings: first, they can exploit the full power of gauge transformations in Eq. 2.2.4, reducing the number of needed contractions and enhancing the computational speed. Secondly, the maximal entanglement between two given subsystems of the TN depends on the chosen bipartition of the system, and hence on the bond dimension χ\chi of the auxiliary link over which the bipartition is performed. Such a feature is known as entanglement clustering [619]. More in detail, any loopless TN geometry admits the following attributes.

A distance

d​i​s​t​(a,b)dist(a,b) between two tensor nodes a,ba,b of the network: it corresponds to the number of links encountered along the shortest path between them. For a loopless TN, such a path is unique: all the nodes which share the same distance dd w.r.t. a central node cc form a level L⁡(d,c)L(d;c). This gives the loopless TN geometry a well defined layered structure w.r.t. each tensor.

A bipartition

of the QMB system: every (auxiliary) link η\eta between two nodes qq and q′q^{\prime} induces a bipartition of state of the whole model. The Hilbert states of the two partitions are spanned by the canonical basis states

{|is⟩:d​i​s​t​(s,q)<d​i​s​t​(s,q′)}and{|is⟩:d​i​s​t​(s,q)>d​i​s​t​(s,q′)}\quantity{\ket{i_{s}}: dist(s,q)<dist(s,q^{\prime})}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\quantity{\ket{i_{s}}: dist(s,q)>dist(s,q^{\prime})} (2.2.5)

respectively, that is by fusing all links ss ultimately connected either to qq or q′q^{\prime} once removed the bipartition link from the network. Then, if A and B are the resulting TN subportions, we can rewrite any pure state |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} using the Schmidt decomposition in Eq. 2.1.24:

|ΨQMB⟩=∑k=1χη|Ak⟩​|Bk⟩​λk\ket{\psiqmb}=\sum_{k=1}^{\chi_{\eta}}\ket{A_{k}}\ket{B_{k}}\lambda_{k} (2.2.6)

for λk\lambda_{k} sorted in a descending order. In these terms, a loopless TN can be seen as a simultaneous Schmidt decomposition over all the auxiliary links. For each network bipartition over a link η\eta, the bond dimension χη\chi_{\eta} provides an upper bound to the Schmidt rank, which in turn contributes to define the bipartite entanglement between the two subsystems (see Eq. 2.1.26). Obviously, the larger the bond dimension, the larger is the amount of quantum correlations encoded by the TN structure for the given bipartition. In these terms, by exploiting the SVD in Eq. 2.1.16, it is possible to reduce the dimension of the auxiliary link η\eta simply by discarding the smallest values λk\lambda_{k} and truncating the sum up to a given threshold χη′\chi_{\eta}^{\prime}, obtaining a truncated state:

|ΨQMBtrunc⟩\displaystyle\ket{\psiqmb^{\rm{trunc}}} =1𝒩k​e​p​t​∑k=1χη′|Ak⟩​|Bk⟩​λk,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\mathcal{N}_{kept}}\sum_{k=1}^{\chi_{\eta}^{\prime}}\ket{A_{k}}\ket{B_{k}}\lambda_{k}, where\displaystyle\rm{where} 𝒩k​e​p​t\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{kept} ≡∑k=1χη′λk.\displaystyle\equiv\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{\chi_{\eta}^{\prime}}\lambda_{k}}. (2.2.7)

The error provided by the truncation, is estimated as in Eq. 2.1.18.

The the computational complexity of a given TN ansatz is then expressed as a polynomial function of the maximal bond dimension χ=maxη⁡χη\chi=\max_{\eta}\chi_{\eta} among all the TN auxiliary links, which represents the maximal level of entanglement between any two partitions formed over an auxiliary link. In these terms loopless TN ansätze display a smother scalings (𝒪⁡(χ3)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{3}) for MPS and 𝒪⁡(χ4)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{4}) for TTN) w.r.t. PEPS [495] or MERA [507], where the presence of loops strongly increase computational costs, at least with 𝒪⁡(χ8)\mathcal{O}(\chi^{8}).

Gauges in loopless Tensor Networks

The absence of loops in the TN geometry allows for a strong speed up of tensor contractions between the network and its conjugate (like the ones in expectation values ⟨ΨQMB|​O​|ΨQMB⟩\bra{\psiqmb}{O}\ket{\psiqmb} for any observable OO) by installing and exploiting gauge transformations like Eq. 2.2.4.

Among all the possible choices of local symmetries, we select the unitary gauge, which will be exploited in the ground state search algorithm of Section 2.4. The unitary gauge is defined w.r.t. a single node T[c]T^{[c]} of the TN, named current gauge center. Starting from nodes of maximal distance d=dm​a​xd=d_{max} from T[c]T^{[c]}, we can install unitary gauges on each level {L(d;c):d=1⋯dm​a​x}\quantity{L(d;c):\; d=1\cdots d_{max}} of the network as follows:

  1. 1.

    for each node q∈L⁡(d,c)q\in L(d;c), perform a QR decomposition with respect to the link η\eta which leads towards the center node cc (see Fig. 2.4a):

    T[q]{s}{α}|η,αη=∑bη=1χηQ[q]{s}{α}|η,bηR[q]bη​αη.T^{[q]}_{\quantity{s}\quantity{\alpha}_{|_{\eta}},\alpha_{\eta}}=\sum_{b_{\eta}=1}^{\chi_{\eta}}Q^{[q]}_{\quantity{s}\quantity{\alpha}_{|_{\eta}},b_{\eta}}R^{[q]}_{b_{\eta}\alpha_{\eta}}. (2.2.8)
  2. 2.

    update T[q]⟶T~[q]≡Q[q]T^{[q]}\longrightarrow\tilde{T}^{[q]}\equiv Q^{[q]} with the semi unitary isometry of the QR decomposition, and contract the upper trapezoidal matrix C[η]≡R[q]C^{[\eta]}\equiv R^{[q]} over the corresponding auxiliary link η\eta into the adjacent tensor T[q′]T^{[q^{\prime}]} from the inner layer L⁡(d−1,c)L(d-1;c) (see Fig. 2.4a). Do it for all the nodes of the level L⁡(d,c)L(d;c).

  3. 3.

    advance inwards d⟶d−1d\longrightarrow d-1 and repeat the previous steps for all the tensors of L⁡(d−1,c)L(d-1;c), up to reach d=1d=1 (see Fig. 2.4b). Notice that this iterative procedure implements a global gauge transformation which does not change the physical state of the network. The computational complexity of such a proceeding (QR decompositions plus R contractions over auxiliary links) is dominated by the QR decomposition ∼𝒪⁡(χZ+1)\sim\mathcal{O}(\chi^{Z+1}), where Z is the maximal number of links of a single tensor in the network (maximal degree of a tensor).

  4. 4.

    move the center from a node cc to a node c′c^{\prime}. This corresponds to the implementation of steps 1 and 2 for each node along the path connecting cc to c′c^{\prime}. Obviously, the non unitary matrix C[η]C^{[\eta]} out coming from the QR decomposition of a node close to cc has to be contracted with the next node on the path towards c′c^{\prime}. For example, if c=q1c=q_{1} and c′=q3c^{\prime}=q_{3} as in Fig. 2.4c, we should have the following steps

    T[q1]{s1}{α1}|ηαη⟶QR∑αηT~[q1]{s1}{α1}|ηαηC[η]αη​bη\displaystyle T^{[q_{1}]}_{\quantity{s_{1}}\quantity{\alpha_{1}}_{|_{\eta}}\alpha_{\eta}}\underset{\rm{QR}}{\longrightarrow}\sum_{\alpha_{\eta}}\tilde{T}^{[q_{1}]}_{\quantity{s_{1}}\quantity{\alpha_{1}}_{|_{\eta}}\alpha_{\eta}}C^{[\eta]}_{\alpha_{\eta}b_{\eta}} (2.2.9)
    ∑bηC[η]αη​bηT[q2]{s2}{α2}|η,η∗bηαη∗⟶T[q2]{s2}{α2}|η,η∗αηαη∗\displaystyle\sum_{b_{\eta}}C^{[\eta]}_{\alpha_{\eta}b_{\eta}}T^{[q_{2}]}_{\quantity{s_{2}}\quantity{\alpha_{2}}_{|_{\eta,\eta^{*}}}b_{\eta}\alpha_{\eta^{*}}}\longrightarrow T^{[q_{2}]}_{\quantity{s_{2}}\quantity{\alpha_{2}}_{|_{\eta,\eta^{*}}}\alpha_{\eta}\alpha_{\eta^{*}}}
    T[q2]{s2}{α2}|η∗αη∗⟶QR∑αη∗T~[q2]{s2}{α2}|η∗αη∗C[η∗]αη∗​bη∗\displaystyle T^{[q_{2}]}_{\quantity{s_{2}}\quantity{\alpha_{2}}_{|_{\eta^{*}}}\alpha_{\eta^{*}}}\underset{\rm{QR}}{\longrightarrow}\sum_{\alpha_{\eta^{*}}}\tilde{T}^{[q_{2}]}_{\quantity{s_{2}}\quantity{\alpha_{2}}_{|_{\eta^{*}}}\alpha_{\eta}^{*}}C^{[\eta^{*}]}_{\alpha_{\eta^{*}}b_{\eta^{*}}}
    ∑bη∗C[η∗]αη∗​bη∗T[q3]{s3}{α3}|η∗bη∗⟶T[q3]{s3}{α3}|η∗αη∗\displaystyle\sum_{b_{\eta^{*}}}C^{[\eta^{*}]}_{\alpha_{\eta^{*}}b_{\eta^{*}}}T^{[q_{3}]}_{\quantity{s_{3}}\quantity{\alpha_{3}}_{|_{\eta^{*}}}b_{\eta^{*}}}\longrightarrow T^{[q_{3}]}_{\quantity{s_{3}}\quantity{\alpha_{3}}_{|_{\eta^{*}}}\alpha_{\eta^{*}}}

    where C[η]C^{[\eta]} and C[η∗]C^{[\eta^{*}]} are the non unitary upper trapezoidal matrices respectively defined on any two links η\eta and η∗\eta^{*} connecting q1→q2q_{1}\to q_{2} and q2→q3q_{2}\to q_{3}.

Aside of the gauge isometrization w.r.t a single tensor node, any loopless TN ansatz admits a canonical form where all the tensors are concurrently isometrized, allowing for multipartite representation of QMB states (see [644, 645, 646]). However, such a canonical form is not suitable for the practical TN contractions that are performed during the variational algorithms, where the whole TN structure is sequentially optimized w.r.t each single tensor (see Section 2.4), which can be more conveniently chosen as the unique gauge center.

Aware of all these features of loopless TN geometries, we can look at two specific realizations: Matrix product states in Section 2.2.3 and (binary) Tree Tensor Networks in Section 2.2.4.

2.2.3 Matrix product states

The simplest yet most diffused and powerful loopless TN ansatz in one dimension, is represented by Matrix product states (MPS), which reproduces the structure of the lattice with a network of tensors, one for each lattice site [646]. As shown in Fig. 2.3(a), each tensor in the bulk of the network has three indices: one physical leg ii of dimension dd, representing the local degrees of freedom, and two auxiliary legs α\alphas of dimension χ\chi connected to the neighboring sites.

More formally, the MPS representation consists in reshaping the generic QMB pure state |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} in Eq. 2.1.1 as follows [486, 647, 487]:

|ΨQMB⟩=∑i1,…,iN=1d∑α1,…,αN=1χAα1,α2[1],i1​Aα2,α3[2],i2,…,AαN−2,αN[N−1],iN−1​AαN−1,α1[N],iN​|i1,i2,…,iN⟩,\ket{\psiqmb}=\sum_{i_{1},\dots,i_{N}=1}^{d}\sum_{\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{N}=1}^{\chi}A^{[1],i_{1}}_{\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}}A^{[2],i_{2}}_{\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}},\dots,A^{[N-1],i_{N-1}}_{\alpha_{N-2},\alpha_{N}}A^{[N],i_{N}}_{\alpha_{N-1},\alpha_{1}}\ket{i_{1},i_2,\dots,i_{\Nsites}}, (2.2.10)

where each 3-rank tensor Aαk,αk+1[k],ikA^{[k],i_{k}}_{\alpha_{k},\alpha_{k+1}} describes the local kthk^{\rm{th}} lattice site with the index iki_{k} and the amount of quantum correlations shared its neighbors through the indices αk,αk+1\alpha_{k},\alpha_{k+1}. In open boundary conditions (OBC), the tensors at the boundaries of an MPS have one trivial auxiliary link α1=αN=1\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{N}=1. Fixing the physical index iki_{k}, the tensor Aαk,αk+1[k],ikA^{[k],i_{k}}_{\alpha_{k},\alpha_{k+1}} is a χ×χ\chi\times\chi complex matrix. In this perspective, Eq. 2.2.10 is a sum of basis elements weighted by matrix products.

In principle, every state of a one-dimensional QMB system can be written exactly in the MPS form, with bond dimension χ=dN/2\chi=d^{N/2} growing exponentially with the lattice sites NN [644]. However, since MPS intrinsically satisfies area law, when dealing with low-energy states of local Hamiltonians, and their real-time dynamics for small-to-intermediate time, an approximate but efficient representation at fixed maximal bond dimension is usually very accurate in capturing the essential features of the systems [501, 485].

In this case, the number of parameters in the MPS representation grows only polynomially with the system size, drastically reducing the overall computational complexity. More in detail, the MPS ground state searching algorithm (based on DMRG) scales like 𝒪⁡(N​d​χ3+N​d2​χ2)\mathcal{O}(Nd\chi^{3}+Nd^{2}\chi^{2}) or 𝒪⁡(N​d3​χ3)\mathcal{O}(Nd^{3}\chi^{3}), depending if the algorithm optimizes a single MPS tensor at a time, or two-tensors simultaneously [490, 488]. Two-site optimization is usually important to avoid local minima or meta-stable configurations during the energy variational minimization [648]. The subspace expansion is an intermediate approach with the benefits of the two-tensor update and a tunable computational cost between the two approaches [484].

2.2.4 Tree Tensor Networks

The other important family of loopless TNs is represented by Tree Tensor Networks (TTN), in which the wave function is decomposed into a hierarchical network of tensors that do not contain internal loops [504, 484]. This way, the network can be efficiently contracted and manipulated in polynomial time by exploiting the unitary gauge transformations detailed in Section 2.2.2.

A particular class of TTN is represented by binary TTN (bTTN), reported in Fig. 2.3c and Fig. 2.3d for one- and two-dimensional lattices. In these structures, tensors in the lowest layer have two physical legs of dimension dd (representing two lattice sites) and an auxiliary leg of dimension χ\chi, whereas, in the upper layers, they have three auxiliary legs of dimensions up to χ\chi. The network intrinsically encodes a renormalization procedure, in which, at each layer, two sites are mapped into a single effective one.

More in detail, bTTN are quite useful for a series of reasons:

  1. 1.

    thanks to their loopless TN geometry, in finite-range models, ground searching algorithms for bTTNs display a numerical complexity of the order 𝒪⁡(N​d2​χ2+N​χ4)\mathcal{O}(Nd^{2}\chi^{2}+N\chi^{4}) [484] (see also Section 2.4). This is a much more favorable scaling concerning equivalent algorithms for other TN structures, and allows reaching quite large values of bond dimensions (χ≈500\chi\approx 500) [507] to keep the variational TTN optimization under control.

  2. 2.

    similarly to MPS, they provide an efficient basis for DMRG-based algorithms, which represent the state-of-the-art technique for the numerical simulation of 1D QMB systems with both short and long-range interactions [638, 639].

  3. 3.

    they can handle both open (OBC) and periodic (PBC) boundary conditions, without the typical limitations of DMRG for periodic systems.

  4. 4.

    any D-dimensional realization of a bTTN admits an equivalent realization in 1D [524, 436, 437, 525]. For instance, to move from a 2D bTTN to the corresponding 1D version (see Fig. 2.3), we just need to rotate each layer of the tree with alternate clockwise and anti-clockwise π/2\pi/2 rotations in the x​yxy plane. This procedure requires the application of a 2D-1D site-ordering that generates a mapping between the 2D physical system and a 1D chain [436] (see Section 2.3). Once the 2D physical model is modeled on a 1D chain, one can apply the TTN variational algorithm discussed in Section 2.4 by using 1D bTTNs.

  5. 5.

    due to their hierarchical structure, bTTNs offer a strong connectivity: rather than MPS, the distance between two physical lattice sites is logarithmically rescaled in the network. As a results, they reveal particularly advantageous to reproduce properly long-range interactions (see also Section 2.3).

Augmented Tree Tensor Networks

The drawback of loopless structures like binary TTN, is that the area law may not be explicitly reproduced in dimensions higher than one [649], which becomes a limiting factor when large systems are addressed. Nonetheless, it is possible to explicitly encode the area law of high dimensional systems in the TTN ansatz by introducing an additional layer of independent disentanglers, acting on different couples of lattice sites and connected to the corresponding physical legs. This process augments the expressive power of TTN, and the resulting ansatz is known as augmented Tree Tensor Network (aTTN) [608]. The computational complexity of variationally optimizing an aTTN structure, which means optimizing both the tensors and the disentanglers, is of the order 𝒪⁡(N​χ4​d4+N​χ​d7)\mathcal{O}(N\chi^{4}d^{4}+N\chi d^{7}). We point out that the scaling of the computational costs with the local dimension dd is particularly severe in the case of aTTN due to the presence of the disentanglers layer.

2.2.5 Tensor Network ansätze with loops

Beyond loopless TN structures like MPS and TTN, there exist other ansätze, which despite their higher computational costs in contractions, offer unique advantages for describing complex QMB systems beyond one dimensions. Below we briefly outline two realizations of these TN ansätze.

Projected Entanglement Pair States (PEPS)

displayed in Fig. 2.3b, represent a generalization of the MPS ansatz to two- or higher-dimensional lattices which directly encode in their structure the area law of entanglement [495]. In this case, each tensor in the bulk has a physical leg of dimension dd, and a number of χ\chi-dimensional auxiliary legs depending on the coordination number of the considered lattice. For example, this coordination number is four in the case of a two-dimensional square lattice, as shown in Fig. 2.3(b). Despite the area law implementation, due to the presence of loops in the TN geometry, an exact contraction of PEPS is an exponentially hard problem, meaning that PEPS can not be efficiently contracted for numerical computing, e.g. scalar products of states or physical observables [493]. To circumvent this problem, approximate contraction methods have been developed during the last years, and are still at the center of current research efforts [495]. But even with exploiting these approximate techniques, the computational complexity for ground state optimization remains quite high, e.g. of the order of 𝒪⁡(N​d2​χ8)\mathcal{O}(Nd^{2}\chi^{8}) [619, 502], limiting the maximum reachable bond dimensions (typical values are of the order χ≈10\chi\approx 10).

Multi-scale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz (MERA)

displayed in Fig. 2.3, extends the capabilities of MPS and TTN by efficiently representing QMB systems with long-range correlations, particularly at criticality. While TTN can capture certain entanglement structures beyond what MPS can handle, they are limited by their tree-like structure, which lacks the loops necessary to efficiently encode the entanglement scaling of critical systems. MERA addresses this limitation by introducing a layered, hierarchical network with loops, allowing for a logarithmic scaling of entanglement entropy and revealing suitable for critical ground states [508, 509].

Unlike TTN, where contractions can be performed in a straightforward and computationally inexpensive manner as detailed in Sections 2.2.2 and 2.4, MERA introduces additional complexity through its disentanglers and isometric tensors, which are necessary for accurately capturing the multi-scale entanglement in critical systems. The presence of loops in MERA increases the complexity of the network and consequently the cost of tensor manipulations. For 1D systems, the scaling of MERA constractions and optimizations is accessible 𝒪⁡(N​χ4)\mathcal{O}(N\chi^{4}) but more expensive than TTNs. Beyond one dimension, e.g. for 2D systems, optimizing MERA is much more challenging and scales with 𝒪⁡(N​χ8)\mathcal{O}(N\chi^{8}). Current research is focusing on developing more efficient contraction and optimization algorithms to enhance its applicability to complex QMB systems [642]. Nonetheless, despite its higher computational, MERA’s ability to capture the intricate entanglement patterns of critical systems makes it a powerful tool in the study of QMB physics.

2.3 Efficient Tensor Network geometries beyond one dimension

If MPS are the established TN ansatz for one-dimensional systems, the development of efficient TN algorithms for higher-dimensional systems is still ongoing [650, 640, 651, 652, 653, 654]. On one side, a possible and frequently used approach lies in the application of consolidated numerical methods based on DMRG (MPS) by suitably mapping the high-dimensional problem onto an equivalent one-dimensional one. Indeed, the DMRG algorithm is often used for analyzing quasi-one-dimensional systems, such as ladder structures [490], and two-dimensional systems, obtaining reliable numerical results in a wide variety of condensed-matter problems [655, 656, 657, 658].

However, using MPS/DMRG on high-dimensional lattices generally involves a significant increase in computational complexity. When adapting an MPS to two dimensions, it requires a careful arrangement of the 2D lattice into a 1D structure. Two main strategies can be implemented: the first one consists in considering the n×n′n\times n^{\prime} 2D lattice as an n′n^{\prime}-legs ladder, then grouping all the n′n^{\prime} sites of each column in a single numerical site, and finally applying the one-dimensional algorithms to the resulting chain [659]. The cost of this approach is the exponential growth with n′n^{\prime} of the local basis dimension, which usually limits the application of this strategy to quasi-two-dimensional systems, in which the number of ladder legs is small with respect to the longitudinal extension.

The second strategy, which we discuss here, lies in covering the two-dimensional lattice by a one-dimensional curve and then applying one-dimensional algorithms to the resulting effective chain. The drawback at this approach is that even if the original model contains only nearest-neighbor interactions, the resulting model on the effective one-dimensional chain shows long-range interactions, that have an influence on the numerical approach efficiency [660]. In detail, the latter strategy induces a specific one-dimensional site-ordering in the 2D lattice, generating a mapping between the 2D physical system and a 1D chain. This procedure can be defined for any mapping

ℳ:i∈[1,n]×[1,n′]→μ∈[1,n​n′]\mathcal{M}:\,i\in[1,n]\times[1,n^{\prime}]\rightarrow\mu\in[1,nn^{\prime}] (2.3.1)

from a n×n′n\times n^{\prime} lattice onto a chain with n​n′n\,n^{\prime} sites, through which it is possible to translate a two-dimensional model into a one-dimensional one. Finally, one can apply 1D TN algorithms, such as DMRG or the TTN variational one discussed in Section 2.4, while accounting for the long-range interactions introduced by the mapping. Long-range interactions eventually require a larger bond dimension to properly describe the system. It follows that the performance of the simulation depends on the capability of the mapping to preserve the locality of the interactions from the original 2D Hamiltonian to the effective new 1D one.

In this section, we quantify the importance of the choice of the site-ordering curve based on the numerical results obtained in [436]. In particular, we consider a square n×nn\times n lattice and compare the numerical precision achieved using the standard snake curve (see Fig. 2.5d) and the Hilbert curve (see Fig. 2.5c) detailed in Section 2.3.2. We demonstrate that, compared to other space-filling curves, the locality-preserving properties of the Hilbert curve leads to a clear improvement of numerical precision, especially for large system sizes, and turns out to provide the best performances for the simulation of 2D lattice systems via 1D TN structures.

2.3.1 Preserving the locality of interactions

Before effectively comparing different 2​D→1​D2D\to 1D mappings, let us deepen the concept of preserving the interaction range (i.e. locality). In the context of numerical simulations with TN algorithms, it would be extremely useful to map a 2D lattice into a 1D chain in a way that preserves locality at most, avoiding long-range interactions of sites that are very far apart from each other. However, it is straightforward to prove that it is impossible to map a DD-dimensional lattice into a D′D^{\prime}-dimensional one, with D′<DD^{\prime}<D, so that two neighboring sites in the DD-lattice are always close together in the D′D^{\prime}-lattice. Let us consider, for instance, nearest neighbour sites: each point of the DD-dimensional square lattice has 2​D2D nearest neighbours, while only 2​D′2D^{\prime} nearest neighbours in the D′D^{\prime}-dimensional one. Thus, after the mapping, at least 2​(D−D′)2(D-D^{\prime}) sites will be placed at a distance larger than one unit. For the specific case of a 2D square lattice and a 1D chain, this implies that the optimal solution would be a mapping such that two out of four nearest neighbours in the 2D lattice remain nearest neighbours in the 1D chain. If we strictly follow this argument, the best choice would be the frequently used snake curve, shown in Fig. 2.5d. However, in this way, the other two nearest neighbours of a generic site of the 2D lattice would be rather far away from each other in the one-dimensional setup, with their distance increasing up to 2​n2n. If our goal is to preserve the locality also for these two other nearest neighbours, the curve that tends to globally satisfy these constraints, outperforming other types of mapping, is exactly the Hilbert curve.

2.3.2 Hilbert curve

Without going into much detail (see [661, 662, 663] for an exhaustive description), the Hilbert curve is a 1D fractal-like self-similar space-filling curve with Hausdörff dimension δ=2\delta=233 3 The fractal or Hausdörff dimension δ\delta is a measure of roughness (or smoothness) for a smooth, differentiable DD-dimensional surface S∈ℝD+1S\in\mathbb{R}^{D+1} with topological dimension DD. If the surface is nondifferentiable and rough, the fractal dimension δ\delta of SS takes values between the topological dimension DD and D+1D+1 [664]. The closer δ\delta to D+1D+1, the better the ability of SS in covering the ℝD+1\mathbb{R}^{D+1} manifold space where the surface is embedded. introduced for the first time in 1891 by the mathematician David Hilbert [665]. Notably, among other interesting properties, it allows to create a mapping between a 1D and a 2D space by keeping and preserving the locality: this implies that two points that are close to each other in the 1D space are close to each other also after folding on the 2D space. The converse is not always strictly true, as unavoidable when passing from two-dimensions to one-dimension. However, even in this case, the curve shows a tendency to preserve the locality as much as possible [662, 661, 663]. For this reason, it finds several applications in computer science [666] and bioinformatics [667].

Effective construction

The basic element of the Hilbert curve is obtained by connecting the elements of a 2×22\times 2 lattice starting from the bottom-left (BL) to the bottom-right (BR) corner as shown in Fig. 2.5a. From this we can now construct the n=4n=4 Hilbert curve via the following procedure: draw the n=2n=2 Hilbert curve into the top-left (TL) an top-right (TR) quadrants, while rotating it clockwise and counterclockwise by 90 degrees in the BL and BR quadrants respectively. Then, by joining these different curve replicas, we end up with the n=4n=4 curve shown in Fig. 2.5b. The generalization to the level nn for covering the n×nn\times n lattice is then straightforward: the 2​n2n curve is obtained by drawing the nn curve in the four main quadrants of the 2​n×2​n2n\times 2n lattice and by applying the just mentioned rules for the rotations in the BL and BR quadrants. In Fig. 2.5c, for example, we report the Hilbert curve for the 8×88\times 8 lattice.

Comparing space filling curves

To get an intuition of how different curves preserve locality, we report in Fig. 2.5c the Hilbert mapping of a generic site of the 2D lattice (within a given quadrant) and its four nearest neighbours: it is evident that all these points that are close on the two-dimensional plane remain fairly close on the one-dimensional chain. On the contrary, this property does not hold for the standard snake mapping, where, as expected, two out of four nearest neighbours are almost always mapped at large distance, as shown in Fig. 2.5d. The only regions in which the Hilbert mapping does not preserve the locality are the inner borders of the main quadrants. In this case, nearest neighbor sites belonging to two adjacent quadrants turn out to be mapped quite far away from each other. Nonetheless, in the limit of large lattices, the number of these points becomes negligible ∼𝒪⁡(n)\sim\mathcal{O}(n) w.r.t the total number of sites.

2.3.3 Numerical evidences

In [436], we compare the performance obtained from the Hilbert and the snake curve on MPS and TTN simulations. We focus on the ground state properties of the 2D Ising model at zero temperature in presence of a uniform transverse magnetic field along the z-direction [668] with the following Hamiltonian:

H^=J​∑⟨i,j⟩σ^ix​σ^jx+λ​∑iσ^iz,\hat{H}=J\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{i}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{j}+\lambda\sum_{i}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{i}, (2.3.2)

where ⟨i,j⟩\langle i,j\rangle refers to the nearest neighbour sites and σ^iα\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{\alpha} is the Pauli matrix in the α\alpha-direction defined on the site ii. The coefficient JJ represents the strength of the interaction between nearest neighbour spins along the xx-axis, whereas λ\lambda determines the strength of the external magnetic field along the zz-axis. In the following, we consider the antiferromagnetic (AF) scenario for J>0J>0, and, without loss of generality, we fix the energy scale by setting J=1J=1.

Ground-state energy density

We simulate the Hamiltonian in Eq. 2.3.2 on a square lattice n×nn\times n with different sizes, up to n=64n=64, and both boundary conditions. To compare the Hilbert and the snake mappings, we express Eq. 2.3.2 as a long-range, one-dimensional Hamiltonian H^S⁡(H)\hat{H}_{S(H)} where sites are sorted according to the snake (S)(S) or the Hilbert (HH) curve. As shown in [436], for both MPS and TTN simulations, the Hilbert curve mapping provides more accurate ground state energies, especially close to the second order critical point [669, 670], stressing the relevance of our analysis for the study of quantum phase transitions. More in detail, as shown in Fig. 2.6, the Hilbert curve shows a faster convergence of the energy as the bond dimension χ\chi is increased.

Local Magnetization

Additionally, it is possible to understand which regions of the lattice contribute to the energy improvement by studying the expectation values of the local magnetization. We measure the local expectation values of the magnetization {⟨σ^kz⟩}1≤k≤n2\quantity{\avg{\Sz_{k}}}_{1\leq k\leq n^{2}} on both the ground states of the two Hamiltonians H^ℋ\hat{H}_{\mathcal{H}} and H^𝒮\hat{H}_{\mathcal{S}} and compute the difference Δ​σ^kz=|⟨σ^kz⟩ℋ−⟨σ^kz⟩𝒮|\Delta\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{k}=|\langle\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{k}\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}-\langle\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{k}\rangle_{\mathcal{S}}|. As shown in Fig. 2.7, Δ​σ^kz\Delta\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{k} seems to be significant all over the lattice quadrants, while vanishing on their edges (the black lines in Fig. 2.5c), where the magnetization values obtained from the two methods are similar. This result aligns with the fact that the Hilbert curve excels at preserving the locality of interactions within the core of the quadrants, while its performance near the edges becomes comparable to that of other orderings, such as the snake. In these terms, we expect to observe similar results also when considering other observables, such as two-point correlation functions.

2.3.4 Distance distributions

For a more rigorous explanation of the previous numerical results, let us introduce two distances dMPSd_{\mathrm{MPS}} and dTTNd_{\mathrm{TTN}}, defined as the number of links connecting two different lattice sites within the MPS and TTN network geometries respectively. Namely, we consider the interaction terms of the 1D Hamiltonians H^𝒮\hat{H}_{\mathcal{S}} and H^ℋ\hat{H}_{\mathcal{H}} of Eq. 2.3.2 and compute the distances dMPSd_{\mathrm{MPS}} and dTTNd_{\mathrm{TTN}} between all the relative couples of sites. We obtain then four sets of distances, each of them labeled by the relative mapping (snake and Hilbert) and the TN geometry (MPS and TTN).

Different curves

In Fig. 2.8, we fix n=16n=16 and plot the distributions of dMPSd_{\mathrm{MPS}} and dTTNd_{\mathrm{TTN}} for the snake (left column) and the Hilbert (right column) mappings: one can qualitatively see that the probabilities at large distances are larger for the snake mapping than for the Hilbert one. This feature is particularly evident in the TTN case, due to the logarithmic scaling of distances within the network.

Different Tensor Network Geometries

Remarkably, when focusing on the same space filling curve (e.g. the Hilbert curve) we can compare the MPS and TTN method the distributions of dMPSd_{\mathrm{MPS}} and dTTNd_{\mathrm{TTN}} on different values of nn. As shown in Fig. 2.9, the fraction of interaction terms with largest distances changes when we move from n=16n=16 to n=32n=32 and decreases faster in the MPS case than in the TTN one. This explains why the improvement achievable with the MPS and the Hilbert curve is larger than the one achievable with TTNs, even though the TTN simulations are overall more accurate than the MPS ones.

2.3.5 Conclusions

These results are particularly interesting, as they provide useful hints for simulating QMB systesm and LGTs beyond one spatial dimension. In particular, the choice of an optimal space filling curve, such as the Hilbert one, to map a d−d-dimensional lattice onto a one-dimensional one, reveals fundamental to minimize long-range interactions on both MPS and TTN ansätze.

While the locality-preserving properties of the Hilbert ordering are directly mapped onto the MPS chain, in the case of TTNs they are enhanced by the logarithmic scaling of distances within the TTN structure. By recalling that the standard TTN methods for two-dimensional systems rely on the construction of a 2D bTTN [608], it is worth noting that the 2D bTTN and the Hilbert curve mapping generate the same long-range interactions within the corresponding networks. Therefore, the former benefits from the mathematical locality-preserving properties of the Hilbert curve.

We have then obtained a systematic strategy to evaluate, given a QMB system defined on a two-dimensional lattice, the more efficient site-ordering to perform simulations by using TNs, based on the analysis of the effective, one-dimensional system generated by the mapping. Our results suggest that 1D variational ground state searching algorithms, such as DMRG, strongly benefits from the choice of the Hilbert curve for treating 2D systems. This can be easily extended to rectangular lattices, such as long narrow cylinders, or on 3D cubic lattice, since it is possible to generalize the Hilbert curve definition also in these cases. Other possible outlooks include the application of this strategy to the study of systems characterized by non-trivial lattice structures and interactions, as for example in spin glasses [671] and quantum chemistry [672].

2.4 Variational ground state search algorithm

We now present the ground-state search algorithm for TTN simulations which has been used for simulating LGTs [524, 525, 437] such as the (2+1)D SU(2) theory in Chapter 3. A pictorial explanation of the algorithm is sketched in Fig. 2.10a. Let us suppose to search for the ground state properties of a QMB Hamiltonian H^QMB\hat{H}_{\rm{QMB}}. Formally, if |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} is the target state, any observable requires the contraction of the Hamiltonian tensor operator with the TN state and its hermitian conjugate: ⟨ΨQMB|H^|ΨQMB⟩\expectationvalue{\ham}{\psiqmb}. To reduce the complexity of the minimization problem, we use a variational approach that optimizes a single tensor TvarT_{\rm{var}} of |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} per step44 4 In practice, we exploit the Krylov sub-space expansion technique to numerically solve the local eigenvalue problem for each tensor [484].. We fix a TvarT_{\rm{var}} as the optimization center and treat all its parameters as variational. Correspondingly, all the other tensors of the TN are kept fixed to form the so-called TN environment. We then contract the environment with the Hamiltonian operator, obtaining an effective Hamiltonian H^eff\hat{H}_{\rm{eff}} which acts only on TvarT_{\rm{var}}. Properly, this is just a local optimization problem, which involves only two single tensors, respectively Tvar∗T_{\rm{var}}^{*} from ⟨ΨQMB|\bra{\psiqmb} and TvarT_{\rm{var}} from |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} 55 5 This step is efficiently carried out by applying the Arnoldi method of the ARPACK library [673]. Then, if we sequentially solve the reduced optimization problem for each TN node, (i.e. by moving the optimization center following the numbered tensors in Fig. 2.10a), the energy expectation value is gradually reduced up to a certain fixed minimal value. The whole series of local optimizations in |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} is also known as sweep sequence.

2.4.1 High level operations

We then then focus on a single local optimization problem [484]. Let us consider a TTN geometry of tensors T[q]T^{[q]} whose nodes q∈{1​…​Q}q\in\quantity{1\dots Q} are mutually joined by auxiliary links ζ\zeta of dimension χζ\chi_{\zeta}. We suppose to use unitary gauges and fix an arbitrary center node TvarT_{\rm{var}} w.r.t. which each tensor of the environment is gauge transformed. Correspondingly, we assume the Hamiltonian as a sum of PP different contributions (e.g. the kinetic energy, the interaction potential, or an external magnetic field):

H^=∑p=1PH^p,\hat{H}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\hat{H}_{p}, (2.4.1)

where each term H^p\hat{H}_{p} is a Tensor Product Operator (TPO) like the following (see Fig. 2.10b):

[H^p]{is}​{js}=∑{γμ}∏s[h^p,k⁡(s)[s]]is​js{γμ}k⁡(s).\quantity[\ham_{p}]_{\quantity{i_{s}}\quantity{j_{s}}}=\sum_{\{\gamma_{\mu}\}}\prod_{s}\quantity[\hop_{p,k(s)}^{[s]}]^{\quantity{\gamma_{\mu}}_{k(s)}}_{i_{s}j_{s}}. (2.4.2)

In this expression, {is}\quantity{i_{s}} and {js}\quantity{j_{s}} label the sets of physical links which connect the Hamiltonian interaction H^p\hat{H}_{p} with ⟨ΨQMB|\bra{\psiqmb} and |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb} respectively; h^p,k⁡(s)[s]\hat{h}_{p,k(s)}^{[s]} is the kthk^{\text{th}} local operator of the specific TPO H^p\hat{H}_{p} acting on the physical site ss of the TN.

Local operators such as h^p,k⁡(s)[s]\hat{h}_{p,k(s)}^{[s]} and h^p,k′​(s′)[s′]\hat{h}_{p,k^{\prime}(s^{\prime})}^{[s^{\prime}]}, concurrently acting on the physical sites ss and s′s^{\prime}, are connected among each other through TPO links like γμ=(k,k′)\gamma_{\mu=(k,k^{\prime})} (see Fig. 2.10b). The sum ∑{γμ}\sum_{\{\gamma_{\mu}\}} runs over all the TPO links {μ}\quantity{\mu} and we define {μ}k⁡(s)⊆{μ}\quantity{\mu}_{k(s)}\subseteq\quantity{\mu} as the set of all the links μ\mu attached to the kthk^{\text{th}} TPO operator h^p,k⁡(s)[s]\hat{h}_{p,k(s)}^{[s]}.

Renormalization

At this point, once fixed a center node cc of the TTN structure defining |ΨQMB⟩\ket{\psiqmb}, we associate to each auxiliary link ζ\zeta of the TTN a renormalized Hamiltonian h^p,𝕂⁡(ζ)[ζ]\hat{h}_{p,\mathbb{K}(\zeta)}^{[\zeta]}, which describes the effective action of the single Hamiltonian TPO in Eq. 2.4.2 onto the subsystem (or partition) SζS_{\zeta}, made of all the environmental sites of the TN separated by ζ\zeta from the current network center cc.

To figure out the situation, let us consider a given node q≠cq\neq c with a proper set of auxiliary links {η}q\quantity{\eta}_{q}. We can suppose that, among these links, the link ζ\zeta is the one through which the node qq communicates with c (see Fig. 2.10c). All the remaining links are then denoted with {ξ}q\quantity{\xi}_{q}, in such a way that {η}q=ζ+{ξ}q\quantity{\eta}_{q}=\zeta+\quantity{\xi}_{q}. Then, we define the renormalized Hamiltonian associated to the link ζ\zeta in the following recursive way:

[h^p,𝕂⁡(ζ)[ζ]]{αξ}​{βξ}{γμ}𝕂⁡(ζ)=∑paired{γμ}∏ξ≠ζ[h^p,𝕂⁡(ξ)[ξ]]αξ​βξ{γμ}𝕂⁡(ξ)where𝕂⁡(ζ)=⋃ξ≠ζ𝕂⁡(ξ).\quantity[\hop_{p,\mathbb{K}(\zeta)}^{[\zeta]}]^{\quantity{\gamma_{\mu}}_{\mathbb{K}(\zeta)}}_{\quantity{\alpha_{\xi}}\quantity{\beta_{\xi}}}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{paired}\\ \quantity{\gamma_{\mu}}\end{subarray}}\prod_{\xi\neq\zeta}\quantity[\hop_{p,\mathbb{K}(\xi)}^{[\xi]}]^{\quantity{\gamma_{\mu}}_{\mathbb{K}(\xi)}}_{\alpha_{\xi}\beta_{\xi}}\qquad\text{where}\qquad\mathbb{K}(\zeta)=\bigcup_{\xi\neq\zeta}\mathbb{K}(\xi). (2.4.3)

In 𝕂⁡(ζ)\mathbb{K}(\zeta), we collect all the physical renormalized Hamiltonians defined on all the links {ξ}q\quantity{\xi}_{q} of the TN node qq with ξ≠ζ\xi\neq\zeta (we recall that both ζ\zeta and ξ\xi are auxiliary links of the TN structure, not of the Hamiltonian TPO). These terms are generally connected by some TPO links {μ}\quantity{\mu}, over which the contractions are performed (and the sum is taken).

The fundamental unit of a renormalized Hamiltonian h^p,𝕂⁡(ξ)[ξ]\hat{h}_{p,\mathbb{K}(\xi)}^{[\xi]} is a single renormalized Hamiltonian operator h^p,𝕂ξ\hat{h}_{p,\mathbb{K}}^{\xi}, where 𝕂\mathbb{K} is the set of all local operators of the TPO h^p,k⁡(s)[s]\hat{h}_{p,k(s)}^{[s]} involved the renormalization:

𝕂⁡(ξ)=⋃s∈Sξk⁡(s)\mathbb{K}(\xi)=\bigcup_{s\in S_{\xi}}k(s) (2.4.4)

Properly, in order to effectively obtain the renormalized Hamiltonian over the link ζ\zeta, we must additionally contract the Hamiltonian operators h^p,𝕂⁡(ξ)[ξ]\hat{h}_{p,\mathbb{K}(\xi)}^{[\xi]} over the links ξ≠ζ\xi\neq\zeta with the node tensor T[q]T^{[q]} and its complex conjugate T[q]∗T^{[q]*}:

[h^p,𝕂⁡(ζ)[ζ]]{γμ}𝕂⁡(ζ)αζ​βζ=∑{αξ}∑{βξ}T[q]αζ​{αξ}[h^p,𝕂⁡(ζ)[ζ]]{γμ}𝕂⁡(ζ){αξ}​{βξ}T[q]∗{βξ}​βζ\quantity[\hop_{p,\mathbb{K}(\zeta)}^{[\zeta]}]^{\quantity{\gamma_{\mu}}_{\mathbb{K}(\zeta)}}_{\alpha_{\zeta}\beta_{\zeta}}=\sum_{\quantity{\alpha_{\xi}}}\sum_{\quantity{\beta_{\xi}}}T^{[q]}_{\alpha_{\zeta}\quantity{\alpha_{\xi}}}\quantity[\hop_{p,\mathbb{K}(\zeta)}^{[\zeta]}]^{\quantity{\gamma_{\mu}}_{\mathbb{K}(\zeta)}}_{\quantity{\alpha_{\xi}}\quantity{\beta_{\xi}}}T^{[q]*}_{\quantity{\beta_{\xi}}\beta_{\zeta}} (2.4.5)

In the unitary gauge, the tensor T[q]T^{[q]} appears as an isometry (see Eq. 2.2.8 et seq.) over the links ξ≠ζ\xi\neq\zeta. Therefore, it is immediately clear that if Eq. 2.4.3 holds 1, so Eq. 2.4.5 does. Obviously, such renormalized Hamiltonians are defined for each kind of interaction p=1​…​Pp=1\dots P.

Effective Hamiltonian

At this point, we exploit the variational feature of the algorithm: for a given center node cc (i.e. the unitary gauge center), we define the effective Hamiltonian H^eff[c]=⟨Ψenv[c]|H^|Ψenv[c]⟩\hat{H}_{\rm{eff}}^{[c]}=\expectationvalue{\ham}{\Psi^{[c]}_{\text{env}}} where Ψenv[c]\Psi^{[c]}_{\text{env}} stands for the result of the TN contractions over all the tensors of the TN except T[c]T^{[c]}, i.e. over the environment of the center node. Then, the energy expectation value E[c]E_{[c]} of the TN state with respect to the given center node cc reads

E[c]=⟨ΨQMB[c]|H^|ΨQMB[c]⟩=⟨T[c]|⟨Ψenv[c]|H^|Ψenv[c]⟩|T[c]⟩=⟨T[c]|H^eff[c]|T[c]⟩.E_{[c]}=\expectationvalue{\ham}{\psiqmb^{[c]}}=\expectationvalue{\expval{\ham}{\Psi^{[c]}_{\text{env}}}}{\tensor^{\qty[c]}}=\expectationvalue{\ham_{\rm{eff}}^{[c]}}{\tensor^{\qty[c]}}. (2.4.6)

Basically, in order to obtain H^eff[c]\hat{H}_{\rm{eff}}^{[c]}, we do not need to contract the entire environment if we have already computed the renormalized Hamiltonians over all the available links of cc. We should have:

H^eff[c]=∑p=1Ph^p,eff[c]where[h^p,eff[c]]{αη}​{bη}=∑{γμ}∏η[h^p,𝕂⁡(η)[η]]αη​bη{γμ}𝕂⁡(η).\hat{H}_{\rm{eff}}^{[c]}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\hat{h}_{p,\rm{eff}}^{[c]}\qquad\text{where}\qquad\quantity[\hop_{p,\rm{eff}}^{[c]}]_{\quantity{\alpha_{\eta}}\quantity{b_{\eta}}}=\sum_{\{\gamma_{\mu}\}}\prod_{\eta}\quantity[\hop_{p,\mathbb{K}(\eta)}^{[\eta]}]_{\alpha_{\eta}b_{\eta}}^{\quantity{\gamma_{\mu}}_{\mathbb{K}(\eta)}}. (2.4.7)

are the renormalized Hamiltonian terms defined over all links {η}c\quantity{\eta}_{c} of the node cc with corresponding indices {αη}\quantity{\alpha_{\eta}} and {bη}\quantity{b_{\eta}}. Hence, the effective Hamiltonian involves the contraction of all renormalized Hamiltonian terms over each tensor link η∈{η}c\eta\in\quantity{\eta}_{c} of the center node cc. Plugging together all the previous steps, we can rewrite the energy expectation value E[c]E_{[c]} as following:
