As an outlook of this study, we plan to develop an analogous formalism in the magnetic basis, where plaquette terms are diagonal [727, 547, 602]. This change of basis should ease TN simulations, which in our case are limited to finite system sizes, but anyway larger than the state-of-the-art of quantum-inspired or quantum simulations of non-Abelian LGTs [569, 610, 728]. Accessing larger system sizes would be a substantial advantage, as it would enable the characterization of correlation functions not distorted by finite-size effects. Correspondingly, larger sizes would allow for studying magnetic effects at small coupling, as in MC simulations [729, 730, 731].

To overcome these limitations (finite gauge representation and finite system sizes), further developments of the numerical simulation architecture are also required: on the hardware side, the possibility of running the computation on a (pre)exascale HPC environment, while on the software side the development of new and improved TN-based algorithms. The latter will be achieved by exploiting the augmented TTN ansatz, which drastically enhances the capability of representing area law-states in high dimensions [608]. These steps will be fundamental for the long-term goal of applying TN methods to large-scale (3+1) lattice QCD and ultimately address open, secular research problems, such as confinement and asymptotic freedom.

From an experimental viewpoint, similarly to the one-dimensional case [578], the dressed-site formalism developed for the (2+1)D SU(2) Hamiltonian could be encoded on quantum hardware. In this perspective, the results presented in this chapter and in [437] represent essential benchmarks for validating current and future experimental implementations [571, 732, 733, 734].

Chapter 4 Non-Ergodic dynamics of LGTs

The nature of equilibration in a isolated interacting quantum many-body (QMB) systems is a fundamental question in physics [735]. Whereas open quantum systems are expected to thermalize due to exchanging energy with a bath [736], the conditions under which an isolated QMB system thermalizes are less intuitive. While the classical counterpart can be easily figured out by using the Liouville theorem and applying the statistical mechanics ensemble on the phase space [737], thermalization in quantum systems is stipulated by the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) [738, 739, 740, 737]. According to the ETH, for an ergodic Hamiltonian, the expectation values of observables in individual energy eigenstates match thermal ensemble averages, and through the process of dephasing, the system’s long-time behavior averages out to these thermal values, leading to thermalization.

So far, ETH has been widely confirmed and numerically verified in several contexts, from strongly correlated models of condensed matter and ultracold atom gases of (softcore and hardcore) bosons [741, 742, 743, 744, 745], spins [746, 747, 748, 749], and fermions [750, 751, 752, 753]. However, in recent years, a new paradigm of weak ergodicity breaking has emerged violating the ETH. In certain ergodic Hamiltonians, there is a polynomial (in system size) number of special non-thermal scar eigenstates that are roughly equally spaced in energy over the whole spectrum [754, 755, 756] and exhibit anomalously low bipartite entanglement entropy [757]. Upon initializing the system in an initial state with a high overlap with these scar eigenstates, the subsequent quench dynamics gives rise to quantum many-body scarring (QMBS), which manifests as prominent oscillations in local observables and persistent revivals in the (local and global) Loschmidt fidelity that last longer than all relevant timescales, thereby circumventing expected thermalization [758, 755, 759, 760, 761, 762, 763]. QMBS has received a lot of attention since its initial discovery in [758] and has been the subject of several quantum simulation experiments [764, 765, 734, 766, 767].

After the discovery of QMBS, it has been shown that the effective model quantum-simulated in [758] is a spin-1/21/2 U⁡(1)\mathrm{U(1)} lattice gauge theory (LGT), where the electric field is represented by a spin-1/21/2 zz-operator [768]. In detail, the robustness of QMBS has been shown to depend on the stability of an underlying gauge symmetry of this model [769]. Later, QMBS have been further observed in spin-SS U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) LGTs [770, 771] and other Abelian LGTs [772, 773, 774], even in two spatial dimensions [775, 776, 777, 778, 779]. Nonetheless, none of these studies tried to explore QMBS in the non-Abelian scenario. Recently, Ref. [780] has shown the emergence of scarring dynamics on a pure (without dynamical matter) (2+1)D SU(2) LGT. In detail, looking at the bipartite entanglement entropy, [780] identified a few scar-eigenstate candidates in a certain parameter regime. However, no experimentally feasible scarred initial states have been proposed, and the type of exhibited scarring vanishes beyond the crudest truncation of the electric field basis.

In this chapter, we bridge this gap discussing the emergence of QMBS in non-Abelian LGTs with dynamical matter and connect the presence of the latter at the origin of such an exotic dynamics. We start from Section 4.1, with a pedagogical introduction to classical thermalization. Then, in Section 4.2, we switch to the corresponding quantum version and expose in Section 4.2.1 the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) for isolated QMB systems in terms of their spectral and dynamical properties. After this introduction, we devote Section 4.3 to the first experimental and numerical observations of scarring dynamics in Rydberg atom chains. In Section 4.3.2, we highlight the strong connection QMB scars and fundamental mechanisms appearing in Abelian LGTs. The original part is in Section 4.4, where we extend such a relation to non-Abelian LGTs by simulating a one-dimensional truncated SU(2) Yang-Mills LGT and observing all the spectral and dynamical properties of a scarring dynamics [438].

4.1 Thermalization in Classical Systems

Before introducing the concept of thermalization in quantum physics, it is useful to first consider its classical counterpart and gain a physical intuition of the mechanism. Thermalization in isolated classical systems refers to the process by which a system evolves over time to reach a state where its macroscopic properties become consistent with those predicted by statistical mechanics. This concept is closely tied to the behavior of the system in its phase space, particularly when the system’s total energy is conserved.

Let us consider a classical system of NN particles without any exchange of energy or matter with the environment. The corresponding phase space Σ\Sigma of the system is defined by a set of 2​N2N variables Γ={𝐫,𝐩}={r1,…,rN,p1,…,pN}\Gamma=\quantity{\vecpos,\vecmom}=\quantity{\pos[1],\dots,\pos[N],\mom[1],\dots, \mom[N]} identifying position and momentum of each particle on a point of the phase space Γ\Gamma. Since the system is isolated, Γ⁡(t)\Gamma(t) moves on a hypersurface of the whole phase space ΣE\Sigma_{E} characterized by constant energy EE.

Then, in principle, the dynamics of the system requires to follow the evolution of Γ⁡(t)\Gamma(t) at each time step along that hypersurface. Namely, for any observable OO, we need to evaluate O⁡(Γ⁡(t))O(\Gamma(t)) ∀t\forall t. Correspondingly, the long-time average of such an observable is given by:

O¯=limT→∞1T​∫0TO⁡(Γ⁡(t))​𝑑t.\bar{O}=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int^{T}_{0}O(\Gamma(t))dt\,. (4.1.1)

If the system is ergodic, we expect that, given enough time, the trajectory Γ⁡(t)\Gamma(t) will pass arbitrarily close to every point of the hypersurfase ΣE\Sigma_{E} at energy EE. More in detail, thanks to the Liouville theorem, we then assume that the time spent in any small region of ΣE\Sigma_{E} is proportional to the phase space volume of that region. This implies that the time average of a function over a long period is statistically equivalent to the predictions made by statistical mechanics, where all accessible microstates at a given energy are equally probable.

In statistical mechanics, the microcanonical ensemble (ME) describes a system with fixed total energy EE and number of particles NN. Theen, the ensemble average of an observable OO corresponds to the uniform average over all possible microstates with energy EE, because all accessible microstates are equally probable:

⟨O⟩ME=∫ΣEO⁡(Γ)​𝑑Γ∫ΣE𝑑Γ.\langle O\rangle_{\rm{ME}}=\frac{\int_{\Sigma_{E}}O(\Gamma)d\Gamma}{\int_{\Sigma_{E}}d\Gamma}\,. (4.1.2)

Let us then assume the system to be in a non-equilibrium initial state where its macroscopic properties do not match the predictions of statistical mechanics. According to classical ergodicity, as the system evolves, the interactions between particles lead to a redistribution of energy and momentum, causing the system to explore the whole hypersurface ΣE\Sigma_{E} of the phase space. Over time, the system “forgets” its initial conditions (except for conserved quantities like energy) and its macroscopic observables settle down to values that match the microcanonical ensemble predictions [737]. Once thermalization is complete, the long-time average in Eq. 4.1.1 matches the microcanonical ensemble average in Eq. 4.1.2 and O¯=⟨O⟩ME\bar{O}=\langle O\rangle_{\rm{ME}}. The system is then said to be in thermal equilibrium.

While a robust proof of ergodicity is typically challenging, a few examples have been demonstrated to display thermalization, such as gases in hard spheres in some volumes, a.k.a. Sinai billiards [781], and the Bunimovich Stadium [782], describing a free particle inside a stadium with hard walls that are circular on the sides and straight in the middle.

Of course, for an integrable system, i.e. with an extensive number of conserved quantities ∼N\sim N, its motion is constrained in a very small subportion of the hypersurface ΣE\Sigma_{E} which strongly depends on the initial conditions, and the whole dynamics reveals (quasi-)periodic. In such cases, ergodicity does not hold, as the statistical mechanics average is not applicable.

4.2 Thermalization in Quantum Systems

While for classical systems the connection between ergodicity of isolated systems and statistical mechanics is quite straightforward, a more accurate analysis is needed to understand how isolated quantum systems reaches thermal equilibrium, as in these case position rr and momentum pp do not commute and we cannot rely on the phase space.

Let us consider a finite non-integrable11 1 If the system has a set of symmetries, we assume that all of them are resolved. NN-body quantum system with NN sufficiently large and a non-degenerate Hamiltonian spectrum:

H^=∑α=1NEα​|Φα⟩⟨Φα|,\hat{H}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{N}E_{\alpha}\outerproduct{\Phi_{\alpha}}{\Phi_{\alpha}}\,, (4.2.1)

where {Eα}α=1​…​N\quantity{E_{\alpha}}_{\alpha=1\dots N} and {|Φα⟩}α=1​…​N\quantity{\ket{\Phi_{\alpha}}}_{\alpha=1\dots N} are the corresponding eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Let us then assume to quench the system with an initial pure22 2 Generalizations of ETH to mixed states are discussed in [737]. state |Ψ⁡(0)⟩=∑αCα​|Φα⟩\ket{\Psi(0)}=\sum_{\alpha}C_{\alpha}\ket{\Phi_{\alpha}}, whose energy is well defined, extensive in NN33 3 This corresponds to assume that each d.o.f. has a finite amount of energy, and the system energy is far above the ground state energy. and robut under (subextensive) fluctuations:

E\displaystyle E =⟨H⟩=⟨Ψ⁡(0)|H|Ψ⁡(0)⟩∼N\displaystyle=\langle H\rangle=\expectationvalue{H}{\Psi(0)}\sim N Δ​E\displaystyle\Delta E =⟨H2⟩−⟨H⟩2∼Nνwith​ν<0.\displaystyle=\sqrt{\langle H^{2}\rangle-\langle H\rangle^{2}}\sim N^{\nu}\qquad\rm{with}\;\nu<0. (4.2.2)

In the Schrödinger picture, the system can be described in terms of the state

|Ψ⁡(t)⟩\displaystyle\ket{\Psi(t)} =∑αCαe−itEα/ℏ|Φα⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\alpha}C_{\alpha}e^{-itE_{\alpha}/\hbar}\ket{\Phi_{\alpha}} where ∑α|Cα|2\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2} =1.\displaystyle=1\,. (4.2.3)

Correspondingly, any generic (local) observable OO can be instantaneously measured as follows

O⁡(t)=⟨Ψ⁡(t)|O|Ψ⁡(t)⟩=∑α,βCα∗​Cβ​ei​t​(Eα−Eβ)​Oα​β=∑α|Cα|2​Oα​α+∑α,α≠βCα∗​Cβ​ei​t​(Eα−Eβ)​Oα​β\begin{split}O(t)&=\expectationvalue{\obs}{\Psi(t)}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}C_{\alpha}^{*}C_{\beta}e^{it(E_{\alpha}-E_{\beta})}O_{\alpha\beta}\\ &=\sum_{\alpha}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}O_{\alpha\alpha}+\sum_{\alpha,\alpha\neq\beta}C_{\alpha}^{*}C_{\beta}e^{it(E_{\alpha}-E_{\beta})}O_{\alpha\beta}\end{split} (4.2.4)

where Oα​β=⟨Φα​|O|​Φβ⟩O_{\alpha\beta}=\expectationvalue{\Phi_{\alpha}|\obs|\Phi_{\beta}}. In analogy to the classical counterpart, we can formally define the long time average resulting from the unitary dynamics of the observable, which is well described by the average value predicted by the diagonal ensemble [741]:

O¯≡limT→∞1T​∫0Td​t​⟨Ψ⁡(t)|O|Ψ⁡(t)⟩=limT→∞1T​∫0Td​t​∑α,βCα∗​Cβ​⟨Φα​|ei​t​H^​O​e−i​t​H^|​Φβ⟩=∑α|Cα|2​Oα​α+∑α,α≠βCα∗​Cβ​Oα​β​limT→∞1T​∫0Tei⁡(Eα−Eβ)​t​𝑑t=∑α|Cα|2​Oα​α≡⟨O⟩DE,\begin{split}\bar{O}&\equiv\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}dt\expectationvalue{\obs}{\Psi(t)}\\ &=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}dt\sum_{\alpha,\beta}C^{*}_{\alpha}C_{\beta}\expectationvalue{\Phi_{\alpha}|e^{it\ham}\obs e^{-it\ham}|\Phi_{\beta}}\\ &=\sum_{\alpha}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}O_{\alpha\alpha}+\sum_{\alpha,\alpha\neq\beta}C^{*}_{\alpha}C_{\beta}O_{\alpha\beta}\cancel{\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}e^{i(E_{\alpha}-E_{\beta})t}dt}\\ &=\sum_{\alpha}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}O_{\alpha\alpha}\equiv\langle O\rangle_{\rm DE},\end{split} (4.2.5)

where the canceled term is exactly due to the dephasing, while ⟨O⟩DE\langle O\rangle_{\rm DE} is the average from the diagonal ensemble. Therefore, after enough time, we expect the observable O⁡(t)O(t) to approach long-time average ⟨O⟩DE\langle O\rangle_{\rm DE} which however depends on the initial quench of the system through the probabilities |Cα|2\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}, as the latters are conserved in time.

This clearly differs from the expected thermalization, according to which the system relaxes to states whose macroscopic quantities are stationary, universal with respect to different initial conditions, and predictable using statistical mechanics [741]. Namely, thermalization in quantum system requires the long-time average in Eq. 4.2.5 to match the prediction of the microcanonical ensemble (ME), which relies on a superposition within the energy shell [E−Δ​E,E+Δ​E][E-\Delta E,E+\Delta E] around the system energy EE in Eq. 4.2.2 and containing NE,Δ​EN_{E,\Delta E} eigenstates:

⟨O⟩ME=1NE,Δ​E​∑α;|Eα−E|<Δ​EOα​α.\langle O\rangle_{\rm ME}=\frac{1}{N_{E,\Delta E}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha;\\ |E_{\alpha}-E|<\Delta E\end{subarray}}O_{\alpha\alpha}\,. (4.2.6)

4.2.1 The Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH)

In order to prove the equivalence between the two ensemble averages (diagonal and microcanonical) and show ergodicity as an emerging properity out of the microscopical properties of realistic QMB systems, we rely on the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH), originally proposed by Deutsch [738] and Srednicki [739] and later widely confirmed [741]. For a detailed review, we recommend the reader to see [740, 737].

According to the ETH, the matrix elements of the observables displaying thermalization can be expressed in the Hamiltonian eigenbasis by the following ansatz:

Oα​β=O(Eα​β)δα​β+e−𝒮(Eα​β)/2fO(Eα​β,ωα​β)Rα​βO_{\alpha\beta}=O(E_{\alpha\beta})\delta_{\alpha\beta}+e^{-\mathcal{S}(E_{\alpha\beta})/2}f_{O}(E_{\alpha\beta},\omega_{\alpha\beta})R_{\alpha\beta} (4.2.7)

where Eα​β=(Eα+Eβ)/2E_{\alpha\beta}=(E_{\alpha}+E_{\beta})/2, ωα​β=(Eα−Eβ)\omega_{\alpha\beta}=(E_{\alpha}-E_{\beta}), and 𝒮⁡(E)∼N\mathcal{S}(E)\sim N is the thermodynamic entropy at energy EE. Correspondingly, O⁡(Eα​β)O(E_{\alpha\beta}) and fO​(Eα​β,ωα​β)=fO​(Eα​β,−ωα​β)f_{O}(E_{\alpha\beta},\omega_{\alpha\beta})=f_{O}(E_{\alpha\beta},-\omega_{\alpha\beta}) are smooth functions of their arguments, and O⁡(Eα​β)O(E_{\alpha\beta}) equals the expectation value of the microcanonical ensemble at energy Eα​βE_{\alpha\beta}. Ultimately, Rα​β=Rβ​α(∗)R_{\alpha\beta}=R_{\beta\alpha}^{(*)} is a real (complex) variable with zero mean and unit variance (⟨|Rα​β|2⟩=1\langle\absolutevalue{R_{\alpha\beta}}^{2}\rangle=1). Right candidates for observables that are proven to satisfy Eq. 4.2.7 are nn-body observables, with n≪Nn\ll N.

No matter of CαC_{\alpha}, if the fluctuations of the system energy (and correspondingly the energy window of the microcanonical ensemble) are sufficiently small, i.e. Δ​E≪1\Delta E\ll 1, then, applying Eq. 4.2.7, we can assume O⁡(Eα​β)O(E_{\alpha\beta}) to be almost constant ∼O⁡(E)\sim O(E) and approximate the long-time average in Eq. 4.2.5 as:

⟨O⟩DE=∑αN|Cα|2​Oα​α∼O⁡(E)​∑αN|Cα|2=O⁡(E).\langle O\rangle_{\rm DE}=\sum_{\alpha}^{N}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}O_{\alpha\alpha}\sim O(E)\sum_{\alpha}^{N}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}=O(E)\,. (4.2.8)

Similarly, the thermal average given by the microcanonical ensamble reads:

⟨O⟩ME=∑αNE,Δ​EOα​αNE,Δ​E∼O⁡(E)​∑αNE,Δ​E1NE,Δ​E=O⁡(E),\langle O\rangle_{\rm{ME}}=\sum_{\alpha}^{N_{E,\Delta E}}\frac{O_{\alpha\alpha}}{N_{E,\Delta E}}\sim O(E)\sum_{\alpha}^{N_{E,\Delta E}}\frac{1}{N_{E,\Delta E}}=O(E)\,, (4.2.9)

so that, in the end, the long-time average matches the microcanonical ensemble precition. Furthermore, using ETH, we can compute the long-time average of the temporal fluctuations of the observable expectation value:

σO2=limT→∞1T​∫0Td​t​[O​(t)2]−⟨O⟩DE2=limT→∞1T​∫0Td​t​∑α,β,γ,δOα​β​Oγ​δ​Cα∗​Cβ​Cγ∗​Cδ​ei​t​(Eα−Eβ+Eγ−Eδ)−⟨O⟩DE2=∑α,α≠βOα​β​Cα∗​Cβ​∑γ,γ≠δOγ​δ​Cγ∗​Cδ​limT→∞1T​∫0Td​t​ei​t​(Eα−Eβ+Eγ−Eδ)=∑α,α≠β|Oα​β|2​|Cα|2​|Cβ|2≤max⁡|Oα​β|2​∑α,β|Cα|2=max⁡|Oα​β|2∝e−𝒮⁡(E).\begin{split}\sigma_{O}^{2}&=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}dt\quantity[\obs(t)^{2}]-\langle O\rangle_{\rm DE}^{2}\\ &=\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}dt\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta}O_{\alpha\beta}O_{\gamma\delta}C^{*}_{\alpha}C_{\beta}C^{*}_{\gamma}C_{\delta}e^{it(E_{\alpha}-E_{\beta}+E_{\gamma}-E_{\delta})}-\langle O\rangle_{\rm DE}^{2}\\ &=\sum_{\alpha,\alpha\neq\beta}O_{\alpha\beta}C^{*}_{\alpha}C_{\beta}\sum_{\gamma,\gamma\neq\delta}O_{\gamma\delta}C^{*}_{\gamma}C_{\delta}\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}dte^{it(E_{\alpha}-E_{\beta}+E_{\gamma}-E_{\delta})}\\ &=\sum_{\alpha,\alpha\neq\beta}\absolutevalue{\obs_{\alpha\beta}}^{2}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}\absolutevalue{C_{\beta}}^{2}\leq\max\absolutevalue{\obs_{\alpha\beta}}^{2}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\absolutevalue{C_{\alpha}}^{2}=\max\absolutevalue{\obs_{\alpha\beta}}^{2}\propto e^{-\mathcal{S}(E)}\,.\end{split} (4.2.10)

Therefore, time fluctuations of the observable expectation values are exponentially small in the system size. Namely, O⁡(t)O(t) is almost equal at any time to the diagonal ensamble average and no time average is needed. In other words, ETH ansatz implies the ergodicity in the strong sense.

The equivalence between the long-time average and the statistical mechanics prediction is similar to the classical counterpart, where ergodicity can be explained in terms of particle collisions and energy redistribution between different d.o.f.. However, in isolated quantum systems, chaos, ergodicity, and thermalization are hidden in the nature of the Hamiltonian eigenstates. In other words, the information of the eventual thermal state is already encoded in the system from the initial quench, and relaxation of observables to their equilibrium values results from the dephasing originated in time evolution [741, 740, 737].

Numerical evidence of ETH has been found in several strongly correlated nonintegrable lattice models of condensed matter and ultracold atom gases, such as hard-core bosons [741, 742], soft-core bosons [743, 744, 745], interacting spin chains [746, 747, 748, 749], and spinless and spinful fermions [750, 751, 752, 753]. Nowadays, ETH is also applied in contexts like quantum gravity and warmholes [783, 784].

Nevertheless, despite a wide variaty of QMB systems were observed displaying ergodicity and thermalization via ETH, some experiments have recently pointed out strong and weak violations of ETH. Apart from integrable systems, strong violations of ETH have been displayed by more interesting phenomena such as many-body localization (MBL) [785], where thermalization is strongly avoided by means of localized quench disorder.

4.3 Quantum Many-Body Scars and Lattice Gauge Theories

Here, we are interested in cases of weak ergodicity breaking, i.e. refferred to a small portion of the spectrum violating ETH, while the overall system behaving ergodically. Such peculiar eigenstates are called scars (like defects of the spectrum) and have been shown to be at the origin of slow dynamics for cold atoms experiments for some intial states [764, 758, 761]. In the following, we review the main features of such an exotic dynamics, starting from the observations in Ryderg atoms chains in Section 4.3.1 to the intimate connection with Abelian LGTs in Section 4.3.2.

4.3.1 Experimental observations of scars in Rydberg atoms

Experimental observation of slow dynamics, have been remarkably encountered in 1D Rydberg atom arrays of NN optical traps, each of them hosting a atom [758]. Every atom is trapped in its electronic ground state (denoted with |↓⟩𝐧\ket{\downarrow}_{\mathbf{n}}), which is quasirenonantly coupled to a single Rydberg state, i.e. a highly excited electronic level (denoted with |↑⟩𝐧\ket{\uparrow}_{\mathbf{n}}). Overall, the Rydberg atom array behaves like a chain of qubits {|↑,↓⟩}𝐧=1​…​N\quantity{\ket{\uparrow,\downarrow}}_{\mathbf{n}=1\dots N}, whose dynamics is ruled by the following Hamiltonian:

H^Ryd=∑𝐧(Ω​σ^𝐧x+δ​σ^𝐧z)+∑𝐧,𝐧′≠𝐧V𝐧,𝐧′​n^𝐧​n^𝐧′,\hat{H}_{\rm{Ryd}}=\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity(\Omega\Sx_{\vecsite} + \delta\Sz_{\vecsite})+\sum_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}\neq\mathbf{n}}V_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\,, (4.3.1)

where σ^𝐧α\hat{\sigma}^{\alpha}_{\mathbf{n}} are Pauli matrices at site 𝐧\mathbf{n}, while the operator n^𝐧=(σ^jz+1)/2\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n}}=(\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{j}+1)/2 measures the presence of a Rydberg excitation (|↑⟩𝐧\ket{\uparrow}_{\mathbf{n}}) at site 𝐧\mathbf{n}. The coefficients Ω\Omega and δ\delta are the Rabi frequency and the detuning of the laser excitation scheme respectively; the former one describes the coupling between the ground and Rydberg states due to an external driving field, while the second one represents the difference between the driving field frequency and the atomic transition frequency. Correspondingly, V𝐧,𝐧′V_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}} couples the interaction between atoms in their Rydberg states at sites 𝐧\mathbf{n} and 𝐧′\mathbf{n}^{\prime}.

In typical experimental realizations of Rydberg arrays made by optical lattices or optical tweezers, the interaction is strong at short range and decays as 1/|𝐧−𝐧′|61/\absolutevalue{\vecsite-\vecsite^{\prime}}^{6} as in the Van der Waals scenario [758, 786, 787]. Such an interaction is typically approximated with the Rydberg-blockade effect, which assumes V𝐧,𝐧′V_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}} as the largest energy scale of the system, avoiding atoms on neighboring sites to be simoultaneously excited to Rydberg states n^𝐧​n^𝐧+𝝁=0\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}}=0 [758]. Within this approximation, the Hamiltonian in Eq. 4.3.1 can be approximated as done by Fendley, Sengupta, and Sachdev (FSS) in [788]:

H^FSS=∑𝐧(Ω​σ^𝐧x+2​δ​n^𝐧)\hat{H}_{\rm{FSS}}=\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity(\Omega\Sx_{\vecsite}+2\delta\nop_{\vecsite}) (4.3.2)

plus the blockade constraint on neighboring sites. In the limit of zero detuning, Eq. 4.3.2 is equivalent to the PXP model [789]:

H^PXP=∑𝐧P^𝐧−𝝁​σ^𝐧x​P^𝐧+𝝁,\hat{H}_{\rm{PXP}}=\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{P}_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu}}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{P}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu}}\,, (4.3.3)

where P^𝐧\hat{P}_{\mathbf{n}} is a projector enforcing the state in 𝐧\mathbf{n} to be in the groundstate. In both these realizations of the Rydberg Hamiltonian, the experimental and numerical observations of the corresponding dynamics pointed out two different behaviors according to the intial quench of the time evolution [758, 764, 761, 768]. Namely, starting from a configuration with all the Rydberg atoms in their groundstate, i.e. |↓,↓,…,↓,↓⟩\ket{\downarrow,\downarrow,\dots,\downarrow,\downarrow} (empty), the system thermalize, as expected from the ETH discussed in Section 4.2.1, and the average value of observables such as the local density n^\hat{n} matches the corresponding statistical mechanics predictions. Correspondingly, the return fidelity with the initial state |⟨Ψ⁡(0)|Ψ⁡(t)⟩|2\absolutevalue{\braket{\Psi(0)}{\Psi(t)}}^{2} quickly vanishes. Conversely, quenching the dynamics from staggered configurations like the following charge-density wave (CDW) states [768]

|↓,↑,↓,↑,↓,↑,…⟩⁡(CDW1)\displaystyle\ket{\downarrow,\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow,\dots}\rm{(CDW1)} |↑,↓,↑,↓,↑,↓,…⟩⁡(CDW2)\displaystyle\ket{\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow,\downarrow,\uparrow,\downarrow,\dots}\rm{(CDW2)} \displaystyle\,, (4.3.4)

the system undergoes an oscillatory behavior of the local density operator n^​(t)\hat{n}(t) (the return fidelity) between the two states {↓,↑}\quantity{\downarrow,\uparrow} (between CDW1 and CDW2) and escapes quantum thermalization (see Fig6b of [758] and Fig1 of [768]). Such a pattern has also been detected by measuring the half-chain entanglement entropy, whose growth in time is slow and oscillating with the same period of density oscillations (see Fig10 of [758]). Moreover, the energy spectrum has revealed the presence of some scar states characterized by a high overlap with the initial quench state [761]. As we will see, the oscillating behavior between CDW1 and CDW2 passing from the full ground state, can be mapped into a process of particle-antiparticle pairs creation and annihilation, which is a foundational mechanism occurring in high-energy [768].

4.3.2 Scars in Abelian Lattice Gauge Theories

Indeed, it has been recently demonstrated that the experimental model of Ryderg atoms can be mapped into a spin-1/21/2 Quantum Link Model (QLM) version of a U(1) LGT [768] and correspondingly, the observation of scarring dynamics can be associated to high-energy physics phenomena such as the Schwinger mechanism [790]. In particular, we can then identify the computational basis of configurations allowed by the Rydberg blockade with the classical configurations of the electric field allowed by Gauss law.

In detail, a Rydberg atom chain in the Rydberg-blockade approximation can be mapped into a (1+1)D realization of the QED Hamiltonian in Eq. 1.4.1:

H^=−w∑𝐧[ψ^𝐧†​U^𝐧,𝝁​ψ𝐧+𝝁+h.c]+m∑𝐧(−1)𝐧ψ^𝐧†ψ^𝐧+J∑𝐧E^𝐧,𝝁2,\hat{H}=-w\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[\hpsi_{\vecsite}^{\dagger}\Apara_{\genlink}\psi_{\vecsite+\latvec}+\hc]+m\sum_{\mathbf{n}}(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}+J\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{E}^{2}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}\,, (4.3.5)

where w=1/2w=1/2, m=m0​c/ℏm=m_{0}c/\hbar, and J=g2/2J=g^{2}/2 are adimensional parameters44 4 Similarly to Eq. 3.1.2, for numerical simulations, we made the Hamiltonian in Eq. 1.4.1 adimensional by multiplying it by a0/(c​ℏ)a_{0}/(c\hbar).. In the finite truncation of U(1) discussed in Section 1.4.2, the gauge fields can be represented by spin-jj variables [533, 531]:

E^𝐧,𝝁\displaystyle\hat{E}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} =S^𝐧,𝝁z​(j)\displaystyle=\hat{S}^{z}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}(j) U^𝐧,𝝁\displaystyle\hat{U}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} =S^𝐧,𝝁+​(j)\displaystyle=\hat{S}^{+}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}(j) [E^𝐧,𝝁,U^𝐧,𝝁]\displaystyle\commutator{\eleE_{\genlink}}{\Apara_{\genlink}} =S^𝐧,𝝁+​(j).\displaystyle=\hat{S}^{+}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}(j)\,. (4.3.6)

At any finite truncation, U(1) Gauss law always requires that G^𝐧​|Ψphys⟩=0\hat{G}_{\mathbf{n}}\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}=0 ∀𝐧\forall\mathbf{n}, where G^𝐧\hat{G}_{\mathbf{n}} is the local generator of the U(1) gauge symmetry defined in Eq. 1.4.4 and constrains the electric fields incoming and outcoming from a local site to match the corresponding amount of charge:

G^𝐧=E^𝐧,𝝁−E^𝐧−𝝁,𝝁−ψ^𝐧†​ψ^𝐧+1−(−1)𝐧2.\hat{G}_{\mathbf{n}}=\hat{E}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}-\hat{E}_{{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu},{\bf\it\mu}}}-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}^{\dagger}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}}+\frac{1-(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}}{2}\,. (4.3.7)

In particular, due to the use of staggered fermions, an empty odd site corresponds to the presence of an anti-particle of charge q¯\bar{q}, while occupied odd sites implies to the presence of a particle of charge qq (assuming that U(1) q<0q<0, as it refers to the electron). Namely, indicating with |Ω⟩𝐧\ket{\Omega}_{\mathbf{n}} an empty matter state in site 𝐧\mathbf{n}, and with |∅⟩𝐧\ket{\varnothing}_{\mathbf{n}} the corresponding absence of charge, we have:

|Ω⟩𝐧,​e​v​e​n\displaystyle\ket{\Omega}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{even}} =|∅⟩𝐧,​e​v​e​n\displaystyle=\ket{\varnothing}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{even}}\qquad\qquad |Ω⟩𝐧,​o​d​d\displaystyle\ket{\Omega}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{odd}} =|q¯⟩𝐧,​o​d​d\displaystyle=\ket{\bar{\charge}}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{odd}} (4.3.8)
ψ^†​|Ω⟩𝐧,​e​v​e​n\displaystyle\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}\ket{\Omega}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{even}} =|q⟩𝐧,​e​v​e​n\displaystyle=\ket{\charge}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{even}}\qquad\qquad ψ^†​|Ω⟩𝐧,​o​d​d\displaystyle\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}\ket{\Omega}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{odd}} =|∅⟩𝐧,​o​d​d.\displaystyle=\ket{\varnothing}_{\mathbf{n},\emph{odd}}\,.
Mapping the Rydberg blockade into the U(1) Gauss law

To understand the connection between the two models, let us reconsider from the Rydberg blockade. When the latter holds, such as in Eqs. 4.3.2 and 4.3.3, the total Hilbert space is restricted to those states without double occupancies on neighboring sites. Then, the effective Hilber space of each pair of neighboring Rydberg atoms along the chain within the Rydberg-blockade approximation is

|1⟩Ryd\displaystyle\ket{1}_{\rm{Ryd}} =|↑,↓⟩\displaystyle=\ket{\uparrow,\downarrow} |2⟩Ryd\displaystyle\ket{2}_{\rm{Ryd}} =|↓,↓⟩\displaystyle=\ket{\downarrow,\downarrow} |3⟩Ryd\displaystyle\ket{3}_{\rm{Ryd}} =|↓,↑⟩.\displaystyle=\ket{\downarrow,\uparrow}\,. (4.3.9)

Correspondingly, in the j=1/2j=1/2 finite truncation of U(1) gauge fields, the effective Hilbert space of a matter site coupled with its attached (left and right) gauge links is made of configurations like |E^𝐧,−𝝁,q𝐧,E^𝐧,+𝝁⟩\ket{\eleE_{\vecsite,-\latvec},\charge_{\vecsite}, \eleE_{\vecsite,+\latvec}}, Denoting E^=+1/2\hat{E}=+1/2 (E^=−1/2\hat{E}=-1/2) with →\rightarrow (←\leftarrow), in the staggered fermion solution we have

|1⟩U⁡(1)even\displaystyle\ket{1}^{\rm{even}}_{\rm{U(1)}} =|→,∅,→⟩\displaystyle=\ket{\rightarrow, \varnothing, \rightarrow} |2⟩U⁡(1)even\displaystyle\ket{2}^{\rm{even}}_{\rm{U(1)}} =|←,q,→⟩\displaystyle=\ket{\leftarrow, q, \rightarrow} |3⟩U⁡(1)even\displaystyle\ket{3}^{\rm{even}}_{\rm{U(1)}} =|←,∅,←⟩\displaystyle=\ket{\leftarrow, \varnothing, \leftarrow} (4.3.10a)
|1⟩U⁡(1)odd\displaystyle\ket{1}^{\rm{odd}}_{\rm{U(1)}} =|→,∅,→⟩\displaystyle=\ket{\rightarrow, \varnothing, \rightarrow} |2⟩U⁡(1)odd\displaystyle\ket{2}^{\rm{odd}}_{\rm{U(1)}} =|→,q¯,←⟩\displaystyle=\ket{\rightarrow, \bar{\charge}, \leftarrow} |3⟩U⁡(1)odd\displaystyle\ket{3}^{\rm{odd}}_{\rm{U(1)}} =|←,∅,←⟩.\displaystyle=\ket{\leftarrow, \varnothing, \leftarrow}\,. (4.3.10b)

One can then associate the effective Hilbert space of neighboring Rydberg atoms in Eq. 4.3.9 with the U(1) gauge invariant configurations of Eq. 4.3.10 (for even and odd sites respectively). Correspondingly, states violating Gauss law are exactly mapped into the nearest-neighbor occupied sites which are strongly suppressed by the Rydberg blockade. A pictorial representation of such a correspondence is given in Fig1 of [768].

We can further identify the Hamiltonian parameters Ω=−w\Omega=-w, δ=−m\delta=-m and the operators

σ^𝐧z\displaystyle\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{\mathbf{n}} ↔(−1)𝐧​2​S^𝐧−𝝁,𝝁z\displaystyle\leftrightarrow(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}2\hat{S}^{z}_{{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu},{\bf\it\mu}}} σ^𝐧x\displaystyle\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{\mathbf{n}} ↔[ψ^𝐧−𝝁†​S^𝐧−𝝁,𝝁+​ψ^𝐧+h.c]\displaystyle\leftrightarrow\quantity[\hpsi_{\vecsite-\latvec}^{\dagger}\spinmat[+]_{\genlinkm}\hpsi_{\vecsite} +\hc] σ^𝐧y\displaystyle\hat{\sigma}^{y}_{\mathbf{n}} ↔−i​(−1)𝐧​[ψ^𝐧−𝝁†​S^𝐧−𝝁,𝝁+​ψ^𝐧+h.c],\displaystyle\leftrightarrow-\text{i}(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}\quantity[\hpsi_{\vecsite-\latvec}^{\dagger}\spinmat[+]_{\genlinkm}\hpsi_{\vecsite} +\hc]\,, (4.3.11)

so that the two Hamiltonians in Eqs. 4.3.5 and 4.3.2 are equivalent.

4.3.3 Gauge theory interpretation of slow dynamics

Remarkably, beyond providing a direct link between Gauss law and the Rydberg blockade mechanism, the connection between Eq. 4.3.2 and Eq. 4.3.5 with the mapping in Eq. 4.3.11 provides an immediate connection between Rydberg-blockade chains experiments and the U(1) LGT. We can then interpret the slow dynamics observed in Rydberg atoms [758] in terms of particle-antiparticle pairs production in high-energy physics. In particular, the two charge density wave states CDW1 and CDW2 of [768] can be mapped into the two uniform electric field states E^𝐧,𝝁=±1/2\hat{E}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}=\pm 1/2. Namely, we can map the empty Rydberg configuration and the ones in Eq. 4.3.4 into the following states:

(CDW1)\displaystyle\rm{(CDW1)} ⟷\displaystyle\longleftrightarrow |→,∅,→,∅,→,∅,→,∅,→⟩\displaystyle\ket{\rightarrow, \varnothing, \rightarrow, \varnothing, \rightarrow, \varnothing, \rightarrow,\varnothing, \rightarrow} (String)\displaystyle{\rm\displaystyle(String)} (4.3.12)
(empty)\displaystyle\rm{(empty)} ⟷\displaystyle\longleftrightarrow |←,q,→,q¯,←,q,→,q¯,←⟩\displaystyle\ket{\leftarrow, \charge\,, \rightarrow, \bar{\charge}\,, \leftarrow, \charge\,, \rightarrow,\bar{\charge}\,, \leftarrow} (Pairs)\displaystyle{\rm\displaystyle(Pairs)}
(CDW2)\displaystyle\rm{(CDW2)} ⟷\displaystyle\longleftrightarrow |←,∅,←,∅,←,∅,←,∅,←⟩\displaystyle\ket{\leftarrow, \varnothing, \leftarrow, \varnothing, \leftarrow, \varnothing, \leftarrow,\varnothing, \leftarrow} (anti−String),\displaystyle{\rm\displaystyle(anti-String)}\,,

where the string (anti-string) refers to a uniform rightward (leftward) electric flux, while pairs refers to the state filled by adjacent particle-antiparticle pairs.

Then, the long-lived oscillations between the CDW1 and CDW2 states observed in the Rydberg-blockade chain are related to the rightward-leftward switch of the electric flux passing throught the intermediate production of particle-antiparticle pairs. Such a pattern is called string inversion and is directly tied to string breaking [790, 791, 792] prototypical of gauge theories including dynamical matter.

Remarkably, this mechanism is disturbed by quantum fluctuations, which are controlled by the dimensionless ratio m/wm/w. In detail, for m<0.655​w=mcm<0.655w=m_{c}, particle-antiparticle pairs are created, which accelerates in an electric field and gradually screens it. Eventually, coherent pair annihilation takes place, leading to a state with an opposite electric flux. Such an inversion happens several times, causing the slow dynamics in the system. This leads to a significant slowdown of thermalization and limits quantum information propagation. Conversely, when the particle mass exceeds a critical value (m>mcm>m_{c}), pair production becomes a virtual process and string inversion does not occur. This marks a different phase of the system’s evolution, preventing the formation of real particle pairs. This transition is related to a quantum phase transition observed in the FSS model in Eq. 4.3.2 at a critical detuning δc\delta_{c} [788] and corresponds to the spontaneous breaking of chiral symmetry in the U(1) LGT [768, 511].

4.4 Scars in Non-Abelian Lattice Gauge Theories

Given the intimate connection between QMBS and LGTs, and the current large effort to quantum simulate the latter [793, 568, 565, 794, 795, 541, 570, 545, 544, 732, 769, 796], it is important to investigate the origin of QMBS in connection to gauge symmetry by exploring its possible occurrence in non-Abelian LGTs with dynamical matter. In particular, investigating a high-energy context of QMBS requires the inclusion of dynamical matter, as demonstrated in the Abelian scenario.

In this section, we report and discuss the exact diagonalization (ED) and matrix product state (MPS) results of [438] that showcase robust QMBS dynamics in a non-Abelian SU(2) LGT with dynamical matter starting in simple initial product states (Section 4.4.1). We show how the QMBS dynamics involve state transfer through meson and baryon-anti-baryon bare states, highlighting the non-Abelian nature of this scarred behavior. In addition to the exotic dynamics observed in Section 4.4.2 and the spectral properties of the model discussed in Section 4.4.3, we enrobust our results with further analyses. In Section 4.4.4, we observe that log-time average of local observables displayed in Fig. 4.1 are not compatible with the thermal relaxation expected for other initial states at the same energy. In Section 4.4.5, we demonstrate how, for other parameter regimes, the spectral and dynamical properites of the two initial product states are compatible with the ergodic behavior predicted by statistical mechanics (microcanonical ensemble). Conversely, we further illustrate how the scars-induced revivals of Fig. 4.1 persist for larges gauge-field trunctations (Section 4.4.6), at larger system sizes (Section 4.4.7), and over longer timescales (Section 4.4.8) for the candidate initial states. These results confirm the overall ergodic nature of the model and regard the observed scarring behavior as a weak violation of ETH and the expected thermalization.

4.4.1 The model

As a prototypical model to probe non-ergodic dynamics in non-Abelian gauge theories, we consider a (1+1)D matter-coupled hardcore-gluon SU(2) LGT [578, 438, 437, 590, 484, 551] such as the one derived in Section 1.3.5. The model describes a matter quark field of mass mm, living on lattice sites 𝐧\mathbf{n}, coupled to a truncated SU(2) gauge field, defined on lattice links | see Fig. 4.1. The quark field is a staggered fermion doublet ψ^𝐧,α\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}, obeying the anticommutation relations in Eq. 1.3.4: {ψ^𝐧,α,ψ^𝐧′,β†}=ℏ​δ𝐧,𝐧′​δα,β\anticommutator*{\hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha}}{\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite^{\prime},\beta}}{=}\hbar\delta_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{\alpha,\beta} [583], where α,β∈{r,g}\alpha,\beta\in\quantity{\rla,\gla} span SU(2) colors. A basis for matter sites is

{|0⟩,|r⟩=ψ^r†​|0⟩,|g⟩=ψ^g†​|0⟩,|2⟩=ψ^r†​ψ^g†​|0⟩}.\quantity{ {\ket{0}},\, {\ket{\rla} = \hpsi^{\dagger}_{\rla}\ket{0}},\, {\ket{\gla} = \hpsi^{\dagger}_{\gla}\ket{0}},\, {\ket{2} = \hpsi^{\dagger}_{\rla} \hpsi^{\dagger}_{\gla}\ket{0}} }. (4.4.1)

Gauge link states can be expanded in the basis |j,mL,mR⟩\ket{j, \mL, \mR}, where mL,mR∈{−j,…,+j}m_{\mathrm{L}},m_{\mathrm{R}}\in\{-j,\ldots,+j\} index spin-jj states, and the link energy density operator is diagonal and coincides with the quadratic Casimir, E^2​|j,mL,mR⟩=j⁡(j​+1)​|j,mL,mR⟩\hat{E}^{2}\ket{j, \mL, \mR}=j(j\mathop{+}1)\ket{j, \mL, \mR} [595]. Adopting a hardcore-gluon truncation, we restrict jj to {0,1/2}\{0,1/2\}, namely keep only basis states reachable from the singlet |00⟩\ket{00} via at most a single application of the parallel transporter U^α​β\hat{U}^{\alpha\beta}: {|00⟩,|r​r⟩,|g​g⟩,|g​r⟩,|r​g⟩}\quantity{\ket{00},\ket{\rla\rla},\ket{\gla\gla},\ket{\gla\rla},\ket{\rla\gla}}, where r(g)=+(−)1/2{\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0}r}({\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0}g})=+(-)1/2.

Correspondingly, non-Abelian Gauss law mandates that physical states are local gauge singlets, G^𝐧ν​|Ψphys⟩≡0,∀𝐧,ν∈{x,y,z}\hat{G}^{\nu}_{\mathbf{n}}\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}\equiv 0,\;\forall\mathbf{n},\,\nu\in\{x,y,z\}, where G^𝐧ν\hat{G}^{\nu}_{\mathbf{n}} are the generators of local rotations at site 𝐧\mathbf{n} and defined in Eq. 1.3.5. In numerical simulations, we enforce this constraint using a dressed site approach, which yields a defermionized qudit model with a 66-dimensional local basis discussed of Eq. 1.3.69 [578].

The dynamics is governed by the Kogut-Susskind (adimensional) Hamiltonian [579] employing staggered fermions and defined in Eq. 1.3.67 on an NN-site lattice with spacing a0a_{0}

H^=12​∑𝐧∑α,β[−i​ψ^𝐧,α†​U^𝐧,𝝁α​β​ψ𝐧+𝝁,β+h.c]+m​∑𝐧,α(−1)𝐧​ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ𝐧,α+g22​∑𝐧E^𝐧,𝝁2.\hat{H}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\quantity[-i\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha}\NApara_{\genlink}\psi_{\vecsite+\latvec,\beta}+\hc]+m\sum_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\psi_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}{+}\frac{g^{2}}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\hat{E}^{2}_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}}. (4.4.2)

where, similarly to Eq. 3.1.2, for the sake of numerical simulations, we rescaled the Hamiltonian with dimensionaless couplings such as m=m0​c/ℏm=m_{0}c/\hbar and g2=q2​a02⋅(c​ℏ​ϵ0)−1g^{2}=q^{2}a_{0}^{2}\cdot(c\hbar\epsilon_{0})^{-1}. Values reported in the Figures refer to these rescaled quantities.

4.4.2 Observing scarred dynamics

To investigate the presence of non-ergodic behavior in this model, we consider the Schrödinger time evolution of different initial states |Ψ⁡(t​=0)⟩\ket{\Psi(t\mathop=0)}, across various parameter regimes. The time evolution is performed on a chain of N=30N=30 sites via MPS methods55 5 In detailed, simulations we obtained from the iTensor Library [797, 798].. As initial configuration, we first consider the polarized bare vacuum (PV), which consists of the matter sites in the bare vacuum configuration, while the gauge sites in the excited electric field state,

|ΨPV⟩=|…​2020​…⟩m​|⋯r​g−g​r2⋯r​g−g​r2⋯⟩g,\ket{\Psi_{\rm{PV}}}{=}\ket{\dots 2020\dots}_{\mathrm{m}}\ket*{\cdots\frac{\rla\gla-\gla\rla}{\sqrt{2}} \cdots\frac{\rla\gla-\gla\rla}{\sqrt{2}} \cdots}_{\mathrm{g}}, (4.4.3)

where |⋅⟩m\ket{\:\cdot\:}_{\mathrm{m}} and |⋅⟩g\ket{\:\cdot\:}_{\mathrm{g}} refer to the matter and gauge subsystems, respectively. Here (mR)𝐧−𝝁,𝐧(m_{\mathrm{R}})_{\mathbf{n}-{\bf\it\mu},\mathbf{n}} and (mL)𝐧,𝝁(m_{\mathrm{L}})_{{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}} around each bulk site 𝐧\mathbf{n} are valence-bonded in a singlet. In the qudit formulation of the model (see Section 1.3.5 and [578]), the state in Eq. 4.4.3 becomes a product state:

|ΨPV⟩=|6⟩​|2⟩​…​|6⟩​|2⟩,\ket{\Psi_{\rm{PV}}}=\ket{6}\ket{2}\dots\ket{6}\ket{2}, (4.4.4)

We identify two regimes avoiding thermalization: the large-mass one, m≫(g2,1)m\gg(g^{2},1), and the large-coupling one, g2≫(m,1)g^{2}\gg(m,1). For each regime, we compute the return fidelity between the initial state and the evolved state, ℱ⁡(t)=|⟨Ψ⁡(t)|Ψ⁡(0)⟩|2\mathcal{F}(t)=\absolutevalue{\braket{\Psi(t)}{\Psi(0)}}^{2}, shown in Fig. 4.1. After an initial complete system relaxation, we observe persistent revivals, signaling a clear deviation from the expected ergodic behavior. The revivals occur approximately periodically, with the period indicated in the figure for both the considered regimes.

The observed dynamics can be understood as a process of persistent particle pair creation out of an initial false vacuum [562, 512, 521]. To see this, we define the (staggered) site occupancy operator,

𝒩^𝐧=(−1)𝐧​∑α[ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧,α−1−(−1)𝐧2],\hat{\mathcal{N}}_{\mathbf{n}}=(-1)^{\mathbf{n}}\sum_{\alpha}\quantity[\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha}\hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha}-\frac{1-(-1)^{\vecsite}}{2}]\,, (4.4.5)

which counts the number of quarks (on even sites) or antiquarks (on odd sites). Then, we compute the average occupancy ϱq​(t)\varrho_{q}(t) of each 𝒩𝐧\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{n}} eigenvalue (single site quark occupancy, q∈{0,1,2}q\in\{0,1,2\}), projecting on the corresponding eigensubspace of 𝒩𝐧\mathcal{N}_{\mathbf{n}} and averaging over all sites nn:

ϱq​(t)=1N​∑𝐧⟨Ψ⁡(t)|δ𝒩𝐧,q|Ψ⁡(t)⟩.\varrho_{q}(t)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\mathbf{n}}\expectationvalue{\delta_{\mathcal{N}_{\vecsite}, q}}{\Psi(t)}\,. (4.4.6)

As lately discussed in Section 4.4.4, they oscillate around average values that do not coincide with the ones predicted by thermal ensembles, confirming deviations from ergodic behavior. Large values of either mass or coupling confine the system dynamics close to the initial state, creating few particle pair excitations in the system. In the large-mass regime, most of the excitations are meson-like (quark and antiquark adjacent pairs with an excited shared gauge link). In the large-coupling regime, the formation of pairs of baryon- (quark pair) and antibaryon- (antiquark pair) like excitations becomes likely as well, as shown by the enhanced double occupancy with respect to the large-mass regime.

Finally, the last row of Fig. 4.1 shows the evolution of the bipartite entanglement entropy defined as 𝒮=−Tr⁡[ϱA​log⁡ϱA]\mathcal{S}=-\Tr[\varrho_{A}\log\varrho_{A}], where AA and BB indicate the two halves of the chain and ϱA=TrB⁡[ϱA​B]\varrho_{A}=\Tr_{B}[\varrho_{AB}] is the reduced density operator of subsystem AA. In both cases, we observe a slow growth of the entanglement entropy after an initial fast increase up to the first fidelity revival peak. The oscillations on top of the growth are driven by the successive fidelity revivals, which indeed have the same period.

In addition to the polarized bare vacuum initial state, we also observe similar scarred-like dynamics for the bare vacuum (V) state: the ground state of the Hamiltonian in Eq. 4.4.2 without the hopping term, made of alternated doubly occupied and empty sites, and trivial links,

|ΨV​(t=0)⟩=|…​2020​…⟩m​|…​0000​…⟩g.\ket{\Psi_{\rm{V}}(t=0)}=\ket{\dots 2020\dots}_{\mathrm{m}}\ket{\dots 0000\dots}_{\mathrm{g}}\,. (4.4.7)

which in the qudit formulation (see Section 1.3.5 and [578]) reads:

|ΨV⟩=|5⟩​|1⟩​…​|5⟩​|1⟩.\ket{\Psi_{\rm{V}}}=\ket{5}\ket{1}\dots\ket{5}\ket{1}. (4.4.8)

The resulting non-ergodic dynamics is displayed on the right-side of Fig. 4.1. Compared to the polarized vacuum case, the oscillation’s period in the fidelity revivals and occupancy is smaller. As discussed in the following section, it can be explained by the many-body spectrum. The large coupling regime is characterized by a faster entanglement growth, consistently with a corresponding lower return fidelity. Although in the regimes considered this product state is energetically close to the true ground state of the model, the observed dynamics is driven by nontrivial physics. This is evident from the significant oscillations observed in the average occupancy, which lead the system significantly away from its initial configuration.

4.4.3 Tower of scar states

To determine whether the observed non-ergodic dynamics originates from QMB scars, we perform ED up to N=10N=10 sites and, for each eigenstate in the many-body spectrum {|Φs⟩}\{\ket{\Phi_s}\}, we compute the overlap

𝒪PV/V=|⟨ΨPV/V|Φs⟩|2\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{PV/V}}=\absolutevalue*{\braket{\Psi_{\mathrm{PV/V}}}{\Phi_s}}^{2} (4.4.9)

and the bipartite entanglement entropy SS with the two considered initial states (polarized, PV, and unpolarized bare vacua, V). These quantities are plotted in Fig. 4.2, for both regimes where we observe revivals in the return fidelity. For each candidate QMBS regime, we find a ‘tower of scar states’ (highlighted by red circles) characterized by a high overlap with the initial product states and entanglement low enough (compared to the rest of the many-body spectrum) to give rise to scarring behavior. In each case, the energy gap between the scar states in the tower, Δ​E\Delta E (reported in Fig. 4.2), approximately matches the frequency of the revivals observed in the return fidelity from Fig. 4.1, Δ​E≈2​π/T\Delta E\approx 2\pi/T. The correspondence between spectral and dynamical features allows us to conclude that QMBS is indeed the underlying mechanism behind the non-ergodic dynamics shown in Fig. 4.1.

4.4.4 Ergodic dynamics for other initial states

In order to prove the scarring behavior as a specific feature of the configurations in Eqs. 4.4.3 and 4.4.7 and not of all the initial states, we consider the microcanonical ensemble (ME) state constructed as a uniform coherent superposition of all eigenstates lying within a small energy window around the quench energy of the polarized vacuum state EPV=⟨ΨPV|H^|ΨPV⟩E_{\rm PV}{=}\expectationvalue*{\ham}{\Psi_{\rm PV}}. Namely, we define the thermal state

|ΨPVME⟩=1NEPV,δ​E​∑s,|Es−EPV|<δ​E|Φs⟩,\ket{\Psi^{\rm ME}_{\rm PV}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{E_{\rm PV},\delta E}}}\sum\nolimits_{s,\>|E_{s}-E_{\rm PV}|<\delta E}\ket{\Phi_s}, (4.4.10)

where δ​E=⟨ΨPV|H^2|ΨPV⟩−EPV2\delta E{=}\sqrt{\expectationvalue*{\ham^2}{\Psi_{\rm PV}}-E_{\rm PV}^{2}} defines the energy shell [EPV−δ​E,EPV+δ​E][E_{\rm PV}{-}\delta E,E_{\rm PV}{+}\delta E], and NEPV,δ​EN_{E_{\rm PV},\delta E} is the number of eigenstates in this energy shell [741].

In Fig. 4.3, we compares the evolution of this state to that of |ΨPV⟩\ket{\Psi_{\rm PV}}, in the identified scarred regimes. As the plot illustrates, the microcanonical state exhibits ergodic behavior: return fidelities relax toward zero (up to minor oscillations attributable to the finite lattice size) and the single occupancy ϱ1\varrho_{1} remains close to its microcanonical ensemble average ⟨ϱ1⟩ME\expectationvalue*{\density_{1}}_{\rm ME} [741]. In contrast, for the polarized vacuum, ϱ1\varrho_{1} widely oscillates around its long-time average (diagonal ensemble) ⟨ϱ1⟩DE\expectationvalue*{\density_{1}}_{\rm DE} largely deviates from the thermal result. We thus conclude that the observed non-ergodic dynamics strictly depends on the initial conditions and escapes an otherwise thermal behavior through the occurrence of scar states in the many-body spectrum.

4.4.5 Ergodic dynamics for other parameter regimes

We have shown that the two considered initial product states polarized bare vacuum (PV) and bare vacuum (V), escape thermalization for the two regimes (m=5,g2=1)(m=5,g^{2}=1) and (m=1,g2=5)(m=1,g^{2}=5). To confirm the scarring nature of the observed non-ergodic dynamics, we investigate the absence of scars states in the many-body spectrum for other parameter regimes. In Fig. 4.4[Left], we look at the overlap of the full many-body spectrum with the two considered initial states PV and V and the corresponding bipartite entanglement entropy for different values of g2=mg^{2}=m.

Rather than in Fig. 4.2, we do not observe a clear emergence of a tower of states, and thus, we expect ergodic dynamics for the two considered states. This is also confirmed by the time evolution of the two initial states for g2=m=1g^{2}=m=1 displayed in Fig. 4.4[Right]. In this case, the fidelity does not exhibit persistent revivals, and the entanglement entropy shows rapid growth compared to the previously observed scarred dynamics. Moreover, as expected for thermalization, the occupancy relaxes to a steady value compatible with the microcanonical ensemble averages.

We leave any further investigations on scarring dynamics for other candidate initial states to future work. To this extent, it could be interesting to investigate the g2=m=0.1g^{2}=m=0.1 case, whose many-body spectrum contains extremely low entanglement entropy states.

4.4.6 Scars at higher gauge link truncation

It is interesting to highlight that the scarring dynamics observed for the minimal truncation in Fig. 4.1, is not a feature of the truncation itself. Indeed, a similar behavior is displayed in the next gauge truncation jmax=1j_{\max}=1, which leads to a dressed-site basis of 10 gauge invariant states. As shown in Fig. 4.5, where we return the fidelity and the entanglement entropy for the same two cases discussed in the main text. Analogously with what has been observed in Abelian LGTs, these results remarkably suggest that the scars dynamics of non-Abelian theories also persist at higher gauge truncations.

4.4.7 Scaling with the system size

Many-body scars represent a polynomial (in number) subset of special non-thermal eigenstates within the full many-body spectrum. This implies that the overlap with the initially considered product states decreases as the system size increases. To investigate this behavior, in Fig. 4.6(a), we plot the return fidelity between the evolved state and two initial scarring states: the polarized bare vacuum (PV) and the bare vacuum (V). Exploiting the slow entanglement growth in the many-body scars regime, we considered system sizes ranging from N=10N=10 to N=50N=50. Although the fidelity peaks decrease with increasing NN as expected, pronounced revivals are still visible even for large chains with N=50N=50 sites. The peaks become sharper, with the fidelity minima approaching zero, accordingly with the expected revivals induced by scars. The maximum amplitude of these peaks follows an exponential scaling in the system size, ℱN=fN\mathcal{F}_{N}=f^{N}, with the extrapolated peak fidelity per site being f=0.97f=0.97 and f=0.98f=0.98 for the PV and V states, respectively. This estimate further demonstrates the robustness of the observed scar dynamics even at large system sizes.

4.4.8 Long-time dynamics

To illustrate how the observed non-ergodic dynamics persist over longer times, we conducted simulations for an extended duration. In Fig. 4.7, we present the same dynamics presented in Fig. 4.1, now up to t=30t=30, nearly ten times longer than previously shown. At this extended duration, we continue to observe persistent revivals and oscillations in both the return fidelity and occupancy. Moreover, in addition to the rapid oscillations with a period T<1T<1 previously discussed, we observe a beating with frequency T∼1T\sim 1 attributed to the non-uniform distribution of scars in energy spacing. Finally, we still observe a slow growth in entanglement at such extended times, consistent with dynamics constrained to the many-body scars subset of the spectrum.

4.5 Summary

In this chapter, we reviewed the foundational concepts of thermalization in isolated quantum many-body (QMB) systems. We discussed how quantum thermalization is governed by the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) [737], which connects the equilibration over time to the dephasing mechanism of the spectrum eigenstates, as seen in a wide variety of models including bosonic, fermionic, and spin systems.

After this introduction, we highlighted the emergence of weak ergodicity breaking in recent studies [758, 764, 761], where a novel class of special non-thermal eigenstates, known as quantum many-body scars (QMBS), was identified. These scarred eigenstates exhibit anomalously low entanglement entropy and result in the system displaying long-lived oscillations and persistent revivals in quench dynamics, effectively violating the predictions of ETH.

This behavior was first observed experimentally in systems of Rydberg atoms, where scarred dynamics manifest in the form of coherent oscillations in local observables and revivals in state fidelity. Furthermore, we explored how this phenomenon extends to LGTs, particularly in U(1) models, where QMBS arise in both spin-1/2 [768] and spin-S formulations [771, 770, 799, 789, 778]. These Abelian gauge theories show robust scarring dynamics, tied to the stability of the underlying gauge symmetry. Scars in these systems are deeply connected to the gauge structure and reveal an interplay between the gauge constraints and non-thermal eigenstates.

The original part was the extension of these results to the non-Abelian scenario. In detail, we presented strong numerical evidence for the occurrence of QMB scars in a non-Abelian SU(2) lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter [438]. In particular, starting from simple experimentally friendly vacuum product states, scarred dynamics manifests as persistent oscillations in local observables and periodic revivals in the state fidelity. This dynamics arises from a state transfer through meson and baryon-antibaryon bare states, which allow the system to escape otherwise expected thermalization.

Even though the results were obtained for a non-Abelian lattice gauge theory model with the gauge-link truncated at the lowest nontrivial irreducible representations, we provided evidence that the observed scar dynamics persists even at higher gauge-link truncations, similar to what has recently been observed for Abelian models [771], hinting at the possible survival of QMBS in the Kogut-Susskind limit of the SU(2) model under consideration. These findings demonstrate that the strong connection between QMBS and LGTs persists even for non-Abelian gauge groups, raising the intriguing question of whether such behavior represents an intrinsic feature of more fundamental theories such as quantum chromodynamics.

All the results we presented open the door to exciting future directions. Given the numerical evidence of scar eigenstates with very low bipartite entanglement entropy throughout the entire spectrum, even in regimes where both mm and gg are quite small, it would be interesting to find simple product states showing large overlap with these eigenstates. Additionally, it would be interesting to map the scarring phase diagram for this model as has been done for the PXP model [800], and see how driving protocols can enhance non-Abelian scarring dynamics [789]. Another venue to pursue is exploring the robustness of the non-Abelian scarring uncovered here in two spatial dimensions, as it has been recently done for Abelian gauge theories [778, 779]. This can shed further light on the nature of this non-Abelian scarring and its possible occurrence in the QFT limit. Furthermore, scarring is known to give rise to complex periodicities in the corresponding dynamical quantum phase transitions of Abelian LGTs [801, 802], and it would be interesting to see if this carries over to the non-Abelian case.

Finally, we stress that, as addressed in [578], the qudit formulation of the proposed model is well-suited for conducting a digital quantum simulation on a recently demonstrated trapped-ion qudit quantum processor [601]. This opens up the intriguing possibility to experimentally observe this exotic non-ergodic dynamics in the near future.

Chapter 5 Simulating Lattice Fermion Theories

The quest for quantum simulation of interacting fermionic models [803, 804, 805] is necessary to reach a novel understanding of collective phenomena both at low and high energies [806, 807, 808, 809, 810], but it is hindered by fundamental challenges [811, 473, 812]. While analog quantum simulation, e.g. with optical lattices, has advanced greatly in recent decades [813, 814, 815, 816, 817, 818, 819, 820, 821, 822, 823, 824, 825, 826, 827, 828, 829, 830, 831], it presents limitations in tailoring exotic interactions. And while fermionic digital quantum processors are still at an early stage of development [549, 832], the well-established conventional digital quantum simulation platforms (e.g. superconducting qubits, trapped ions, Rydberg arrays, quantum dots) [552, 553, 554, 555, 556] are built on distinguishable, spatially localized qubits (qudits). In this framework, a Fermion Encoding is the analytical process to exactly convert a fermionic algebra (mutually-anticommuting operations) into a genuinely local algebra (mutually-commuting operations) of qudits.

Such encoding can not be carried out free of cost. Traditional strategies focused on encoding NN Dirac orbitals into NN qubits. By construction, these strategies can not preserve locality and, as a result, end up encoding the ubiquitous two-body interactions into cumbersome WW-body interactions (with WW often addressed as Pauli weight). Alongside recent efforts, which were able to reduce WW from linear to logarithmic in NN [557, 559], a separate sector of strategies arose: encodings attempting to preserve locality [833, 834, 592, 835]. They exhibit a flat Pauli weight (WW does not scale with NN) at the price of requiring a number of qubits larger (but still linear scaling) than the number NN of fermion orbitals. For non-gauge lattice fermion theories, Ref. [717] showed that it is sufficient to add one qubit for each lattice bond to achieve local encoding (a generalization to lattice gauge fermionic theories was also recently introduced [550, 551]). The extra qubits play the role of an effective, discrete lattice gauge field with pure gauge dynamics akin to the Toric Code Hamiltonian [836]. The formal mapping is well understood [837], but evidence of practical feasibility of the local encoding for numerical simulation or digital quantum simulation is still the subject of active research [838, 839].

This chapter is based on the twofold study of Ref. [439] on the feasibility of the local fermion encoding for classical and quantum simulation, as summarized in Fig. 5.1: on one hand side, we investigate its performance for ground-state numerical simulations based on tensor network (TN) ansatz states. On the other side, we numerically test its applicability and scalability for digital quantum simulation on a generic platform (considering standard 1-qubit and 2-qubit programmable dynamical resources), by numerically emulating the noiseless quantum simulation processing in real-time. Equipped with these methods, we investigate the equilibrium and out-of-equilibrium properties of the spin-12\frac{1}{2} Hubbard model on a two-dimensional square lattice, with TN simulations. At zero temperature, we can access system sizes that allow us to identify the transition between liquid and insulating (crystalline spin-lattice) phases. In real-time dynamics, for a ladder in the t−Jt-J model limit, we observe spin and charge time-evolution displaying distinct time-scales, an effect that in 1D Hubbard chains is a precursor of the spin-charge separation phenomenon, see for example the recent experiments [840, 552, 841], whereas in 2D it only governs short time scales before the polaron picture and strongly-correlated effects set in [842, 843, 816].

The chapter is structured as follows: in Section 5.1, we revisit the gauge-based encoding to locally remove the fermionic matter, or gauge defermionization. Such an approach can be seen as a generalization of the dressed-site formalism developed in Section 1.2, as in this case there are no gauge fields. We devote Section 5.2 to the implementation of the encoding on a tree-tensor network (TTN) ansatz and show ground state simulation results of the 2D Hubbard model. Finally, in Section 5.3, we detail our prescription for digital quantum simulation of the 2D Hubbard model, based on gauge defermionization, and numerically emulate the digital quantum simulation to observe spin-charge separation effects in two-dimensional lattice samples.

5.1 Gauge Defermionization of Lattice Fermion Theories

In this section, we revisit and extend a known technique, based on lattice gauge theories, to eliminate fermionic matter from 2D lattice models [550, 551]. The strategy consists of developing an analytical mapping from an input fermion lattice Hamiltonian (here we consider it to be a pure non-gauge fermion theory) to a lattice gauge Hamiltonian, with a ℤ𝟚\mathbb{Z_{2}} gauge symmetry, equipped with appropriate gauge constraints. Then, by applying the dressed-site formalism developed in Section 1.2, the resulting theory can be manipulated so that the fermionic parity at each (dressed) site is protected, thus resulting in a theory where operator algebras at different sites always commute, as in a local spin theory.

Our formulation of the defermionization technique can be applied to any 2D fermion lattice Hamiltonian, regardless of the lattice system (it works on Honeycomb and Kagome lattices as well as irregular lattices), as long as few general constraints are satisfied: (i) the global parity of fermions is protected; (ii) Hamiltonian terms that flip the local fermion parity must be nearest-neighbor; (iii) the full system must be under open boundary conditions (OBC), i.e. every closed path on the lattice must be topologically shrinkable to a point. These conditions are often satisfied in solid state Hamiltonians and cold atoms systems [844]

Therefore, without any loss of generality, a general fermion Hamiltonian on a two-dimensional lattice Λ\Lambda with N=Nx×NyN=N_{x}\times N_{y} sites 𝐧\mathbf{n} reads:

H^0=∑𝐧,k∑α,β[[hα,β​ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k,β+h.c]+[Δα,β​ψ^𝐧,α​ψ^𝐧+𝝁k,β+h.c]]+V​({n^𝐧,α}),\begin{split}\hat{H}_{0}=&\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\quantity[ \qty[h_{\alpha,\beta}\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k],\beta}+\hc]+ \qty[\Delta_{\alpha,\beta} \, \hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec[k],\beta}+\hc]]+V\quantity( \{ \nop_{\vecsite,\alpha} \}),\end{split} (5.1.1)

where the fermion fields satisfy the usual Dirac anti-commutation relations

{ψ^𝐧,α†,ψ^𝐧′,β}\displaystyle\quantity{ \hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha}, \hpsi_{\vecsite^{\prime},\beta}} =i​ℏ​δ𝐧,𝐧′​δα,β\displaystyle=i\hbar\delta_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{\alpha,\beta} {ψ^𝐧,α,ψ^𝐧′,β}\displaystyle\quantity{ \hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha}, \hpsi_{\vecsite^{\prime}, \beta}} =0,\displaystyle=0, (5.1.2)

and can exhibit an internal degree of freedom, here labeled by the flavor indices α,β\alpha,\beta.

The interaction potential VV term, which is a function of the fermion densities n^𝐧,α=ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧,α\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}=\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}, can in principle have any range and shape, and even include chemical potentials. For instance, it can also account local terms that do not conserve the spin, like bα,β​ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧,βb_{\alpha,\beta}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\beta}, or local s-wave superconducting terms as Δ​ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧,β†\Delta\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\beta}.

Conversely, the hopping hα,βh_{\alpha,\beta} and the double creation/annihilation Δα,β\Delta_{\alpha,\beta} processes (the latter often seen in superconductors) are the terms that break local fermion parity: their single-site algebras do not commute between distant sites (i.e. they are not genuinely local), and this is the source of all the numerical difficulty when simulating lattice fermions.

While in one spatial dimension, the Jordan-Wigner transformation [557] provides an easy solution to this problem, tackling the mapping in higher dimensions requires sophisticated, often cumbersome techniques [592, 497]. In this perspective, converting a fermion algebra into a genuinely local (spin-like) algebra using introducing a lattice gauge field is an elegant strategy, which is also practical from a numerical simulation standpoint, as we discuss later on.

5.1.1 Mapping into a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theory

We now perform a set of exact algebraic manipulations to the Hamiltonian of Eq. 5.1.1 until we reach a defermionized form. The very first step is to promote the total fermion parity operator at site 𝐧\mathbf{n} to a gauge transformation (for the matter sites MM) that behaves like a parity operator, or an element of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} group:

G𝐧[M]=exp(i​π​∑αψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧,α)=G𝐧[M]†=(G𝐧[M])−1.G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]}=\rm{exp}\quantity(i \pi{\textstyle{\sum_{\alpha}}}\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha} \hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha})=G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]\dagger}=(G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]})^{-1}. (5.1.3)

Under G𝐧[M]G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]}, operators that preserve total fermion parity, such as densities n^𝐧,α\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}, are left invariant, while operators that flip the total fermion parity, such as ψ^𝐧,α(†)\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}^{(\dagger)}, acquire a sign. Namely:

G𝐧[M]​n^𝐧,α​G𝐧[M]\displaystyle G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]}\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]} =n^𝐧,α\displaystyle=\hat{n}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha} G𝐧[M]​ψ^𝐧,α​G𝐧[M]\displaystyle G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]} =−ψ^𝐧,α\displaystyle=-\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha} (5.1.4)

At this stage, we promote the gauge transformation into a gauge symmetry. This task is performed by adding an auxiliary quantum lattice field, the gauge field, on the bonds (𝐧,𝝁)(\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}) of the lattice. The local Hilbert space for a gauge site should correspond to the regular representation space for the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} group [595], so it should be a two-level system, or a qubit, equipped with the (genuinely local) algebra of Pauli matrices {σ^x,σ^y,σ^z}\quantity{\Sx,\Sy,\Sz}.

Being ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} an Abelian gauge group, the left- G𝐧,𝝁[L]G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[L]} and right- G𝐧,𝝁[R]G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[R]} groups of transformations of the gauge field must commute and square to the identity. Without loss of generality, we can set them both to the same operator: G𝐧,𝝁[L]=G𝐧,𝝁[R]=σ^𝐧,𝝁zG_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[L]}=G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[R]}=\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}. Thanks to this auxiliary field, we equip the gauge-violating terms of the Hamiltonian with a parallel transporter operator. We replace

ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β⟶ψ^𝐧,α†​U^𝐧,𝝁​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β,\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},\beta}\quad\longrightarrow\quad\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},\beta}, (5.1.5)

that transforms covariantly under the gauge field groups:

G𝐧,𝝁[L]​U^𝐧,𝝁​G𝐧,𝝁[L]=G𝐧,𝝁[R]​U^𝐧,𝝁​G𝐧,𝝁[R]=−U^𝐧,𝝁G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[L]}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[L]}{=}G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[R]}\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[R]}{=}-\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}} (5.1.6)

Again, without loss of generality, we set U^𝐧,𝝁=σ^𝐧,𝝁x\hat{U}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}=\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}. Overall, this procedure translates into modifying the fermion parity-flipping terms from Eq. 5.1.1 according to

hα,β​ψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β\displaystyle h_{\alpha,\beta}\,\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},\beta} ⟶hα,β​ψ^𝐧,α†​σ^𝐧,𝝁x​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β\displaystyle\longrightarrow\quad h_{\alpha,\beta}\,\hat{\psi}^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},\beta} (5.1.7)
Δα,β​ψ^𝐧,α​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β\displaystyle\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},\beta} ⟶Δα,β​ψ^𝐧,α​σ^𝐧,𝝁x​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β.\displaystyle\longrightarrow\quad\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}\,\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n},\alpha}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},\beta}\,.

With this modification, the Hamiltonian satisfies a gauge symmetry around every site, precisely G𝐧[total]=G𝐧[M]​∏𝝁G𝐧,𝝁[L/R]G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[\rm{total}]}=G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[M]}\prod_{{\bf\it\mu}}G_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{[L/R]}. Consequently, we have to choose a symmetry sector (for each of these symmetries) to play the role of physical space. As it is common for lattice gauge theories, we consider the quantum states invariant under all the G𝐧[total]G_{\mathbf{n}}^{[\rm{total}]}, i.e. which satisfy

[exp⁡(i​π​∑αψ^𝐧,α†​ψ^𝐧,α)​∏𝝁σ^𝐧,𝝁z]​|Ψphys⟩=|Ψphys⟩,\quantity[\exp\left(i \pi\sum_{\alpha} \hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha} \hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha}\right) \prod_{\latvec} \Sz_{\vecsite,\latvec}]\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}{=}\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}, (5.1.8)

in order to be the physical states |Ψphys⟩\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}. This equation plays the role of effective Gauss’ Law of the resulting gauge theory, and the condition can be satisfied at every site only if the total number of fermions in the system is even. To simulate an odd number of fermions, one or more virtual bonds, going out of the system, must be added to keep track of the appropriate parity gauge flux.

5.1.2 Restoring equivalence with Plaquette Operators

It is then possible to check that, under the Gauss’ Law of Eq. 5.1.8, the gauge-theory modification in Eq. 5.1.7 does not change the actual dynamics given by the original Hamiltonian as in Eq. 5.1.1, but only when the lattice is a non-cyclic graph (such as a 1D chain, or a dendrimer lattice). For each (product state) fermion configuration, the extra degrees of freedom introduced by the gauge fields are completely locked by Gauss’ Law; thus all residual degeneracy is removed, and all the matrix elements of H^0\hat{H}_{0} are unaltered.

Conversely, when lattice cycles are present, the modification changes the dynamics. In fact, for each elementary closed cycle of sites, or plaquette □∈Λ\square\in\Lambda, one Gauss’ Law operator becomes linearly dependent on others, thus contributing to degeneracy with a 2-fold space. Moreover, when a fermion winds around a closed cycle, all of the gauge fields in its path undergo a σ^x\hat{\sigma}^{x} flip, thus the final state may differ from the original one. If we want to restore the dynamics of the original model, we have to add more physical contents to the plaquette, either in terms of an additional pure gauge field Hamiltonian or in terms of extra symmetries.

Fortunately, a simple recipe to do either is inspired by Kitaev’s Toric Code [836]. The idea is to add a plaquette Hamiltonian term with a σ^x\hat{\sigma}^{x} for each gauge link of the plaquette, that is

H^p=−∑□∈Λ∏⟨𝐧,𝐧′⟩∈□σ^x𝐧,𝐧′=−∑□∈Λ(⌜σ^x⌝σ^xσ^x⌞σ^x⌟).\begin{split}\hat{H}_{p}&=-\sum_{\square\in\Lambda}\prod_{\langle\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}\rangle\in\square}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}=-\sum_{\square\in\Lambda}\quantity(\begin{array}{ccc} \ulcorner& \Sx& \urcorner\\ \Sx& & \Sx\\ \llcorner& \Sx& \lrcorner\\ \end{array}).\end{split} (5.1.9)

Notably, each of these plaquette operators commutes with the lattice gauge Hamiltonian and can be equivalently cast as a (gauge) symmetry. Moreover, plaquettes also commute with Gauss’ laws, because a vertex and a plaquette always share either zero or two bonds, regardless of the lattice system, and [σ^1x​σ^2x,σ^1z​σ^2z]=0[\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{1}\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{2},\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{1}\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{2}]=0.

We can then map the original lattice fermion Hamiltonian, Eq. 5.1.1, to a dynamically-equivalent, ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-invariant lattice gauge model, which reads

H^1=∑𝐧,k∑α,β[hα,β​ψ^𝐧,α†​σ^𝐧,𝝁x​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β+Δα,β​ψ^𝐧,α​σ^𝐧,𝝁x​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β​h.c]+V​({n^𝐧,α}),\begin{split}\hat{H}_{1}=\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\quantity[h_{\alpha,\beta}\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha}\Sx_{\vecsite,\latvec} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec,\beta} +\Delta_{\alpha,\beta} \hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha} \Sx_{\vecsite,\latvec} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec,\beta} \hc]+V\quantity(\{ \nop_{\vecsite,\alpha} \}),\end{split} (5.1.10)

with the constraints

[ei​π​∑αn^𝐧,α​∏𝝁vertexσ^𝐧,𝝁z]​|Ψphys⟩\displaystyle\quantity[e^{i \pi\sum_{\alpha} \nop_{\vecsite,\alpha}} \prod_{\latvec}^{\rm{vertex}} \Sz_{\vecsite,\latvec}]\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}} =|Ψphys⟩,\displaystyle=\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}, [∏⟨𝐧,𝐧′⟩plaquetteσ^𝐧,𝐧′x]​|Ψphys⟩\displaystyle\quantity[\prod_{\avg{\vecsite,\vecsite^{\prime}}}^{\rm{plaquette}} \Sx_{\vecsite, \vecsite^{\prime}}]\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}} =|Ψphys⟩.\displaystyle=\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}. (5.1.11)

Indeed, the combined constraints in Eq. 5.1.11 completely resolve the 2-fold degeneracy introduced by the plaquette, and each closed path of moving fermions returns to its original state with the correct amplitude and phase. Therefore, the whole mapping holds for the subspace of the Hilbert space satisfying Eq. 5.1.11. Any excitations from the ground state of Eq. 5.1.9 break the encoding validity. A rigorous proof of the equivalence between Eq. 5.1.1 and Eqs. 5.1.10 and 5.1.11 was provided for a number-conserving theory on the square lattice in [550]; the generalization to other cases is fairly straightforward.

Notice that the degeneracy is not fully removed in periodic boundary conditions (PBC), where each winding dimension introduces an additional closed cycle. This case requires the additional constraint of a full σ^x\hat{\sigma}^{x} string along each winding dimension, but we will not treat this case here, because the theory becomes non-local.

5.1.3 Fermionic Rishons

So far, it seems that we have increased the complexity of the fermion lattice theory. In this last step, we will locally manipulate the gauge fields and achieve defermionization explicitly, ending with an algebra of genuinely local operators only.

Similarly to the rishon decomposition discussed in Sections 1.3.3 and 1.4.3, we split each gauge field, living on the (𝐧,𝝁)(\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}) lattice link, in a pair of spinless fermion modes (rishons) c^𝐧,𝝁(†)\hat{c}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{(\dagger)} and c^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁(†)\hat{c}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},-{\bf\it\mu}}^{(\dagger)}, equipped with another symmetry. These new Dirac fermion operators belong to dressed sites 𝐧\mathbf{n} and 𝐧+𝝁\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu} respectively and satisfy the usual anti-commutation relations between themselves and with the physical matter fermions

{c𝐧,𝝁†,c^𝐧′,𝝁′}\displaystyle\quantity{c^{\dagger}_{\vecsite, \latvec}, \cop_{\vecsite^{\prime}, \latvec^{\prime}}} =δ𝐧​𝐧′​δ𝝁​𝝁′\displaystyle=\delta_{\mathbf{n}\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{{\bf\it\mu}{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}} {c^𝐧,𝝁,c^𝐧′,𝝁′}\displaystyle\quantity{\cop_{\vecsite, \latvec}, \cop_{\vecsite^{\prime}, \latvec^{\prime}}} =0\displaystyle=0 {ψ^𝐧,c^𝐧′,𝝁}\displaystyle\quantity{\hpsi_{\vecsite},\cop_{\vecsite^{\prime},\latvec}} =0.\displaystyle=0\,. (5.1.12)

The combined 4-dimensional space of the two modes is then reduced back to the 2-dimensional space of a qubit by imposing that the total number of rishon fermions on a bond must be an even number. This constraint can again be cast as a link symmetry, requiring that

expi​π​(c^𝐧,𝝁†​c^𝐧,𝝁+c^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁†​c^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁)(|Ψphys⟩)=|Ψphys⟩.\exp[i \pi( \cop_{\vecsite,\latvec}^{\dagger} \cop_{\vecsite,\latvec}{+}\cop_{\vecsite+\latvec,-\latvec}^{\dagger} \cop_{\vecsite+\latvec,-\latvec})]{\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}}{=}\ket{\Psi_{\rm{phys}}}. (5.1.13)

We then convert the gauge fields Pauli algebra into an operator algebra acting on the rishon pair:

σ^𝐧,𝝁z\displaystyle\hat{\sigma}^{z}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}} →1−2​c^𝐧,𝝁†​c^𝐧,𝝁=1−2​c^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁†​c^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁\displaystyle\to 1-2\hat{c}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}=1-2\hat{c}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},-{\bf\it\mu}}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},-{\bf\it\mu}} σ^𝐧,𝝁x\displaystyle\hat{\sigma}^{x}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}} →I^​γ^𝐧,𝝁​γ^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁,\displaystyle\to\hat{I}\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbf{n}+{\bf\it\mu},-{\bf\it\mu}}, (5.1.14)

where now γ^𝐧,𝝁=c^𝐧,𝝁+c𝐧,𝝁†=γ^𝐧,𝝁†\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}{=}\hat{c}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}{+}c^{\dagger}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}{=}\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{\dagger} is a Majorana operator on the rishon fermion, which squares to the identity γ^𝐧,𝝁2=1\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}}^{2}{=}1 but still anti-commutes with other fermions {γ^𝐧,𝝁,γ^𝐧′,𝝁′}=2​δ𝐧,𝐧′​δ𝝁,𝝁′\{\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbf{n},{\bf\it\mu}},\hat{\gamma}_{\mathbf{n}^{\prime},{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}\}{=}2\delta_{\mathbf{n},\mathbf{n}^{\prime}}\delta_{{\bf\it\mu},{\bf\it\mu}^{\prime}}. These operators defined at Eq. 5.1.14 respect the fermion parity symmetry on the bond, and on the even parity sector, they act exactly as Pauli matrices.

We can then plug this exact manipulation into the gauge theory Hamiltonian, resulting in

H^2=∑𝐧,k∑α,β[i​hα,β​ψ^𝐧,α†​γ^𝐧,𝝁​γ^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β+i​Δα,β​ψ^𝐧,α​γ^𝐧,𝝁​γ^𝐧+𝝁,−𝝁​ψ^𝐧+𝝁,β+h.c]+V,\begin{split}\hat{H}_{2}&{=}\sum_{\mathbf{n},k}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\quantity[i h_{\alpha,\beta}\hpsi^{\dagger}_{\vecsite,\alpha} \majo_{\vecsite,\latvec} \majo_{\vecsite+\latvec,-\latvec} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec,\beta} {+} i\Delta_{\alpha,\beta}\hpsi_{\vecsite,\alpha} \majo_{\vecsite,\latvec} \majo_{\vecsite+\latvec,-\latvec} \hpsi_{\vecsite+\latvec,\beta} +\hc]+V\,,\end{split} (5.1.15)

where we have to add the new link parity symmetry to the constraints, thus
